options.label: Plebeians elected by lot
options.rationale: Plebeians were shut out at first.

questions.explanation: Patricians held the magistracies, and the Senate was made up of former magistrates.

levels.title: The Twelve Tables
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why Rome wrote down its laws and what that changed.
levels.summary: Around 450 BCE Rome wrote its laws on the Twelve Tables in the Forum, so patrician judges could no longer bend unwritten custom.

cards.headline: A law you can’t read is a law someone else controls.
Law in public
cards.body: Around 450 BCE, Rome wrote down its laws on the Twelve Tables and displayed them in the Forum. Plebeians had demanded it: until then, patrician judges could interpret unwritten custom as they pleased. Now anyone could check the rules, at least in principle.

cards.headline: Everyday rules
cards.body: The Twelve Tables covered ordinary life: debt, property, family and damage to others. They became the foundation of Roman law. According to Cicero, boys still memorized them at school centuries later.

cards.fact: The original tablets are lost.
cards.context: They were probably destroyed when the Gauls sacked Rome. The laws survive only in quotations by later writers.

cards.headline: Written law: established
learned: The Twelve Tables were written around 450 BCE
They were displayed publicly in the Forum
They limited patrician judges
They covered debt, property and family

questions.prompt: What were the Twelve Tables?

options.label: A list of Rome’s seven kings

questions.explanation: The Twelve Tables were Rome’s first written law code, displayed in the Forum around 450 BCE.

questions.prompt: Why did plebeians want the laws written down?

options.label: So they could vote on each law again
So patrician judges couldn’t bend unwritten custom
So the laws could be sent to other cities
options.rationale: The point was fairness at home.

options.label: So priests could read them aloud

questions.explanation: Written, public laws meant patricians could no longer interpret custom however they liked.

questions.prompt: From Level 14: the Twelve Tables were a win in which struggle?

options.label: The war against the Etruscans
options.rationale: The Tables were an internal reform.

questions.explanation: Written laws were one of the plebeians’ gains in the Conflict of the Orders.

levels.title: Tribunes of the Plebs
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the tribunes’ power to protect plebeians, including the veto.
levels.summary: Tribunes, elected by plebeians, could veto any magistrate and were sacrosanct. Ten of them protected ordinary citizens.

cards.headline: The most powerful word in Roman politics meant “I forbid.”
Protectors of the plebs
cards.body: The tribunes of the plebs were officials elected by plebeians to protect them from abuses by magistrates. Their number eventually rose to ten. A tribune’s door was expected to stay open day and night, so any plebeian could ask for help.

cards.headline: I forbid
cards.body: A tribune could block the act of any magistrate simply by declaring “Veto,” Latin for “I forbid.” Tribunes were also sacrosanct: harming one was a religious crime. That protection let them stand up to consuls. Because plebeians elected them, tribunes answered to ordinary citizens rather than to the old families.

cards.headline: Tribunes: understood
learned: Tribunes were elected by plebeians
Eventually there were ten
They could veto any magistrate
They were sacrosanct

questions.prompt: What does veto mean in Latin?
questions.explanation: Veto means “I forbid”: a tribune could use it to block any magistrate.

questions.prompt: Why couldn’t an angry consul simply arrest a troublesome tribune?

options.label: Tribunes were sacrosanct; harming one was a religious crime
Tribunes had their own private army
Tribunes lived outside the city
options.rationale: Their doors were open in Rome.

questions.explanation: Sacrosanctity made harming a tribune a religious crime, protecting them from powerful magistrates.

questions.prompt: From Level 12: one consul could block the other. Whose actions could a tribune block?
questions.explanation: A tribune’s veto could stop the act of any magistrate, even a consul.

levels.title: Cincinnatus and the Citizen Ideal
levels.objective: After this level you can retell the story of Cincinnatus and explain the Roman idea of civic duty.
levels.summary: Called from his plow in 458 BCE to save Rome, Cincinnatus won and gave up power after 16 days: the model Roman citizen.

cards.headline: Rome’s favorite hero was a farmer who gave power back.
Called from the plow
cards.body: In 458 BCE, according to tradition, a Roman army was trapped by enemies. The Senate made Cincinnatus dictator to rescue it. The messengers found him plowing his small farm.

cards.headline: Power returned
cards.body: Cincinnatus won the war and then resigned after about 16 days, long before his time ran out, and went back to his farm. Romans told the story to celebrate the mos maiorum, “the custom of the ancestors”: duty, discipline and service to the state.

cards.fact: An American city carries his name.
cards.context: Cincinnati is named after the Society of the Cincinnati, which took its name from the farmer who gave power back.

cards.headline: Civic virtue: understood
learned: Cincinnatus was called from his plow in 458 BCE
He saved a trapped Roman army
He resigned after about 16 days
Romans prized duty: the mos maiorum

questions.prompt: What was Cincinnatus doing when Rome called on him?
questions.explanation: Messengers found Cincinnatus plowing his small farm.

questions.prompt: Why did Romans admire Cincinnatus so much?

options.label: He gave up supreme power once the crisis passed
He became king after the war

questions.explanation: He used supreme power only as long as needed, then returned to his farm: the ideal of civic duty.

questions.prompt: From Level 12: Cincinnatus held which emergency office, limited to six months?
questions.explanation: The dictatorship gave supreme power for at most six months; Cincinnatus gave it up after about 16 days.

levels.title: The Gauls Sack Rome
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the Gallic sack of Rome and how it changed Roman defense.
levels.summary: Around 390 BCE Gauls under Brennus won at the Allia and sacked Rome. “Woe to the conquered.” Rome answered with a great stone wall.

cards.headline: Around 390 BCE, Rome learned it could be captured.
Disaster at the Allia
cards.body: In about 390 BCE, an army of Gauls led by a chief named Brennus crushed the Romans at the Allia River. The Gauls then marched into Rome and sacked it. Some sources date the sack to 387 BCE.

cards.headline: Woe to the conquered
cards.body: According to Livy, when the Romans protested the ransom the Gauls demanded, Brennus threw his sword onto the scales and said “Vae victis”: woe to the conquered. Legend adds that Juno’s sacred geese warned the defenders of the Capitoline of a night attack.

cards.fact: Rome built a wall.
cards.context: After the sack, Rome surrounded itself with a strong stone wall, later called the Servian Wall.

cards.headline: The sack: survived
learned: Gauls under Brennus sacked Rome around 390 BCE
Rome lost at the Allia River
“Vae victis”: woe to the conquered
Rome then built the Servian Wall

questions.prompt: Who sacked Rome around 390 BCE?
questions.explanation: A Gallic army led by Brennus won at the Allia River and sacked Rome.

questions.prompt: How did Rome respond to the Gallic sack?

options.label: It moved the capital to Veii
It paid the Gauls to guard the city
It built a strong stone wall around the city

questions.explanation: After the sack, Rome built the stone wall later called the Servian Wall.

questions.prompt: From Level 15: what probably happened to the original Twelve Tables when the Gauls sacked Rome?

options.label: They were carried off to Gaul and kept
They were hidden in the Vestals’ temple

questions.explanation: The original tablets were probably lost in the sack; the laws survive only in later quotations.

levels.title: Conquering Italy
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Rome came to control the Italian peninsula, and the role of roads and alliances.
levels.summary: Rome beat the Samnites, built the Via Appia from 312 BCE and made defeated peoples allies. By about 264 BCE it controlled Italy.

cards.headline: Rome won Italy with armies, roads and allies.
Wars in the hills
cards.body: In the Samnite Wars, from 343 to 290 BCE, Rome fought the tough hill peoples of central and southern Italy. Victory there, and over other rivals, left Rome in control of nearly all the peninsula south of the Po Valley by about 264 BCE.

cards.headline: Roads and allies
cards.body: In 312 BCE Rome began the Via Appia, its first great road, to move armies south quickly. Defeated peoples became allies who supplied soldiers instead of paying tribute, and some were granted citizenship. Each war made Rome’s army bigger.

cards.fact: A victory that cost too much.
cards.context: King Pyrrhus of Epirus beat Roman armies, but his losses were so heavy that a “Pyrrhic victory” now means a win that costs too much.

cards.headline: Italy: united
learned: Rome fought the Samnite Wars, 343–290 BCE
The Via Appia was begun in 312 BCE
Defeated peoples became allies
By about 264 BCE Rome controlled Italy

questions.prompt: What was the Via Appia?
questions.explanation: Begun in 312 BCE, the Via Appia was Rome’s first great road, built to move armies south.

questions.prompt: How did Rome keep conquered Italian peoples loyal?

options.label: It made them allies who supplied soldiers
It forced them all to move to Rome
It let each city choose a king

questions.explanation: Defeated peoples became allies who sent soldiers rather than tribute, and some gained citizenship.

questions.prompt: From Level 12: which Roman officials led the armies in these wars?
questions.explanation: Consuls commanded Rome’s armies, including in the wars that won Italy.

levels.title: Checkpoint: How the Republic Worked
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how consuls, Senate, assemblies and tribunes balanced one another.
levels.summary: Consuls led, the Senate advised, the assemblies elected and legislated, and tribunes could veto: a mixed constitution Polybius admired.

cards.headline: Chapter 2 finale. How do you stop anyone from becoming a king?
cards.body: You spread power around, and let each part hold the others back.

cards.headline: Checks and balances
cards.body: The Greek historian Polybius admired Rome’s government as a mix of three kinds of rule. The consuls were like kings, the Senate like an aristocracy, and the assemblies like a democracy. Each part checked the others, so none could take over. Polybius, a Greek taken to Rome as a hostage, wrote to explain how Rome had come to dominate the Mediterranean.

cards.headline: Chapter 2 complete
learned: Consuls led and commanded armies
The Senate advised, and was heeded
Assemblies elected and legislated; tribunes could veto
Each part checked the others

questions.prompt: In Rome’s assemblies, what did citizens do?
questions.explanation: Citizens met in assemblies to elect magistrates and pass laws.

questions.prompt: Which officials could block any magistrate with a single word?
questions.explanation: Tribunes could stop any magistrate by declaring “Veto.”

questions.prompt: Why did Polybius think Rome’s government was stable?

options.label: Rome had the largest army in the world
options.rationale: His point was about the constitution.

options.label: One wise ruler made every decision
Each part of the government checked the others

questions.explanation: Consuls, Senate and assemblies each had power, and each held the others in check.

questions.prompt: Which change ended the Conflict of the Orders?

options.label: Plebeians were allowed to join the army
Plebeian assembly votes became binding on all Romans
Patricians were banned from the Senate

questions.explanation: The Hortensian law of 287 BCE made the plebeian assembly’s votes binding on everyone.

questions.prompt: Chapter 2 recap: what links one-year consuls, the six-month dictatorship and Cincinnatus?

options.label: Power should be held only for a limited time
Power should pass from father to son
Power should belong to the priests
Power should go to the richest family

questions.explanation: Short terms and Cincinnatus’s early resignation all express the Republic’s rule: power is temporary.

levels.title: Carthage, Queen of the Sea
levels.objective: After this level you can describe Carthage and why it clashed with Rome.
levels.summary: Carthage, founded by Phoenicians in 814 BCE, ruled the western seas. In 264 BCE it and Rome went to war over Sicily: the Punic Wars.

cards.headline: Once Rome held Italy, it looked across the water and found a rival.
A city of traders
cards.body: Carthage was founded by Phoenician settlers from Tyre, traditionally in 814 BCE, on the coast of what is now Tunisia. It grew rich from trade and became the leading naval power of the western Mediterranean.

cards.headline: Sicily in between
cards.body: Sicily lies between Italy and North Africa. In 264 BCE a local conflict there drew in both powers, and Rome and Carthage went to war. The wars that followed are called Punic, from the Latin Punicus, “Phoenician.”

cards.fact: Carthage was older than Rome.
cards.context: Its traditional founding date of 814 BCE comes even before Rome’s own, 753 BCE. By the time the two met, Carthage had ruled the sea for centuries.

cards.headline: Carthage: introduced
learned: Carthage was founded by Phoenicians, traditionally 814 BCE
It was the western Mediterranean’s naval power
Rome and Carthage went to war over Sicily in 264 BCE
Punic means Phoenician

questions.prompt: Who founded Carthage?
questions.explanation: Phoenicians from Tyre founded Carthage, traditionally in 814 BCE.

questions.prompt: Why are Rome’s wars with Carthage called the Punic Wars?

options.rationale: The name has a different source.

levels.title: The First Punic War
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Rome built a navy and won the First Punic War.
levels.summary: In 264–241 BCE a land power learned to fight at sea. With a new fleet and the corvus, Rome beat Carthage and took Sicily.

cards.headline: To beat a sea power, Rome had to become one, almost from scratch.
A navy from nothing
cards.body: The First Punic War lasted from 264 to 241 BCE. Rome had little experience at sea, but it built a large war fleet to take on Carthage, the leading naval power of the western Mediterranean.

cards.headline: Turning sea battles into land battles
cards.body: Roman ships carried the corvus, a boarding bridge with a spike at its end. Dropped onto an enemy deck, it let Roman soldiers storm across. Sea battles became the kind of fight Rome was good at.

cards.fact: Sicily became Rome’s first province.
cards.context: Victory gave Rome its first territory outside Italy. It would not be the last.

cards.headline: First Punic War: won
learned: The First Punic War ran from 264 to 241 BCE
Rome built a war fleet
The corvus turned sea fights into boarding fights
Sicily became Rome’s first province

options.label: A boarding bridge with a spike
A signal fire on the coast

questions.explanation: The corvus was a spiked boarding bridge that let Roman soldiers storm enemy ships.

questions.prompt: Why did the corvus suit the Romans so well?

options.label: Their ships were faster than Carthage’s
It let their soldiers fight on enemy decks
It could sink ships from far away
It hid their ships from view

questions.explanation: Rome’s strength was its infantry; the corvus turned sea battles into fights between soldiers.

levels.title: Hannibal Crosses the Alps
levels.objective: After this level you can retell Hannibal’s march over the Alps with his army and elephants.
levels.summary: In 218 BCE Hannibal led an army with war elephants from Spain over the Alps into Italy, beginning the Second Punic War.

cards.headline: The attack Rome never expected came over the mountains, with elephants.
A general sworn against Rome
cards.body: According to tradition, Hannibal’s father made him swear as a boy never to be a friend of Rome. As a Carthaginian general based in Spain, Hannibal invaded Italy and began the Second Punic War, which lasted from 218 to 201 BCE.

cards.headline: Over the Alps
cards.body: In 218 BCE Hannibal marched his army, including war elephants, from Spain over the Alps. The crossing cost him many men and most of the elephants. But he reached Italy and began winning battles almost at once. He would stay and fight in Italy for about 15 years.

cards.headline: The Alps: crossed
learned: The Second Punic War ran from 218 to 201 BCE
Hannibal invaded Italy from Spain
He crossed the Alps with war elephants
The march was costly, but he won early battles

options.label: By sea from Carthage to Ostia
Through Greece and across the Adriatic

questions.explanation: Hannibal marched from Spain over the Alps into Italy in 218 BCE.

options.label: His whole army
options.rationale: He reached Italy and won battles.

options.label: Many men and most of his elephants
His command, which went to his brother

questions.explanation: The crossing was brutal, but Hannibal reached Italy with enough of his army to win.

options.label: Carthage had no ships at all

questions.explanation: After building a fleet in the First Punic War, Rome could contest the sea, so a land invasion avoided it.

levels.title: Disaster at Cannae
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what happened at Cannae and why it is still studied.
levels.summary: At Cannae in 216 BCE Hannibal encircled a much larger Roman army and destroyed it. Rome lost tens of thousands, yet refused to make peace.

cards.headline: Rome’s biggest army walked into a trap it couldn’t escape.
The trap
cards.body: At Cannae in 216 BCE, Hannibal faced a much larger Roman army. He let the center of his line fall back as the Romans pushed forward. Then his wings and cavalry closed around them from both sides. It was a double envelopment.
cards.callout: Center falls back, wings close in

cards.headline: A catastrophe, and a refusal
cards.body: Ancient sources report Roman losses in the tens of thousands, one of the worst defeats in Roman history. Yet Rome refused to make peace. Hannibal had won a battle. He had not won the war, because Rome would not quit. Cannae is still studied as the classic example of encirclement.

cards.headline: Cannae: studied

Rome still refused to make peace

levels.title: Fabius the Delayer
levels.objective: After this level you can explain Fabius Maximus’s strategy of avoiding battle and why it worked.
levels.summary: Fabius shadowed Hannibal and cut his supplies instead of fighting. Mocked as the Delayer, he was proved right as Italy’s allies held firm.

cards.headline: Sometimes the best way to beat a genius is to refuse to fight him.
Don’t fight, follow
cards.body: Fabius Maximus refused to meet Hannibal in a pitched battle. Instead he shadowed Hannibal’s army and cut off its supplies. Romans first mocked him as Cunctator, “the Delayer.” After Cannae, the name became praise.

cards.headline: Why it worked
cards.body: Hannibal was far from home and needed Italian cities to join him. But most of Rome’s allies stayed loyal, so he never got the reinforcements he needed. Time, and Hannibal’s distance from home, were on Rome’s side.

cards.fact: His name became a strategy.
cards.context: A “Fabian strategy” still means wearing down a stronger enemy by avoiding a decisive battle, exactly as Fabius did.

cards.headline: Delay: vindicated

He cut off Hannibal’s supplies instead
“The Delayer” became a compliment
Italy’s loyal allies starved Hannibal of men

options.label: The Conqueror
options.rationale: His fame came from not fighting.

questions.explanation: Cunctator, “the Delayer,” began as an insult and became praise.

options.rationale: The issue was supplies and allies.

questions.explanation: Without battles to win over Italian cities, Hannibal’s army slowly ran short of supplies and men.

levels.title: Scipio and Zama
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Scipio Africanus defeated Hannibal at Zama.
levels.summary: Scipio took Spain, invaded Africa and beat Hannibal at Zama in 202 BCE. Carthage lost its empire and fleet and paid a huge indemnity.

cards.headline: Rome finally beat Hannibal by making him come home.
Take the war to Africa
cards.body: Publius Cornelius Scipio drove the Carthaginians out of Spain. Then, in a bold gamble, he invaded Africa and threatened Carthage itself. Carthage recalled Hannibal from Italy to defend the city.

cards.headline: Zama, 202 BCE
cards.body: At the Battle of Zama in 202 BCE, Scipio defeated Hannibal and won the Second Punic War. Carthage lost its overseas territories and most of its fleet, and had to pay Rome a huge indemnity.
cards.callout: Zama, 202 BCE: the war is won

cards.fact: He was named for his victory.
cards.context: Scipio was given the name Africanus, after the continent where he won the war.

levels.title: Rome Turns East
levels.objective: After this level you can describe how Rome came to dominate Greece and the Hellenistic kingdoms.
levels.summary: Rome beat Macedon and came to control Greece, destroying Corinth in 146 BCE. Meanwhile Greek culture conquered Rome from within.

cards.headline: Rome conquered Greece. Then Greece conquered Rome right back.
Wars with Macedon
cards.body: In a series of wars against the kingdom of Macedon, ending in 148 BCE, Rome came to control Greece. In 196 BCE the Roman general Flamininus had proclaimed the Greek cities free. Yet Roman influence over them only kept growing.

cards.headline: Captive Greece
cards.body: Greek art, literature and philosophy deeply shaped Roman culture. Wealthy Romans learned Greek, hired Greek tutors and copied Greek statues. The poet Horace later wrote that captive Greece took its fierce conqueror captive.

cards.fact: Corinth was destroyed in 146 BCE.
cards.context: In the same year that Carthage fell, Rome also destroyed the great and wealthy Greek city of Corinth.

cards.headline: The east: won

levels.title: Carthage Must Be Destroyed
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how and why Rome destroyed Carthage in 146 BCE.
levels.summary: Cato demanded that Carthage be destroyed. In the Third Punic War (149–146 BCE) Rome did it, and Carthage became the province of Africa.

cards.headline: One senator ended every speech the same way: Carthage must be destroyed.
A rival that recovered
cards.body: After Zama, Carthage recovered its wealth through trade. In the Senate, Cato the Elder was said to end his speeches, whatever the topic, with the demand that Carthage must be destroyed.

cards.headline: The end of Carthage
cards.body: In the Third Punic War, from 149 to 146 BCE, Rome besieged, captured and destroyed Carthage. Its lands became the Roman province of Africa. The same year, Rome destroyed Corinth in Greece.

cards.fact: The salted earth is a myth.
cards.context: The famous story that Rome sowed salt on Carthage’s fields was invented much later. Carthage was eventually refounded as a Roman colony and became one of the empire’s great cities.

levels.title: The Legion
levels.objective: After this level you can describe how a Roman legion was organized, equipped and trained.
levels.summary: Republican legions had 4,000 to 5,000 citizen infantry in flexible maniples, three lines deep, armed with the gladius and pila.

cards.headline: Citizens under arms
cards.body: In the Republic, a legion had roughly 4,000 to 5,000 infantry. In the earlier Republic, legionaries were property-owning citizens who bought their own equipment. Each carried a short stabbing sword, the gladius, and heavy throwing javelins called pila.

cards.headline: Flexible blocks
cards.body: Legions fought in maniples, small units that could move and turn independently. They were arranged in three lines: the young hastati in front, the principes behind them, and the veteran triarii at the back.

cards.fact: The pilum was built to bend.
cards.context: Its long iron shank was designed to bend on impact, so an enemy couldn’t simply throw it back at the Romans.

Early legionaries were property-owning citizens
They carried the gladius and pila

options.label: He surrounded them from both sides

questions.explanation: A double envelopment trapped the Romans so their numbers couldn’t help them.

levels.title: Checkpoint: Master of the Mediterranean
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how the Punic Wars turned Rome into a Mediterranean power.
levels.summary: From 264 to 146 BCE Rome beat Carthage three times and conquered Greece. It now ruled the Mediterranean through provinces.

levels.title: The Gracchi Brothers
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the land reforms of the Gracchi and why they ended in violence.
levels.summary: As estates swallowed small farms, the tribunes Tiberius and Gaius Gracchus pushed land and grain reforms. Both were killed.

cards.headline: Two brothers tried to give land to the poor. Both were killed for it.
Rich estates, poor farmers
cards.body: Rome’s conquests brought wealth, but not to everyone. By the 2nd century BCE, rich Romans had built huge estates worked by enslaved people, while many small farmers lost their land. In 133 BCE the tribune Tiberius Gracchus proposed giving public land to poor citizens.

cards.headline: Blood in the Forum
cards.body: Many senators saw a threat to their power and property. Tiberius was killed by a mob of senators and their supporters, the worst political bloodshed in Rome in centuries. His brother Gaius pushed wider reforms, including cheap grain for citizens, and was killed in 121 BCE.

cards.fact: A dangerous precedent.
cards.context: The deaths of the Gracchi showed that political disputes in Rome could now be settled with violence rather than votes.

cards.headline: The Gracchi: remembered
learned: Estates grew as small farmers lost land
Tiberius Gracchus proposed land reform in 133 BCE

questions.explanation: Killing sitting reformers showed that votes and vetoes could be overruled by force.

questions.explanation: Both brothers were tribunes of the plebs, the office created to protect ordinary citizens.

levels.title: Marius Remakes the Army
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Marius’s reforms tied soldiers to their generals.
levels.summary: Seven-time consul Marius opened the legions to landless volunteers paid by the state. Soldiers began to look to generals, not the Senate.

cards.headline: The man who saved Rome from invaders also changed whom its soldiers served.
An army of the poor
cards.body: Gaius Marius was elected consul an unprecedented seven times. Facing a shortage of recruits, he enrolled poor citizens with no property, equipped and paid by the state. He led them to victory over the invading Cimbri and Teutones in 102 and 101 BCE.

cards.headline: Loyal to the general
cards.body: The new soldiers had no farms to return to. They looked to their general, not the Senate, for pay and for land when they retired. An army that depended on its commander could be turned against Rome itself.

cards.fact: Every legion got an eagle.
cards.context: Marius made the silver eagle, the aquila, the standard of every legion. Losing it in battle was a disgrace.

cards.headline: The army: remade

He enrolled landless volunteers
Soldiers began serving their general
Every legion carried an eagle

levels.title: Sulla Marches on Rome
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why Sulla’s march on Rome broke a taboo.
levels.summary: In 88 BCE Sulla led his army against Rome itself, fought Marius’s side in a civil war, then ruled as dictator with no time limit.

cards.headline: In 88 BCE a Roman general did the unthinkable: he attacked Rome.
The march
cards.body: In 88 BCE Sulla marched his army on Rome itself, something no Roman general had done before. His soldiers followed him, not the Senate. He and Marius, with their supporters, then fought a civil war for control of the city.

cards.headline: Lists of the doomed
cards.body: Victorious, Sulla took the dictatorship with no time limit. He published proscription lists: anyone named could be killed and their property seized. He reformed the constitution to strengthen the Senate, and then, surprisingly, retired.
cards.callout: Proscription: a list of people who could be killed

cards.headline: Why it mattered
cards.body: Sulla showed that an army loyal to its general could be turned against Rome itself. His soldiers followed him rather than the Senate. Later generals, Julius Caesar among them, would remember the example.

cards.headline: Sulla: understood
learned: Sulla marched on Rome in 88 BCE
Civil war followed between Sulla and Marius
Proscriptions let enemies be killed
He ruled as dictator with no time limit

questions.explanation: A traditional dictator served at most six months; Sulla took the office with no time limit.

levels.title: Spartacus
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the slave revolt led by Spartacus and how it ended.
levels.summary: In 73 BCE the gladiator Spartacus led a slave revolt that grew to tens of thousands. Crassus crushed it in 71 BCE.

cards.headline: A gladiator escaped his school and raised an army that shook Rome.
The breakout
cards.body: In 73 BCE Spartacus, a gladiator from Thrace, escaped from a gladiator school at Capua with a band of fellow fighters. Enslaved people from Italy’s great estates joined him. His army grew to tens of thousands and defeated several Roman forces.

cards.headline: A brutal end
cards.body: In 71 BCE the wealthy general Marcus Crassus crushed the revolt. Some 6,000 captured rebels were crucified along the Appian Way as a warning. Spartacus himself became a lasting symbol of resistance to oppression.

cards.headline: Why Rome was afraid
cards.body: The great estates that the Gracchi had tried to break up were worked by enslaved people. That is why a slave army frightened wealthy Romans so much: their fortunes depended on the very people now in revolt.

cards.headline: The revolt: ended
learned: Spartacus was a Thracian gladiator
His revolt began at Capua in 73 BCE
Crassus crushed it in 71 BCE
Some 6,000 rebels were crucified

levels.title: Pompey the Great
levels.objective: After this level you can describe Pompey’s rise and his conquests in the East.
levels.summary: Pompey rose under Sulla, won huge commands, swept the pirates from the sea in 67 BCE and remade the East. He called himself Magnus.

cards.headline: He called himself “the Great” before most Romans agreed he was.
A general of special commands
cards.body: Pompey first rose to fame as a young commander fighting for Sulla. Later the Roman people voted him extraordinary commands that gave him power over huge areas for years at a time. In 67 BCE he cleared the Mediterranean of pirates in about three months.

cards.headline: Remaking the East
cards.body: Pompey then defeated King Mithridates and reorganized the eastern Mediterranean. He made Syria a Roman province and captured Jerusalem in 63 BCE. He took the name Magnus, “the Great,” in imitation of Alexander the Great.

cards.fact: Pompey swept the pirates from the Mediterranean in about three months.
cards.context: The campaign of 67 BCE was one of the extraordinary commands the Roman people voted him, and its speed made him a hero.

levels.title: Cicero Against Catiline
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the Catiline conspiracy and Cicero’s role as consul.
levels.summary: Cicero, a “new man” and Rome’s great orator, became consul in 63 BCE and exposed Catiline’s plot, but executed conspirators without trial.

cards.headline: Rome’s greatest speaker won his biggest fight with words, then paid for it.
A new man
cards.body: Cicero was a “new man,” the first in his family to reach the Senate. His speeches made him Rome’s greatest orator. Hundreds of his letters survive, which makes him the best-documented person of the late Republic.

cards.headline: The conspiracy
cards.body: Cicero was elected consul for 63 BCE. That year he exposed a conspiracy by Catiline to seize power and denounced him in a series of famous speeches. He then had several conspirators executed without trial. That decision later led to his exile.

cards.fact: Hundreds of Cicero’s letters survive.
cards.context: They make him the best-documented person of the late Republic. We can follow his hopes, worries and quarrels in his own words.

cards.headline: Cicero: heard
learned: Cicero was a “new man” and a great orator
He was consul in 63 BCE

questions.explanation: Cicero was one of the two consuls for 63 BCE.

levels.title: The First Triumvirate
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the informal alliance of Caesar, Pompey and Crassus.
levels.summary: In 60 BCE Caesar, Pompey and Crassus pooled their power. Julia’s death in 54 BCE and Crassus’s at Carrhae in 53 BCE broke it apart.

cards.headline: Three ambitious men agreed to share Rome. It couldn’t last.
A private deal
cards.body: In 60 BCE Julius Caesar, Pompey and Crassus formed an informal alliance, later called the First Triumvirate. Each gained something the Senate had refused him: Caesar a consulship, Pompey land for his veterans, and Crassus favors for his allies. Pompey married Caesar’s daughter Julia to seal it.

cards.headline: Falling apart
cards.body: Julia died in 54 BCE, weakening the bond between her husband and her father. Then Crassus, the richest man in Rome and the victor over Spartacus, was killed in 53 BCE after a disastrous defeat by the Parthians at Carrhae. Only two rivals were left.

cards.fact: Pompey married Caesar’s daughter Julia to seal the alliance.
cards.context: Her death in 54 BCE removed the family tie between the two most powerful men in Rome.

levels.title: Caesar in Gaul
levels.objective: After this level you can describe Caesar’s conquest of Gaul and why it made him so powerful.
levels.summary: From 58 to 50 BCE Caesar conquered Gaul, beat Vercingetorix at Alesia, raided Britain, and gained wealth and a loyal veteran army.

cards.headline: Caesar spent eight years conquering Gaul, and wrote the history of it himself.
The conquest
cards.body: Between 58 and 50 BCE, Julius Caesar conquered Gaul, roughly modern France and Belgium. At Alesia in 52 BCE he defeated the Gallic leader Vercingetorix. He also led two expeditions to Britain, in 55 and 54 BCE.

cards.headline: Wealth, an army and a story
cards.body: The conquest gave Caesar enormous wealth and a veteran army loyal to him. He also wrote his own account, the Commentaries on the Gallic War, describing himself in the third person. Readers in Rome learned the war from Caesar’s point of view.

cards.fact: Caesar wrote about himself in the third person.
cards.context: His Commentaries on the Gallic War read as if an observer were describing Caesar’s deeds, which made his own story look like plain history.

levels.title: Crossing the Rubicon
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why crossing the Rubicon meant civil war.
levels.summary: In 49 BCE Caesar led his army across the Rubicon into Italy: civil war. He beat Pompey at Pharsalus in 48 BCE.

cards.headline: A small river. One step across. No way back.
The boundary
cards.body: The Rubicon was a small river marking the boundary between Caesar’s province and Italy. A general had to leave his army behind before crossing it. In January 49 BCE Caesar crossed with his army anyway. He is said to have declared “alea iacta est”: the die is cast.

cards.headline: Caesar against Pompey
cards.body: The crossing started a civil war. Caesar defeated Pompey at Pharsalus in Greece in 48 BCE. Pompey fled to Egypt, where he was murdered. Today, “crossing the Rubicon” means passing a point of no return.

cards.fact: “Alea iacta est”: the die is cast.
cards.context: Caesar is said to have spoken these words as he crossed the Rubicon in 49 BCE. Once a die is thrown, the throw can’t be taken back.

cards.headline: Chapter 4 finale. Beware the Ides of March.
cards.body: How a century of crisis ended with a murder in the Senate.

cards.headline: Dictator for life
cards.body: After his victory in the civil war, Caesar was made dictator in 44 BCE, and then dictator for life. To many senators this looked like the kingship Rome had sworn never to allow again.

cards.headline: The Ides of March
cards.body: On the Ides of March, 15 March 44 BCE, Caesar was stabbed to death at a meeting of the Senate. The conspirators were led by Brutus and Cassius. Brutus claimed descent from the Brutus who had expelled Rome’s last king. They hoped to restore the Republic, but Caesar’s murder only led to more civil war.

levels.title: Octavian, Caesar's Heir
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Caesar's young heir built power after the assassination.
levels.summary: Caesar’s will made his 18-year-old great-nephew Octavian his heir. Octavian joined Antony and Lepidus, and they crushed the assassins at Philippi.

cards.headline: Caesar’s will named an heir almost no one expected: an 18-year-old.
The heir
cards.body: Caesar’s will adopted his 18-year-old great-nephew Octavian as his son and heir. Octavian took the name Gaius Julius Caesar and used it to win over Caesar’s soldiers and supporters. The name was his greatest asset.

cards.headline: Three men again
cards.body: In 43 BCE Octavian, Mark Antony and Lepidus formed the Second Triumvirate, an alliance given legal power for five years. At Philippi in 42 BCE, Antony and Octavian defeated Brutus and Cassius, who both took their own lives.
cards.callout: Unlike the First, the Second Triumvirate was legal

cards.fact: Cicero was killed in the proscriptions of 43 BCE.
cards.context: The triumvirs revived Sulla’s lists of enemies. Cicero had attacked Antony in fierce speeches, and his name was on the list.

cards.headline: The heir: rising
learned: Caesar adopted Octavian in his will
The Second Triumvirate formed in 43 BCE
Cicero died in the proscriptions
The assassins lost at Philippi

questions.prompt: How was Octavian related to Julius Caesar?

options.label: Caesar’s great-nephew, adopted in his will
His younger brother, a fellow general
options.rationale: He was a generation or two younger.

options.label: His son by Cleopatra, born in Egypt
His rival general in Gaul
options.rationale: Octavian was a teenager when Caesar died.

questions.explanation: Caesar’s will adopted his great-nephew Octavian as his son and heir.

questions.prompt: Why did Caesar’s name matter so much to Octavian?

options.label: It made him consul automatically at 18
It won over Caesar’s soldiers and supporters
It let him skip the Senate’s approval
It made the assassins surrender
options.rationale: He had to defeat them in battle.

questions.explanation: Caesar’s veterans and supporters rallied to the man who carried his name.

questions.prompt: From Level 40: whom did Antony and Octavian defeat at Philippi in 42 BCE?

options.label: Catiline and his fellow plotters
options.rationale: Cicero dealt with them in 63 BCE.

questions.explanation: Brutus and Cassius, who led the plot against Caesar, were defeated at Philippi.

levels.title: Antony and Cleopatra
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the alliance of Mark Antony and Cleopatra and why it alarmed Rome.
levels.summary: Antony ruled the East and allied with Cleopatra, last of the Ptolemies. When he gave her Roman lands, Octavian called him a traitor.

cards.headline: A Roman general and an Egyptian queen formed a partnership Rome called treason.
The queen of Egypt
cards.body: Cleopatra VII was the last active ruler of Egypt’s Ptolemaic dynasty, a Greek-speaking family descended from a general of Alexander the Great. She had earlier been Julius Caesar’s ally and lover, and had a son, Caesarion, whom she said was Caesar’s.

cards.headline: Antony in the East
cards.body: After Philippi, Mark Antony took charge of Rome’s eastern provinces and allied with Cleopatra. He married Octavian’s sister Octavia in 40 BCE, but later left her for Cleopatra. In 34 BCE, in the Donations of Alexandria, he gave Roman lands in the East to Cleopatra and her children.

cards.fact: Octavian turned the romance into a weapon.
cards.context: He portrayed Antony as a traitor under the spell of a foreign queen, and opinion in Rome turned against Antony.

cards.headline: The alliance: met
learned: Cleopatra was the last Ptolemaic ruler
Antony ruled the East and allied with her
He gave Roman lands to her children
Octavian called him a traitor

questions.prompt: Which ruling family did Cleopatra belong to?
questions.explanation: Cleopatra VII was the last active ruler of the Ptolemaic dynasty of Egypt.

questions.prompt: Why did the Donations of Alexandria anger Romans?

options.label: Antony gave Roman lands to Cleopatra’s family
Antony moved the Senate to Alexandria
Cleopatra refused to trade grain with Rome
options.rationale: The anger was about Roman land.

options.label: Antony freed all of Egypt’s slaves
options.rationale: The anger was about Roman land.

questions.explanation: Handing Roman territory to Cleopatra’s family let Octavian paint Antony as a traitor.

questions.prompt: From Level 41: after which battle did Antony take charge of the East?
questions.explanation: After Antony and Octavian beat Brutus and Cassius at Philippi, Antony took charge of the eastern provinces.

levels.title: Actium
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the Battle of Actium and its consequences.
levels.summary: In 31 BCE Agrippa’s fleet beat Antony and Cleopatra at Actium. Both died in 30 BCE, Egypt became Roman, and Octavian stood alone.

cards.headline: One sea battle decided who would rule the Roman world.
War on a queen
cards.body: In 32 BCE Rome declared war on Cleopatra, not on Antony, so the conflict looked like a foreign war rather than another civil war. Octavian’s closest friend, Marcus Agrippa, was his leading general and admiral, and commanded his fleet.

cards.headline: The battle
cards.body: On 2 September 31 BCE, Octavian’s fleet defeated Antony and Cleopatra at Actium, off western Greece. The next year, as Octavian took Alexandria, Antony and Cleopatra both took their own lives.

cards.headline: Master of the Roman world
cards.body: Egypt became a Roman province under Octavian’s personal control, and its grain helped feed Rome. After Actium, one man stood alone at the top of the Roman world.

cards.headline: Actium: decided
learned: Rome declared war on Cleopatra
Agrippa won at Actium in 31 BCE
Antony and Cleopatra died in 30 BCE
Egypt became a Roman province

questions.prompt: Who commanded Octavian’s fleet at Actium?

options.label: Mark Antony
options.rationale: He was on the other side.

questions.explanation: Agrippa, Octavian’s closest friend, commanded his fleet.

questions.prompt: Why did Rome declare war on Cleopatra rather than on Antony?

options.label: To make it look like a foreign war

questions.explanation: A war against a foreign queen was easier to rally Romans behind than one more civil war.

questions.prompt: From Level 42: what had Antony done that let Octavian call him a traitor?

options.label: Surrendered his legions to the Parthians
Killed Octavian’s sister
options.rationale: He left her; he didn’t kill her.

options.label: Given Roman lands to Cleopatra and her children

questions.explanation: The Donations of Alexandria handed Roman territory to Cleopatra’s family.

levels.title: Augustus, First Emperor
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Augustus ruled as emperor while claiming to restore the Republic.
levels.summary: In 27 BCE Octavian “restored” the Republic and became Augustus. He kept the old offices but held the legions, and ruled for about 40 years.

cards.headline: He said he was giving power back. He kept almost all of it.
The settlement of 27 BCE
cards.body: In 27 BCE Octavian claimed to restore the Republic, and the Senate gave him the name Augustus, “the revered one.” He called himself princeps, “first citizen,” and avoided the title of king.

cards.headline: Old forms, new power
cards.body: The Senate, consuls and elections continued. But Augustus controlled most of the legions and the key frontier provinces. Historians call his system the Principate, from princeps. He ruled until his death in 14 CE, about 40 years as emperor.
cards.callout: Principate: rule by the princeps, the “first citizen”

cards.fact: Augustus wrote his own record of achievements.
cards.context: Called the Res Gestae, it was inscribed on bronze pillars outside his tomb. It lists his victories, his buildings and his gifts to the Roman people.

cards.headline: The first emperor: crowned without a crown
learned: Octavian became Augustus in 27 BCE
He called himself princeps
The old offices survived without real power
He ruled until 14 CE

questions.prompt: What did Augustus call himself?

options.label: Rex, the old title of king
Dictator for life
options.rationale: That title helped get Caesar killed.

questions.explanation: Augustus called himself princeps, “first citizen,” and avoided the title of king.

questions.prompt: Why did Augustus keep the Senate, consuls and elections?

options.label: The Senate and consuls held the real power
The army demanded it
options.rationale: The army was loyal to him.

options.label: To make his rule look like the Republic

questions.explanation: Keeping the old forms let one man’s power look like the Republic, not a monarchy.

questions.prompt: From Level 9: why did Augustus avoid the title of king?

options.label: Romans had hated the title since the last king
Only Etruscans were allowed to be kings
options.rationale: The issue was Roman hatred of kings.

options.label: The Senate had no power to crown anyone
options.rationale: The issue was Roman hatred of kings.

questions.explanation: After the last king was expelled, rex was so hated that even Rome’s most powerful leaders avoided it.

levels.title: The Pax Romana
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the Pax Romana and what peace made possible.
levels.summary: From Augustus to Marcus Aurelius, about 200 years of relative peace let trade, people and ideas move freely across the empire.

cards.headline: For about 200 years, most of the Roman world lived in peace.
The Roman peace
cards.body: The Pax Romana, “Roman peace,” was a period of about 200 years of relative peace and stability across the empire, beginning with Augustus. It is usually dated from 27 BCE to 180 CE, the death of the emperor Marcus Aurelius.

cards.headline: What peace made possible
cards.body: With the seas and roads safe, trade flowed across the Mediterranean. Goods, people and ideas moved from one end of the empire to the other, and cities grew and prospered.

cards.fact: The Pax Romana wasn’t free of war.
cards.context: Fighting went on at the frontiers. What the peace meant was that the empire’s interior was largely spared from war.

cards.headline: The peace: understood
learned: The Pax Romana lasted about 200 years
It ran from Augustus to Marcus Aurelius
Trade and cities flourished
Fighting went on at the frontiers

questions.prompt: Roughly how long did the Pax Romana last?
questions.explanation: The Pax Romana lasted about 200 years, from 27 BCE to 180 CE.

questions.prompt: How did the Pax Romana help trade?

options.label: Safe seas and roads let goods move freely
It closed the frontiers to foreign goods
It ended the use of coins

questions.explanation: Peace made travel safe, so trade, people and ideas moved freely.

questions.prompt: From Level 1: what did Romans call the Mediterranean at the heart of this trade?
questions.explanation: Romans called the Mediterranean Mare Nostrum, “our sea.”

levels.title: A City of Marble
levels.objective: After this level you can describe how Augustus rebuilt Rome and why buildings mattered politically.
levels.summary: Augustus restored temples, Agrippa built baths and the first Pantheon, and the Ara Pacis celebrated peace. Every building sent a message.

cards.headline: “I found Rome a city of brick and left it a city of marble.”
Building an image
cards.body: According to the historian Suetonius, Augustus boasted that he found Rome a city of brick and left it a city of marble. By his own count in the Res Gestae, he restored 82 temples in a single year. His buildings advertised his piety and linked his rule to Rome’s gods.

cards.headline: A friend who built
cards.body: Augustus’ friend Agrippa paid for major public works in Rome, including baths and aqueducts. He also built the first Pantheon. The domed Pantheon standing today is a later rebuilding under the emperor Hadrian.

cards.fact: The Ara Pacis, the Altar of Augustan Peace, was dedicated in 9 BCE.
cards.context: Its carvings show members of Augustus’ family in procession, a family portrait in marble celebrating the peace he had brought.

cards.headline: Rome: rebuilt
learned: Augustus boasted of a city of marble
He restored 82 temples in one year
Agrippa built the first Pantheon
The Ara Pacis celebrated his peace

questions.prompt: How many temples did Augustus say he restored in a single year?
questions.explanation: In the Res Gestae, Augustus says he restored 82 temples in one year.

questions.prompt: Why did Augustus pour money into temples and monuments?

options.label: Rome had almost no stone buildings before him
options.rationale: He boasted of turning brick to marble.

options.label: To show his piety and tie his rule to the gods
To house the Senate’s new members
To prepare Rome for a siege

questions.explanation: His buildings advertised his piety and the peace he had brought.

questions.prompt: From Level 7: Roman religion aimed to keep the pax deorum. What was it?

options.label: A temple to the god of war
options.rationale: It was a relationship, not a building.

questions.explanation: The pax deorum was the peace between Rome and its gods, kept by correct ritual. Restoring temples served it.

levels.title: Virgil and the Aeneid
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what the Aeneid is and why Augustus's Rome valued it.
levels.summary: Virgil’s Aeneid follows the Trojan Aeneas to Italy. It gave Rome an epic to rival Homer’s, and Augustus’ family a heroic ancestor.

cards.headline: Rome’s greatest poem is about a refugee from a burning city.
The poem
cards.body: Virgil, who lived from 70 to 19 BCE, was the greatest poet of Augustan Rome. His Aeneid is an epic poem in 12 books, modeled on Homer’s Iliad and Odyssey. It tells how the Trojan prince Aeneas escaped burning Troy and, guided by fate, came to Italy.

cards.headline: A poem for Augustus
cards.body: The Julian family, including Caesar and Augustus, claimed descent from Aeneas through his son Iulus. So the poem gave Augustus a heroic ancestor. Its hero is famous for pietas: dutiful devotion to the gods, his family and his country.
cards.callout: Pietas: duty to gods, family and country

cards.fact: Virgil wanted the Aeneid burned.
cards.context: He died before finishing it and asked for the manuscript to be destroyed. Augustus had it published instead.

cards.headline: The Aeneid: read
learned: Virgil was Augustan Rome’s great poet
The Aeneid follows Aeneas from Troy to Italy
Augustus’ family claimed Aeneas as ancestor
Aeneas stands for pietas, duty

questions.prompt: Who is the hero of the Aeneid?

options.label: Romulus
options.rationale: He comes much later in Rome’s story.

questions.explanation: The Aeneid follows the Trojan prince Aeneas from Troy to Italy.

questions.prompt: Why did the Aeneid suit Augustus so well?

options.label: It gave his family a heroic ancestor in Aeneas
It described his victory at Actium in full
It was written in Greek for the East

questions.explanation: The Julian family claimed descent from Aeneas, so Rome’s founding epic honored Augustus’ own line.

questions.prompt: From Level 2: Aeneas was one founding legend. Who, in the other, founded the city itself?
questions.explanation: Legend said the twins Romulus and Remus were raised by a wolf, and Romulus founded and named Rome.

levels.title: Months Named for Emperors
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the Julian calendar and how July and August got their names.
levels.summary: Caesar’s Julian calendar of 46 BCE gave us 365 days and leap years. Two months were renamed for him and for Augustus.

cards.headline: Two of your months are named after Roman rulers.
Caesar fixes the year
cards.body: In 46 BCE Julius Caesar introduced the Julian calendar, with 365 days and a leap day every fourth year, an average of 365.25 days. He based the reform on the advice of the astronomer Sosigenes of Alexandria.

cards.headline: New names
cards.body: The Roman year once began in March, so Quintilis meant “fifth month.” It was renamed Julius, our July, in honor of Julius Caesar. Sextilis was renamed Augustus, our August, in honor of Augustus in 8 BCE.

cards.fact: The Julian calendar was slightly too long.
cards.context: It drifted against the seasons, so in 1582 Pope Gregory XIII replaced it with the Gregorian calendar we use today.

cards.headline: The calendar: set
learned: Caesar’s calendar began in 46 BCE
It had 365 days and a leap day
July honors Caesar and August honors Augustus
The Gregorian calendar replaced it in 1582

questions.prompt: Which month is named after Julius Caesar?
questions.explanation: Quintilis was renamed Julius, our July, in Caesar’s honor.

questions.prompt: Why does the Julian calendar add a leap day every fourth year?

options.label: To honor Augustus with an extra day
To make every month the same length
To fit the Roman festival cycle
A year is about 365 and a quarter days long

questions.explanation: Three 365-day years and one 366-day year average 365.25 days.

questions.prompt: From Level 40: Caesar didn’t live long with his new calendar. When was he killed?
questions.explanation: Caesar was killed on the Ides of March, 15 March 44 BCE, two years after his calendar began.

levels.title: Teutoburg Forest
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the disaster in the Teutoburg Forest and how it fixed the Rhine frontier.
levels.summary: In 9 CE Arminius led three legions under Varus into an ambush and destroyed them. Rome gave up on Germany and held the Rhine.

cards.headline: In 9 CE three Roman legions marched into a German forest. They never came out.
The ambush
cards.body: In 9 CE, Germanic warriors led by Arminius destroyed three Roman legions under the governor Varus in the Teutoburg Forest. Arminius had served with the Roman army and was trusted by Varus, whom he led into an ambush.

cards.headline: The river becomes a border
cards.body: After the disaster, Rome gave up plans to conquer Germany east of the Rhine, and the river became a lasting frontier. Archaeologists believe the battlefield lies near Kalkriese in Germany, where Roman weapons and coins have been found.

cards.fact: “Quintilius Varus, give me back my legions!”
cards.context: According to the historian Suetonius, Augustus cried out these words after hearing of the disaster.

cards.headline: The frontier: fixed
learned: Arminius ambushed Varus in 9 CE
Three legions were destroyed
The Rhine became the frontier
Augustus mourned his lost legions

questions.prompt: Who led the Germanic warriors in the Teutoburg Forest?

options.label: Spartacus
options.rationale: He led a slave revolt in Italy.

questions.explanation: Arminius, who had served with the Roman army, led the ambush.

questions.prompt: What lasting effect did the Teutoburg disaster have?

options.label: Rome abandoned the province of Gaul
Rome gave up conquering Germany past the Rhine

questions.explanation: Rome gave up conquering Germany east of the Rhine, which became a lasting frontier.

questions.prompt: From Level 29: a legion had roughly 4,000 to 5,000 infantry. About how many were in three?
questions.explanation: Three legions of 4,000 to 5,000 infantry each make roughly 12,000 to 15,000 soldiers.

levels.title: Milestone: From Republic to Empire
levels.objective: After this level you can trace Rome's path from republic to empire and explain what changed and what stayed.
levels.summary: From the Gracchi to Augustus, violence and loyal armies turned the Republic into one-man rule that kept the Republic’s old forms.

cards.headline: Milestone: halfway to Mastery. How did a republic become an empire?
cards.body: In about a century, Rome went from the Gracchi to an emperor. Let’s trace the path.

cards.headline: Same forms, new master
cards.body: The change from Republic to Empire kept republican forms, such as the Senate and the consuls, while real power passed to one man. Even the word emperor is borrowed from the army: it comes from imperator, a title soldiers gave to a victorious commander.

events.label: Tiberius Gracchus proposes land reform
Sulla marches on Rome
Caesar crosses the Rubicon
Caesar is assassinated
Octavian wins at Actium
Octavian becomes Augustus

items.label: Republic
points: Power limited by time and colleagues

items.label: Principate
points: Senate and consuls kept, but weaker

cards.headline: Milestone: halfway to Mastery
learned: Republican forms survived under one ruler
Emperor comes from imperator
Loyal armies carried generals to power
Octavian became Augustus in 27 BCE

questions.prompt: In what year did Octavian receive the name Augustus?
questions.explanation: In 27 BCE the Senate gave Octavian the name Augustus.

questions.prompt: What did Marius change about who could serve in the legions?

options.label: He enrolled poor citizens with no property
He replaced soldiers with mercenaries from Gaul

questions.explanation: Marius enrolled landless citizens, equipped and paid by the state.

questions.prompt: Where did Octavian’s fleet defeat Antony and Cleopatra?
questions.explanation: Agrippa’s fleet won at Actium, off western Greece, in 31 BCE.

questions.prompt: Why did the Republic’s forms survive under Augustus?

options.label: They made one man’s rule look like a republic
The Senate still controlled the legions
The consuls could still overrule Augustus
Rome had no other way to name its years

questions.explanation: Keeping the Senate and consuls let Augustus hold real power without looking like a king.

questions.prompt: Where does the word “emperor” come from?

options.label: Rex, the Latin title of Rome’s kings
Augustus, “the revered one”
options.rationale: That was a name the Senate gave.

questions.explanation: Emperor comes from imperator, the title soldiers gave a victorious commander.

questions.prompt: Why did loyal armies matter so much in the fall of the Republic?

options.label: They kept the peace in Italy
options.rationale: They were used in civil wars.

options.label: Generals could use loyal soldiers to seize power
They protected the Senate from ambitious generals

questions.explanation: Since Marius, soldiers looked to their general, so Sulla, Caesar and Octavian could turn armies into political power.

questions.prompt: Which of these came first on the road from Republic to Empire?
questions.explanation: Sulla marched on Rome in 88 BCE, decades before Caesar and Octavian followed his example.

levels.title: Tiberius
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the reign of Tiberius and the problem of succession.
levels.summary: Tiberius, Augustus’ adopted stepson, ruled from 14 to 37 CE, much of it from Capri. Rome had no rule for choosing the next emperor.

cards.headline: Following Rome’s first emperor may have been the hardest job in the world.
The reluctant heir
cards.body: Augustus had no surviving son. After other chosen successors died, he adopted his stepson Tiberius as heir. Tiberius became emperor on Augustus’ death in 14 CE and ruled until 37 CE. Rome never had a fixed law of succession, so each emperor had to choose an heir, often by adoption.

cards.headline: Rule from an island
cards.body: In his later years Tiberius withdrew to the island of Capri and ruled from there. In Rome, Sejanus, commander of the Praetorian Guard, grew powerful until Tiberius had him executed in 31 CE.

cards.fact: The Praetorian Guard was the emperor’s bodyguard, stationed in Rome itself.
cards.context: Soldiers that close to the emperor could protect him. They could also turn on him.

cards.headline: Tiberius: met
learned: Augustus adopted his stepson Tiberius
Tiberius ruled from 14 to 37 CE
He withdrew to Capri
Rome had no law of succession

questions.prompt: How was Tiberius related to Augustus?

options.label: His younger brother, a fellow consul
His stepson, adopted as his heir
His nephew, the son of Octavia

questions.explanation: Augustus adopted his stepson Tiberius as heir after other successors died.

questions.prompt: Why was every change of emperor a possible crisis?

options.label: The Senate elected emperors every year
Emperors had to be born in Rome itself
Rome had no fixed law of succession
Only generals over sixty could rule

questions.explanation: Without a law of succession, each emperor had to pick an heir, and rivals could contest the choice.

questions.prompt: From Level 44: Tiberius took over the position Augustus had created. What had Augustus called himself?

options.label: Rex, the old title of king

questions.explanation: Augustus called himself princeps, and his successors inherited the role.

levels.title: Caligula
levels.objective: After this level you can separate what is known about Caligula from later rumor.
levels.summary: Caligula, “little boot,” began popular in 37 CE and became autocratic. His own guard killed him in 41 CE. Many tales about him are hostile rumor.

cards.headline: Most of what you’ve heard about Caligula was written by people who hated him.
Little Boot
cards.body: Gaius, known as Caligula, became emperor in 37 CE. Caligula means “little boot,” a nickname soldiers gave him as a child, when he wore a small soldier’s uniform in his father’s camp. He was popular at first, but his rule soon became autocratic and extravagant.

cards.headline: Stories and evidence
cards.body: Most accounts of Caligula come from later writers hostile to him, so historians treat the wildest stories with caution. The tale that he planned to make his horse a consul may be a joke or an exaggeration.
cards.callout: Ask who wrote a story, and why

cards.fact: Caligula was murdered by officers of his own guard in 41 CE.
cards.context: The Praetorian Guard, meant to protect the emperor, ended his reign.

cards.headline: Caligula: sifted
learned: Caligula means “little boot”
He ruled from 37 to 41 CE
His guard murdered him
Hostile sources shape his legend

questions.prompt: What does the nickname Caligula mean?

options.label: Little soldier
options.rationale: Close, but it was about his footwear.

questions.explanation: Soldiers called the child Gaius “little boot” because of his small uniform.

questions.prompt: Why do historians doubt many stories about Caligula?

options.label: He banned all writing during his reign
The stories were all written in Greek
His coins show he was a gentle ruler
They come from later writers who hated him

questions.explanation: Hostile later writers had reasons to exaggerate, so their wildest claims need caution.

questions.prompt: From Level 51: which force, meant to protect the emperor, killed Caligula?
questions.explanation: Officers of the Praetorian Guard, stationed in Rome, murdered Caligula in 41 CE.

levels.title: Claudius Conquers Britain
levels.objective: After this level you can describe Claudius's reign and the invasion of Britain.
levels.summary: The guard made Claudius emperor in 41 CE. The scholar few took seriously invaded Britain in 43 CE, where Boudica later rose in revolt.

cards.headline: The emperor nobody took seriously conquered a land Caesar only raided.
The unlikely emperor
cards.body: After Caligula’s murder, the Praetorian Guard made his uncle Claudius emperor in 41 CE. Claudius had a limp and a stammer, and his family kept him out of public life. He was a scholar who wrote histories, now lost, and he relied on freedmen, formerly enslaved people, as powerful officials.

cards.headline: Britain becomes Roman
cards.body: In 43 CE Claudius launched the invasion of Britain, which became a Roman province. In about 60 CE Boudica, queen of the Iceni, led a revolt that burned London before the Romans crushed it.

cards.fact: Caesar had raided Britain twice, in 55 and 54 BCE.
cards.context: Claudius’ invasion came nearly a century later, and this time Rome stayed.

cards.headline: Britain: conquered
learned: The guard made Claudius emperor in 41 CE
He was a scholar kept out of public life
He invaded Britain in 43 CE
Boudica revolted around 60 CE

questions.prompt: When did Claudius launch the invasion of Britain?
questions.explanation: Claudius invaded Britain in 43 CE, and it became a province.

questions.prompt: Why was Claudius an unexpected emperor?

options.label: His family had kept him out of public life
He had never been to Rome before
options.rationale: He grew up in the imperial family.

options.label: He was born a Gaulish prince
He had led a revolt against Caligula
options.rationale: The guard chose him after the murder.

questions.explanation: With a limp and a stammer, Claudius was kept out of public life until the guard made him emperor.

questions.prompt: From Level 38: what had Julius Caesar achieved in Britain?

options.label: Full conquest of the whole island

questions.explanation: Caesar led two expeditions to Britain but did not conquer it.

levels.title: Nero and the Great Fire
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the Great Fire of Rome and Nero's reputation.
levels.summary: Nero became emperor at 16. After the fire of 64 CE he blamed the Christians and built a palace on the ruins. His death in 68 CE ended Augustus’ line.

cards.headline: Rome burned for six days, and people have blamed Nero ever since.
The young emperor
cards.body: Nero, Claudius’ adopted son, became emperor in 54 CE at the age of 16. Facing revolt, he took his own life in 68 CE, ending the Julio-Claudian dynasty, the family line of Augustus.

cards.headline: The Great Fire
cards.body: In 64 CE a great fire burned in Rome for six days. Three of the city’s 14 districts were destroyed and seven more badly damaged. Nero blamed the Christians in Rome and had many of them executed. On land cleared by the fire, he built a vast palace, the Golden House.

cards.fact: Nero did not fiddle while Rome burned.
cards.context: The fiddle did not yet exist, and the historian Tacitus says Nero was away at Antium when the fire began.

cards.headline: Nero: judged
learned: Nero became emperor at 16 in 54 CE
Rome burned for six days in 64 CE
He blamed the Christians
His death in 68 CE ended Augustus’ line

questions.prompt: Whom did Nero blame for the Great Fire?
questions.explanation: Nero blamed the Christians in Rome and had many executed.

questions.prompt: Why is “Nero fiddled while Rome burned” a myth?

options.label: He was dead before the fire began
He played the flute, not the fiddle
options.rationale: The fiddle didn’t exist at all.

options.label: The fire happened under Caligula
options.rationale: It was in 64 CE, under Nero.

options.label: The fiddle didn’t exist, and he was away

questions.explanation: The instrument was invented much later, and Tacitus places Nero at Antium when the fire started.

questions.prompt: From Level 53: Nero was the adopted son of which emperor?
questions.explanation: Nero was Claudius’ adopted son and succeeded him in 54 CE.

levels.title: The Year of the Four Emperors
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what happened in 69 CE and what it revealed about imperial power.
levels.summary: In 69 CE four men ruled in turn, each backed by an army. Vespasian won, proving that emperors could be made far from Rome.

cards.headline: In a single year, Rome had four emperors.
69 CE
cards.body: After Nero’s death in 68 CE came the Year of the Four Emperors, 69 CE. Galba, Otho, Vitellius and Vespasian each held power in turn. Each claimant was backed by an army, showing that the legions could make and unmake emperors.

cards.headline: The winner
cards.body: Vespasian, a general commanding in Judaea, won the civil war and founded the Flavian dynasty. The historian Tacitus wrote that the year revealed a secret of empire: an emperor could be made somewhere other than Rome.

cards.fact: Vespasian came from a family of modest rank.
cards.context: He did not belong to the old Roman nobility. Command of an army now mattered more than an ancient name.

cards.headline: The year: survived
learned: Four emperors ruled in 69 CE
Each was backed by an army
Vespasian won and founded the Flavians
Emperors could be made far from Rome

questions.explanation: Vespasian won and founded the Flavian dynasty.

questions.prompt: What did 69 CE reveal about imperial power?

options.label: The Senate could choose emperors freely
Armies far from Rome could make emperors

questions.explanation: Since Marius, soldiers depended on their commander for pay and land, so their loyalty followed him.

levels.title: The Flavians and the Colosseum
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the Flavian dynasty and the building of the Colosseum.
levels.summary: Vespasian and his sons Titus and Domitian ruled until 96 CE. They built the Colosseum on the grounds of Nero’s palace.

cards.headline: The Colosseum stands where an emperor’s private lake used to be.
A family of soldiers
cards.body: In 70 CE Vespasian’s son Titus captured Jerusalem and destroyed its Temple. Titus succeeded Vespasian and was followed by his brother Domitian, whose harsh rule ended with his murder in 96 CE.

cards.headline: The Colosseum
cards.body: Vespasian began the Colosseum, and Titus opened it in 80 CE with games that lasted 100 days. It could hold about 50,000 spectators. It stood on the site of a lake in the grounds of Nero’s Golden House, giving the land back to public use.

cards.fact: The Colosseum’s real name was the Flavian Amphitheatre.
cards.context: The name Colosseum came later, probably from a colossal statue of Nero that stood nearby.

cards.headline: The Colosseum: opened
learned: Titus took Jerusalem in 70 CE
The Colosseum opened in 80 CE
It held about 50,000 people
It was built on Nero’s palace grounds

questions.prompt: About how many spectators could the Colosseum hold?
questions.explanation: The Colosseum held about 50,000 spectators.

questions.prompt: Why did building on Nero’s palace grounds send a message?

options.label: It hid the damage from the Great Fire
It gave a hated ruler’s land back to the people
It honored Nero as the Flavians’ ancestor
It was the only flat land left in Rome

questions.explanation: Turning Nero’s private lake into a public arena showed the new dynasty sharing Rome with its people.

questions.prompt: From Level 54: what had Nero built on land cleared by the Great Fire?

options.label: A temple to the god Janus
A new wall around the city
A vast palace, the Golden House
A harbor for the grain ships

questions.explanation: Nero built the Golden House on land cleared by the fire; the Flavians built the Colosseum on its grounds.

levels.title: Pompeii and Vesuvius
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the eruption of Vesuvius and why Pompeii is so valuable to historians.
levels.summary: In 79 CE Vesuvius buried Pompeii and Herculaneum. The ash that killed the towns preserved them, and Pliny the Younger described it all.

cards.headline: A volcano destroyed a town, and by burying it, saved it for us.
The eruption
cards.body: In 79 CE Mount Vesuvius erupted and buried the towns of Pompeii and Herculaneum. Titus was emperor. Pliny the Younger described the eruption in letters to the historian Tacitus. His uncle, Pliny the Elder, died trying to rescue people.

cards.headline: A town frozen in time
cards.body: Pompeii was buried under several meters of ash and pumice, which preserved buildings, paintings and everyday objects. Its walls still carry painted notices and scratched graffiti, including election slogans. Together they give historians a rare snapshot of ordinary town life.

cards.fact: Plaster casts show victims in their final moments.
cards.context: In the 1800s, excavators poured plaster into hollows left in the ash by victims’ bodies, recording their final positions.

cards.headline: Pompeii: uncovered
learned: Vesuvius erupted in 79 CE
It buried Pompeii and Herculaneum
Pliny the Younger described it
The ash preserved a whole town

questions.prompt: Which two towns did Vesuvius bury in 79 CE?
questions.explanation: The eruption buried Pompeii and Herculaneum.

questions.prompt: Why is Pompeii so valuable to historians?

options.label: It was the empire’s richest and largest city
Its people wrote the first Roman history
Ash preserved ordinary town life as it was
It was the only town the eruption spared

questions.explanation: Buried under ash, Pompeii kept buildings, paintings, objects and graffiti that usually disappear.

questions.prompt: From Level 56: which emperor, who opened the Colosseum a year later, ruled when Vesuvius erupted?
questions.explanation: Titus was emperor in 79 CE and opened the Colosseum in 80 CE.

levels.title: Trajan's Empire at Its Largest
levels.objective: After this level you can describe Trajan's conquests and the empire at its greatest extent.
levels.summary: Trajan, born in Spain, conquered Dacia and pushed into Mesopotamia. In 117 CE the empire reached its greatest extent.

cards.headline: The empire reached its largest size under an emperor born in Spain.
The best emperor
cards.body: Trajan, born in Spain, was the first emperor from outside Italy. He ruled from 98 to 117 CE, and the Senate gave him the title Optimus, “the best.” His reign fell in the middle of the Pax Romana, when the empire’s interior was largely at peace even as its armies fought on the frontiers.

cards.headline: Conquest
cards.body: Trajan conquered Dacia, roughly modern Romania, in two wars ending in 106 CE. Under him the empire reached its greatest extent, in 117 CE, after he conquered lands as far as Mesopotamia.

cards.fact: Trajan’s Column tells the story of the Dacian wars in stone.
cards.context: A spiral band of carvings winds up the column from base to top, showing the campaigns scene by scene.

cards.headline: The empire: at its largest
learned: Trajan was born in Spain
He ruled from 98 to 117 CE
He conquered Dacia
The empire peaked in 117 CE

questions.prompt: Why is 117 CE a landmark year for the empire?

options.label: Rome was sacked by the Gauls again

questions.explanation: In 117 CE, after Trajan’s conquests, the empire was at its largest.

levels.title: Hadrian and His Wall
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why Hadrian consolidated the frontiers and built his wall.
levels.summary: Hadrian gave up some conquests, toured the frontiers and fortified them. His wall ran about 118 km across northern Britain.

cards.headline: Hadrian’s answer to an empire too big to grow: guard its edges.
Holding, not growing
cards.body: Hadrian, Trajan’s successor, ruled from 117 to 138 CE. He gave up some of Trajan’s eastern conquests and spent much of his reign traveling through the provinces, inspecting armies and frontiers. In Rome he rebuilt the Pantheon, first built by Agrippa, as the domed temple still standing today.

cards.headline: The wall
cards.body: Hadrian’s Wall, begun in 122 CE, ran about 118 km across northern Britain. It had small forts about every Roman mile, and larger forts along its length.
cards.callout: Hadrian’s Wall: begun 122 CE, about 118 km long

cards.fact: Hadrian was the first emperor to wear a full beard.
cards.context: He loved Greek culture, and he wore his beard in the Greek style.

cards.headline: The frontier: guarded
learned: Hadrian ruled from 117 to 138 CE
He gave up some conquests
His wall crossed northern Britain
He rebuilt the Pantheon

options.label: Egypt
options.rationale: The wall is in the far north.

questions.explanation: Hadrian’s Wall ran about 118 km across northern Britain.

questions.prompt: What did Hadrian’s frontier policy show?

options.label: He chose to hold the empire, not expand it
Rome had lost most of its legions in Dacia
He meant to invade all of Scotland next
Britain had become the empire’s richest land

questions.explanation: He gave up some conquests and fortified the frontiers he kept.

questions.prompt: From Level 46: who built the first Pantheon, which Hadrian rebuilt?
questions.explanation: Agrippa built the first Pantheon; the domed building standing today is Hadrian’s rebuilding.

levels.title: Checkpoint: The Five Good Emperors
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the era of the Five Good Emperors, ending with Marcus Aurelius.
levels.summary: From 96 to 180 CE, emperors chosen by adoption gave Rome its steadiest era. Marcus Aurelius passed power to his son Commodus, and it ended.

cards.headline: Chapter 6 finale. Five emperors in a row who ruled well. Then it ended.
cards.body: How Rome found good rulers for most of a century, and how it lost them.

cards.headline: Choosing the best
cards.body: Nerva, Trajan, Hadrian, Antoninus Pius and Marcus Aurelius, who ruled from 96 to 180 CE, are known as the Five Good Emperors. Each of the first four chose his successor by adoption, picking a capable adult rather than relying on a son. The historian Edward Gibbon called it the time when the human race was most happy and prosperous.

cards.headline: The philosopher emperor
cards.body: Marcus Aurelius, a Stoic philosopher, wrote his private reflections, the Meditations, while on campaign. A deadly epidemic, the Antonine Plague, swept the empire from about 165 CE. Marcus was succeeded by his own son Commodus, whose disastrous reign ended the era.

cards.headline: Chapter 6 complete

The first four chose heirs by adoption
Marcus Aurelius wrote the Meditations
His son Commodus ended the era

questions.explanation: Marcus Aurelius, the philosopher emperor, was the last of the five.

options.label: Claudius

With the eruption of Vesuvius in 79 CE
