questions.explanation: The Pax Romana is usually dated from 27 BCE to 180 CE, when Marcus Aurelius died.

levels.title: A Day in the City
levels.objective: After this level you can describe daily life in the city of Rome, from apartment blocks to the forum.
levels.summary: Perhaps a million people crowded into Rome. Most rented rooms in risky apartment blocks; the rich lived in houses built around an atrium.

cards.headline: A million people, one city, and hardly anyone had a kitchen or a bath at home.
Apartment life
cards.body: By the time of Augustus, Rome had perhaps around 1 million inhabitants. Most lived in insulae, crowded apartment blocks several stories high, usually without running water or private baths. The upper floors were the cheapest, and fire and collapse were constant dangers.

cards.headline: Houses and the Forum
cards.body: Wealthy Romans lived in a domus, a private house built around an open hall called the atrium. Public life centered on the Forum, with its temples, law courts, markets and platforms for speeches.

cards.fact: Augustus gave Rome its first fire brigade.
cards.context: He created the vigiles, freedmen who fought fires and patrolled at night, and he limited new buildings to about 20 meters high.

cards.headline: The city: explored
learned: Rome had perhaps a million people
Most lived in insulae
The rich lived in a domus
The Forum was the center of public life

options.label: In private houses with an atrium

options.label: They had the best views of the Forum

levels.title: Slavery in Rome
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how slavery shaped Roman society and what freed slaves could become.
levels.summary: Enslaved people, taken by war, piracy and birth, did every kind of work. Many were freed, and a citizen’s freed slave became a citizen.

cards.headline: In Rome, a doctor, a teacher and a miner could all be enslaved.
Property under the law
cards.body: Enslaved people made up a large share of the population of Roman Italy. People were enslaved through war, piracy and trade, and children born to enslaved mothers were enslaved too. Under Roman law an enslaved person was property, with no legal rights of their own.

cards.headline: Every kind of work
cards.body: Enslaved people worked in mines, on farms and in households. Some served as teachers, doctors and secretaries. Romans also often freed enslaved people, a practice called manumission.

cards.fact: A citizen’s freed slave usually became a Roman citizen.
cards.context: Their children had full rights. Some freedmen grew rich, and Claudius used freedmen as powerful officials.

cards.headline: Slavery: understood
learned: Enslaved people were legally property
War, piracy and birth fed slavery
Manumission freed many
Freed slaves of citizens became citizens

options.label: Selling a slave at public auction

questions.explanation: Manumission was the freeing of an enslaved person, which Romans did often.

questions.explanation: His army of escaped enslaved people grew to tens of thousands and defeated several Roman forces.

levels.title: Bread and Circuses
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the grain dole and public games and why rulers provided them.
levels.summary: Rome fed about 200,000 citizens with free grain and staged huge free games. A poet mocked it as “bread and circuses.”

cards.headline: A Roman poet said his people wanted only two things: bread and circuses.
Free grain
cards.body: Rome gave free grain to many citizens living in the city. Under Augustus about 200,000 people received it. Much of that grain came from Egypt, which was under the emperor’s personal control.

cards.headline: Free games
cards.body: Public games, ludi, began as religious festivals and grew into huge free entertainments. Emperors and politicians paid for games and food to win popularity and keep the city calm.

cards.fact: “Bread and circuses” was a complaint.
cards.context: The poet Juvenal said that the Roman people, who once handed out commands, now wanted only these two things. He meant that citizens had traded political power for free food and shows.

cards.headline: Bread and circuses: explained
learned: Rome fed citizens with free grain
About 200,000 received it
Games began as religious festivals
Juvenal mocked “bread and circuses”

questions.explanation: Under Augustus about 200,000 people in Rome received free grain.

options.label: The law required it of every consul
To win popularity and keep the city calm
Because farmers refused to sell grain

questions.explanation: Feeding and entertaining the crowd kept rulers popular and the city calm.

questions.explanation: Gaius Gracchus pushed wider reforms, including cheap grain, before he was killed in 121 BCE.

levels.title: Gladiators
levels.objective: After this level you can separate the reality of gladiator fights from popular myth.
levels.summary: Gladiator fights began as funeral games. Most fighters were enslaved or condemned, fought in set types, and were often spared.

cards.headline: Thumbs down meant death? Probably not the way the movies show it.
Who fought
cards.body: Gladiator fights probably began as funeral games to honor the dead, first recorded in Rome in 264 BCE. Most gladiators were enslaved people, prisoners of war or condemned criminals, but some free men volunteered.

cards.headline: How they fought
cards.body: Gladiators fought in types with set equipment, such as the net-and-trident retiarius against the helmeted secutor. They were expensive to train, and many fights did not end in death: a beaten fighter could be spared.

cards.fact: No one knows exactly what the thumb meant.
cards.context: Roman writers mention a “turned thumb” deciding a gladiator’s fate, but not which way it turned. The thumbs-down of films is a modern guess.

cards.headline: Gladiators: unmasked
learned: Fights began as funeral games
Most gladiators were enslaved or condemned
They fought in set types
Many beaten fighters were spared

questions.explanation: The first recorded fights in Rome, in 264 BCE, were funeral games.

options.label: They were expensive to train and replace
Killing in the arena was illegal

questions.explanation: A trained gladiator was a costly investment, so many beaten fighters lived to fight again.

levels.title: Chariot Racing
levels.objective: After this level you can describe chariot racing, the Circus Maximus and the racing factions.
levels.summary: The Circus Maximus held about 150,000 fans. Four color factions raced four-horse chariots seven laps, and rivalries could turn into riots.

cards.headline: Rome’s biggest crowds didn’t watch gladiators. They watched chariots.
The Circus Maximus
cards.body: The Circus Maximus, Rome’s great racetrack, could hold about 150,000 spectators. A standard race was seven laps around the central barrier, the spina. The most prestigious races used four-horse chariots, called quadrigae: teams of four horses running side by side.

cards.headline: Reds, Whites, Blues and Greens
cards.body: Charioteers raced for four factions, the Reds, Whites, Blues and Greens, each with passionate fans. Supporters cheered for colors more than for drivers, though successful charioteers could become rich and famous.

cards.fact: Racing fans nearly toppled an emperor.
cards.context: In 532 CE fans of the Blues and Greens rioted together in Constantinople in the Nika revolt, nearly overthrowing the emperor Justinian.

questions.explanation: About 150,000 spectators is roughly three times the Colosseum’s 50,000.

levels.title: The Baths
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what Roman baths were like and why they mattered socially.
levels.summary: Cheap, heated public baths had hot, warm and cold rooms. Romans went to exercise, talk and do business, not just to wash.

cards.headline: For a Roman, the bath was the gym, the café and the office.
Hot, warm, cold
cards.body: Large public baths, thermae, had hot, warm and cold rooms: the caldarium, tepidarium and frigidarium. They were heated by the hypocaust: hot air from furnaces flowed under raised floors and through the walls.

cards.headline: Why Romans went
cards.body: Baths were social centers where Romans exercised, talked, did business and relaxed, and entry was cheap. The Baths of Caracalla, opened in the 3rd century CE, could serve about 1,600 bathers at a time.

cards.fact: Romans cleaned themselves without soap.
cards.context: Bathers oiled their skin and scraped it clean with a curved metal tool, the strigil. The oil and dirt came off together.

cards.headline: The baths: visited
learned: Baths had hot, warm and cold rooms
The hypocaust heated the floors
Baths were social centers
Bathers used oil and a strigil

questions.explanation: The caldarium was the hot room; the tepidarium was warm and the frigidarium cold.

questions.explanation: Romans exercised, talked, did business and relaxed at the baths.

levels.title: What Romans Ate
levels.objective: After this level you can describe what rich and poor Romans ate, including garum.
levels.summary: Most Romans ate grain, oil, wine and beans; the rich reclined at banquets. Almost everyone loved garum, a fermented fish sauce.

cards.headline: The Romans’ favorite sauce was made from fermented fish.
Everyday food
cards.body: Most Romans lived on grain, eaten as porridge or bread, with olive oil, wine, vegetables and beans. Street counters called thermopolia sold hot food to city dwellers, many of whom had no kitchen at home.

cards.headline: Fish sauce and feasts
cards.body: Garum, a fermented fish sauce, was one of the most popular seasonings in the Roman world. It was made in coastal factories, especially in Spain, and shipped around the empire in clay jars called amphorae. Wealthy Romans dined in the triclinium, reclining on couches around a table.

cards.fact: No Roman ever ate a tomato.
cards.context: Tomatoes, potatoes and maize came from the Americas more than a thousand years later. A Roman cookbook attributed to Apicius survives, full of fish sauce but no tomato.

levels.title: Latin, the Language That Lived On
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Latin spread and became the Romance languages.
levels.summary: Latin spread west with soldiers and settlers, and spoken Latin became Italian, French, Spanish, Portuguese and Romanian.

cards.headline: Rome fell, but its language is still spoken by hundreds of millions of people.
From Latium to the West
cards.body: Latin was first spoken in Latium, the region around Rome. It spread through the western provinces with soldiers, settlers and officials, while Greek stayed the common language of the East.

cards.headline: Latin’s children
cards.body: Everyday spoken Latin, often called Vulgar Latin, gradually developed into the Romance languages: Italian, French, Spanish, Portuguese and Romanian. English is not one of them, but a large share of its vocabulary comes from Latin, much of it through French.

cards.fact: Latin outlived the empire that spread it.
cards.context: It remained the language of the Western Church, law and scholarship for centuries after the Western Empire fell. Romanian descends from the Latin spoken in the province of Dacia.

cards.headline: Latin: still alive

levels.title: Roman Women
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the rights and roles of Roman women, and their limits.
levels.summary: Roman women couldn’t vote or hold office, and early law gave them male guardians. Yet many owned property, ran businesses and wielded influence.

cards.headline: She couldn’t vote, but she might own a business and advise an emperor.
Limits
cards.body: Roman women could not vote or hold political office. Under early Roman law a woman needed a male guardian for legal matters, though the rule weakened over time. Girls were often married in their early to mid teens, usually to older men.

cards.headline: Wealth and influence
cards.body: Many Roman women owned property, ran businesses and inherited wealth. Livia, the wife of Augustus, was one of the most influential people in Rome. Women also served as priestesses: the Vestal Virgins tended the sacred fire of Vesta.

cards.fact: Julius Caesar’s daughter was simply called Julia.
cards.context: Roman daughters usually took a feminine form of the family name, so sisters could share the same name.

levels.title: Checkpoint: Everyday Rome
levels.objective: After this level you can connect housing, work, food, entertainment and religion into a picture of daily life.
levels.summary: Cramped homes pushed Roman life into public spaces. Patrons, household gods, free grain and games held the city together.

cards.headline: Chapter 7 finale. Put a whole Roman day together.
cards.body: Where Romans lived, ate, washed, worshiped and cheered, and why so much of it happened in public.

cards.headline: Life in public
cards.body: Life in Rome combined grand public spaces, such as baths, forums and arenas, with crowded and risky housing for most people. Because homes were cramped, much of Roman life happened in public: in the streets, baths, forums and arenas.

cards.headline: The ties that bound
cards.body: Many Romans were clients of a wealthy patron, greeting him in the morning in return for help and protection. At home, households honored the Lares and Penates, guardian spirits of the home and its food.
cards.callout: Patron and client: help in return for loyalty

cards.headline: Chapter 7 complete
learned: Most Romans lived in cramped insulae
Life happened in public spaces
Clients served wealthy patrons
Grain, games and baths kept the city calm

questions.prompt: What were insulae?
questions.explanation: Insulae were apartment blocks several stories high, where most Romans lived.

questions.prompt: What did Roman law consider an enslaved person to be?

options.label: A member of the patron’s family
A soldier owed to the state

questions.explanation: Under Roman law an enslaved person was property, with no legal rights of their own.

questions.prompt: Why did so much Roman life happen in public places?

options.label: The law banned gatherings at home
Private homes were taxed by the hour

questions.explanation: With most people in small insulae, the baths, forums and streets became everyone’s living room.

questions.prompt: What did a client give a wealthy patron?

options.label: A share of every harvest by law
options.rationale: It was loyalty, not a tax.

questions.explanation: Clients greeted their patron each morning in return for help and protection.

questions.prompt: Chapter 7 recap: how did grain, games and baths help keep Rome calm?

options.label: They were paid for by the poor
They gave city people food, fun and space
They kept citizens out of the Forum
They trained citizens for the legions

questions.explanation: Free grain, games and cheap baths made life in a crowded city bearable, and won rulers popularity.

levels.title: All Roads Lead to Rome
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Roman roads were built and why they mattered.
levels.summary: Layered, drained and as straight as the land allowed, over 80,000 km of main roads carried armies first, then everyone else.

cards.headline: Some Roman roads are still in use after two thousand years.
Built in layers
cards.body: Major Roman roads were built in layers: a foundation of large stones, then gravel or rubble, topped with paving stones. They ran as straight as the ground allowed and were cambered, curved slightly, so rainwater drained off.
cards.callout: Camber: a slight curve that sheds water

cards.headline: Why roads mattered
cards.body: Roads were built first for the army, letting legions march quickly. They also carried trade, officials and the imperial post. At its height the network included more than 80,000 km of main roads.

cards.fact: The word mile comes from Rome.
cards.context: Milestones along the roads marked distances in Roman miles of 1,000 paces, mille passus in Latin.

cards.headline: The roads: traveled
learned: Roads were built in layers
They were cambered to drain rain
They served the army first
Milestones measured Roman miles

questions.prompt: Why were Roman roads cambered?

options.label: To mark the edge of each province
So carts could pass each other

questions.explanation: A slight curve let rainwater run off instead of pooling and breaking the road.

questions.prompt: Who were Roman roads built for first?

options.label: Merchants carrying grain to Rome
options.rationale: They came to use them too.

options.label: The army, to move legions quickly

questions.explanation: Roads let legions march quickly, and trade and officials followed.

questions.prompt: From Level 19: what was Rome’s first great road?
questions.explanation: The Via Appia, begun in 312 BCE, was built to move armies quickly to the south.

levels.title: Aqueducts
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how aqueducts carried water to Roman cities using gravity.
levels.summary: Aqueducts ran on a gentle downhill slope, mostly underground. By the 3rd century CE, 11 of them fed the city of Rome.

cards.headline: Rome moved rivers’ worth of water for miles with no pumps at all.
Downhill all the way
cards.body: Aqueducts carried water by gravity, along a gentle, steady downhill slope from springs in the hills. Most of an aqueduct’s length ran underground or at ground level; the famous arches carried it across valleys.

cards.headline: Water for a city
cards.body: Rome’s first aqueduct, the Aqua Appia, was built in 312 BCE by Appius Claudius. By the 3rd century CE, 11 aqueducts supplied the city, feeding fountains and the great public baths. Frontinus, Rome’s water commissioner around 97 CE, wrote a book about them.

cards.fact: The Pont du Gard still stands in southern France.
cards.context: This three-tier aqueduct bridge rises about 49 m above the river it crosses.

cards.headline: Water: delivered
learned: Aqueducts ran on gravity
Most of their length was hidden
Rome’s first was built in 312 BCE
11 aqueducts fed Rome

questions.prompt: What moved water through a Roman aqueduct?
questions.explanation: Aqueducts ran on a gentle, steady downhill slope, so gravity did the work.

questions.prompt: Why did aqueducts need arches in some places?

options.label: To show off the emperor’s wealth
To keep the slope steady across valleys
To hold up the city walls

questions.explanation: Arches carried the channel across dips in the land, keeping the gentle slope unbroken.

questions.prompt: From Level 19: Appius Claudius built Rome’s first aqueduct. What else did he begin?
questions.explanation: Appius Claudius began both the Aqua Appia and the Via Appia in 312 BCE.

levels.title: Roman Concrete
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what made Roman concrete so durable.
levels.summary: Lime and volcanic ash made a concrete that set underwater and shaped domes. Lumps of lime even helped it heal its own cracks.

cards.headline: Some Roman harbor walls have stood in seawater for two thousand years.
Ash and lime
cards.body: Roman concrete mixed lime with volcanic ash, called pozzolana, and chunks of rock or brick. Pozzolana is named after Pozzuoli, near Naples, where the ash was dug. Concrete made with it could set even underwater, which let Romans build harbors in the sea.
cards.callout: Pozzolana: volcanic ash from near Naples

cards.headline: New shapes
cards.body: Concrete let Romans build arches, vaults and domes on a scale never seen before. Walls were usually faced with brick or stone, so the concrete core was hidden from view.

cards.fact: Roman concrete could repair itself.
cards.context: A 2023 study found that lumps of lime in the mix could react with water seeping into cracks and seal them.

cards.headline: Concrete: set
learned: Concrete mixed lime and volcanic ash
It set underwater
It made domes and vaults possible
Lime lumps helped seal cracks

questions.prompt: What volcanic ingredient went into Roman concrete?
questions.explanation: Roman concrete mixed lime with volcanic ash called pozzolana.

questions.prompt: Why could Romans build harbors out in the sea?

options.label: They drained the sea with pumps

questions.explanation: Concrete made with volcanic ash set even underwater.

questions.prompt: From Level 46: Augustus boasted he found Rome a city of brick and left it a city of what?
questions.explanation: Augustus claimed he left Rome a city of marble; much of it was marble facing over concrete and brick.

levels.title: The Pantheon
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the Pantheon and its record-breaking dome.
levels.summary: Hadrian’s Pantheon has the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world, lit only by its oculus. As a church it survived intact.

cards.headline: The largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world was built by the Romans.
A perfect sphere
cards.body: Pantheon means “of all the gods.” Its dome, about 43 m across, is still the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world. The height from the floor to the top of the dome equals its diameter, so a complete sphere would fit inside.

cards.headline: Light and lightness
cards.body: An open hole at the top, the oculus, about 8 m wide, is the building’s only source of natural light. The dome gets thinner toward the top, and lighter stone was mixed into the concrete higher up.
cards.callout: Oculus: the open “eye” at the top

cards.fact: The Pantheon survived by changing religion.
cards.context: In 609 CE it became a Christian church, which helped it survive intact while other temples were stripped.

cards.headline: The Pantheon: entered
learned: Pantheon means “of all the gods”
Its 43 m dome is still a record
The oculus is its only light
It survived as a church

questions.prompt: What does the name Pantheon mean?
questions.explanation: Pantheon means “of all the gods.”

questions.prompt: Why was the Pantheon’s dome made lighter toward the top?

options.label: To reduce the weight pressing down on it
Because the builders ran out of stone

questions.explanation: A thinner dome with lighter stone higher up puts less weight on the structure below.

questions.prompt: From Level 59: which emperor rebuilt the Pantheon as it stands today?

options.label: Augustus
options.rationale: His friend Agrippa built the first one.

questions.explanation: Hadrian rebuilt the Pantheon first built by Agrippa.

levels.title: Running the Provinces
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how governors, taxes and local elites ran the provinces.
levels.summary: Governors ran provinces, split by Augustus between the Senate and himself. Taxes came from a census, and local elites did most of the work.

cards.headline: Rome ran an empire of millions with a surprisingly small staff.
Governors and taxes
cards.body: Augustus split the provinces: peaceful ones had governors chosen by the Senate, while frontier provinces with armies were run by his own deputies. Provinces paid taxes on land and on people, and a census counted them for taxation.

cards.headline: Local help
cards.body: Rome ran its provinces with few officials, relying on local elites to govern their own cities and collect taxes. In the Republic, tax collection had often been contracted out to private companies of publicani, who were notorious for abuses.

cards.fact: Pontius Pilate was a provincial governor.
cards.context: He was the Roman prefect who governed Judaea from 26 to 36 CE.

cards.headline: The provinces: run
learned: Governors ran the provinces
Augustus kept the armed provinces
A census set the taxes
Local elites did most of the governing

questions.prompt: Who collected taxes for Rome in many Republican provinces?
questions.explanation: Tax collection was often contracted out to publicani, notorious for abuses.

questions.prompt: Why did Augustus keep the frontier provinces for himself?

options.label: That was where the armies were
The Senate refused to govern them

questions.explanation: Frontier provinces held the legions, and controlling them meant controlling the army.

questions.prompt: From Level 30: which was Rome’s first province?
questions.explanation: Rome’s provinces began with Sicily, taken after the First Punic War.

levels.title: Becoming Roman
levels.objective: After this level you can explain Roman citizenship and how it spread to all free people in 212.
levels.summary: Citizenship brought legal privileges. It spread to Italy, then to towns, soldiers and individuals, until Caracalla gave it to almost all free people in 212 CE.

cards.headline: In 212 CE, millions of people became Roman citizens on the same day.
What citizenship meant
cards.body: Roman citizens had legal privileges, such as the right to appeal to Rome and protection from certain punishments. According to the Book of Acts, Paul of Tarsus, a Roman citizen, used his right to appeal to the emperor.

cards.headline: How it spread
cards.body: After the Social War of 91–88 BCE, Rome granted citizenship to its Italian allies. It then spread through the provinces by grants to towns, individuals and soldiers. Non-citizen soldiers, the auxiliaries, received it after about 25 years of service.

cards.fact: In 212 CE Caracalla made almost every free person a citizen.
cards.context: After centuries of gradual grants, being Roman became a status shared across the whole empire.

cards.headline: Citizenship: granted
learned: Citizens had legal privileges
Italians gained citizenship after 88 BCE
Auxiliaries earned it by service
Caracalla extended it in 212 CE

questions.prompt: Which emperor granted citizenship to almost all free people in 212 CE?
questions.explanation: Caracalla’s grant of 212 CE made almost all free inhabitants citizens.

questions.prompt: How could an auxiliary soldier become a citizen?

options.label: By paying a fee in Rome

questions.explanation: Auxiliaries, non-citizen soldiers, received citizenship after about 25 years of service.

questions.prompt: From Level 62: how else could an enslaved person become a citizen?

options.label: By being freed by a Roman citizen
By fighting well in the arena
By moving to the city of Rome
By learning to read and write Latin

questions.explanation: A person freed by a Roman citizen usually became a citizen.

levels.title: Roman Law
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the key ideas of Roman law and how they reached modern legal systems.
levels.summary: Jurists developed Roman law for a thousand years after the Twelve Tables. Justinian’s code carried it into the law of much of the world.

cards.headline: If you live in France, Brazil or Japan, your law has Roman roots.
Lawyers who shaped the law
cards.body: Roman legal experts, the jurists, wrote opinions that developed and explained the law. They held, for example, that the burden of proof rests on the person who makes a claim, not on the one who denies it.
cards.callout: Burden of proof: whoever claims must prove

cards.headline: Justinian’s code
cards.body: In the 6th century CE the emperor Justinian had Roman law collected into the Corpus Juris Civilis, the “body of civil law.” It shaped the civil law systems used across continental Europe, Latin America and many other countries.

cards.fact: English law still speaks Latin.
cards.context: Many legal terms are Latin words, such as alibi, which means “elsewhere.”

cards.headline: The law: laid down
learned: Jurists developed Roman law
The claimant bears the burden of proof
Justinian’s code collected the law
Civil law systems grew from it

questions.prompt: Which emperor had Roman law collected into the Corpus Juris Civilis?
questions.explanation: Justinian had Roman law collected in the 6th century CE.

questions.prompt: Under the Roman rule on burden of proof, who must prove a claim?
questions.explanation: The burden of proof rests on whoever makes the claim, not on the one who denies it.

questions.prompt: From Level 15: when did Rome first write down its laws, in the Twelve Tables?
questions.explanation: Around 450 BCE Rome wrote down its laws in the Twelve Tables, displayed in the Forum.

levels.title: Money and Trade
levels.objective: After this level you can describe Roman coins, trade routes and the economy of the Mediterranean.
levels.summary: The silver denarius carried the emperor’s face everywhere. Amphorae carried wine, oil and fish sauce, and traders reached India.

cards.headline: In Rome there is a hill made entirely of broken jars.
Coins with a message
cards.body: The denarius, a silver coin, was the standard Roman coin for centuries. Coins carried the emperor’s portrait and short messages, spreading his image across the empire. Over time emperors reduced the silver in the denarius, and by the 3rd century CE it held very little.

cards.headline: Goods on the move
cards.body: Wine, olive oil and fish sauce moved around the Mediterranean in amphorae, clay jars made for shipping. Roman traders sailed to India, and Chinese silk reached Rome through many middlemen along the Silk Road.

cards.fact: Monte Testaccio is an artificial hill.
cards.context: It is made of fragments of millions of broken olive oil amphorae, dumped in Rome after their oil was used.

cards.headline: Trade: mapped
learned: The denarius was Rome’s silver coin
Coins spread the emperor’s image
Amphorae carried oil, wine and garum
Trade reached India and China

questions.prompt: What was the denarius?
questions.explanation: The denarius was the standard silver coin of Rome for centuries.

questions.prompt: Why did emperors put their portraits on coins?

options.label: To prove the coins were gold
Because the law required a face
To spread their image across the empire

questions.explanation: Coins passed through countless hands, carrying the emperor’s face and messages everywhere.

questions.prompt: From Level 67: which fish sauce was shipped around the empire in amphorae?
questions.explanation: Garum was made in coastal factories, especially in Spain, and shipped in amphorae.

levels.title: Life on the Frontier
levels.objective: After this level you can describe forts, soldiers and communities on the Roman frontier.
levels.summary: Auxiliaries held standard forts along the limes. Towns grew beside them, and the Vindolanda tablets let us read their letters.

cards.headline: At a fort in northern Britain, a commander’s wife sent a birthday invitation.
Forts on the limes
cards.body: The fortified frontier of the empire was called the limes. Much of it was held by auxiliaries, non-citizen soldiers recruited from the provinces. Forts followed a standard plan: a rectangle with rounded corners, four gates and a headquarters building at the center.

cards.headline: Towns beside the forts
cards.body: Civilian settlements grew up beside frontier forts, with traders, craftsmen and soldiers’ families. On Hadrian’s Wall, small forts stood about every Roman mile.

cards.fact: We can read letters written on the frontier.
cards.context: At Vindolanda, near Hadrian’s Wall, archaeologists found hundreds of wooden writing tablets, including a birthday invitation from one commander’s wife to another.

cards.headline: The frontier: held
learned: The limes was the fortified frontier
Auxiliaries held much of it
Towns grew beside the forts
Vindolanda preserved frontier letters

questions.prompt: What was the limes?
questions.explanation: The limes was the fortified frontier of the empire.

questions.prompt: Why are the Vindolanda tablets so valuable?

options.label: They list every emperor in order
They are the only Latin writing found

questions.explanation: Letters like a birthday invitation reveal ordinary life that official histories leave out.

questions.prompt: From Level 76: what did auxiliaries receive after about 25 years of service?
questions.explanation: Non-citizen auxiliaries received Roman citizenship after about 25 years.

levels.title: Checkpoint: How Rome Held an Empire
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how roads, law, citizenship, the army and trade held the empire together.
levels.summary: Roads, a shared army, citizenship, law and trade held the empire together, and Roman ways spread through the provinces.

cards.headline: Chapter 8 finale. How do you hold together an empire from Britain to Egypt?
cards.body: Not with soldiers alone. Here is the rest of the answer.

cards.headline: More than force
cards.body: Rome held its empire together with roads, a shared army, citizenship, law and trade, not by force alone. Local elites ran their own cities, and in 212 CE almost every free person became a citizen.

cards.headline: Becoming Roman
cards.body: Historians call the spread of Roman language, culture and ways of life in the provinces Romanization. Towns across the West built forums, baths and amphitheaters on the Roman model. Latin spread across the West with soldiers, settlers and officials.

cards.headline: Chapter 8 complete
learned: Roads, army, law and trade held the empire
Local elites ran their cities
Citizenship spread to nearly all
Romanization spread Roman ways

questions.prompt: What did Roman milestones measure?
questions.explanation: Milestones marked distances in Roman miles of 1,000 paces.

questions.prompt: What happened in 212 CE?

options.label: Rome was sacked by the Gothic army
Almost all free people became citizens
Hadrian’s Wall was begun in the north

questions.explanation: In 212 CE Caracalla granted citizenship to almost all free inhabitants.

questions.prompt: How did Rome govern so much with so few officials?

options.label: Local elites ran their own cities
Every province had a legion in each town
The emperor visited every city yearly

questions.explanation: Rome relied on local elites to govern their cities and collect taxes.

questions.prompt: What is Romanization?

options.label: The conquest of Italy by Rome
The spread of Roman roads only

questions.explanation: Romanization is the spread of Roman language, culture and ways of life in the provinces.

questions.prompt: Chapter 8 recap: which pair did most to bind the empire’s peoples to Rome?

options.label: Gladiator games and chariot races
options.rationale: They entertained, but didn’t bind the provinces.

options.label: Aqueducts and baths
options.rationale: They served cities, not the whole empire.

questions.explanation: Citizenship and a shared law gave provincials a stake in Rome, alongside roads, trade and the army.

levels.title: The Crisis of the Third Century
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the chaos of the third century, when emperors rose and fell rapidly.
levels.summary: From 235 to 284 CE, more than 20 emperors came and went, an emperor was captured, and the empire split in three before Aurelian reunited it.

cards.headline: More than 20 emperors in about 50 years. Most of them were murdered.
Everything at once
cards.body: From 235 to 284 CE, the Crisis of the Third Century, the empire suffered civil wars, invasions, plague and economic trouble. Emperors had reduced the silver in the denarius until it held very little, and prices soared.

cards.headline: An emperor in chains
cards.body: In 260 CE the emperor Valerian was captured by the Persian king Shapur I, the only Roman emperor taken prisoner by a foreign enemy. For a time the empire split into three, with a Gallic Empire in the west and Palmyra under Queen Zenobia in the east.

cards.fact: Aurelian put the pieces back together.
cards.context: In the 270s he reunited the empire and built new walls around Rome itself.

cards.headline: The crisis: survived
learned: The crisis ran from 235 to 284 CE
More than 20 emperors ruled
Valerian was captured by Persia
Aurelian reunited the empire

questions.prompt: Which emperor was captured by the Persians in 260 CE?
questions.explanation: Valerian was captured by Shapur I, the only emperor taken prisoner by a foreign enemy.

questions.prompt: Why did prices soar during the crisis?

options.label: Coins held less and less silver

questions.explanation: Emperors cut the silver in the denarius, so each coin was worth less and prices rose.

questions.prompt: From Level 55: what had 69 CE revealed that the third century showed again?

options.label: Emperors had to be born in Rome
Armies could make and unmake emperors

questions.explanation: In both periods, armies raised their own commanders to the throne and removed others.

levels.title: Diocletian Divides the Empire
levels.objective: After this level you can explain Diocletian's reforms and the Tetrarchy.
levels.summary: Diocletian ended the crisis in 284 CE with four emperors, smaller provinces and price controls, then retired to his palace at Split.

cards.headline: One emperor wasn’t enough. Diocletian tried four.
Rule of four
cards.body: Diocletian became emperor in 284 CE and ended the half century of crisis. He created the Tetrarchy, “rule of four”: two senior emperors, called Augusti, and two junior ones, called Caesars. It was meant to put an emperor near every threatened frontier and give the empire a planned succession.
cards.callout: Tetrarchy: two Augusti and two Caesars

cards.headline: Reforms
cards.body: Diocletian split the provinces into smaller units and separated civil from military command. In 301 CE his Edict on Maximum Prices tried, and failed, to stop inflation by fixing prices.

cards.fact: Diocletian did what no emperor had done: he retired.
cards.context: In 305 CE he stepped down voluntarily and moved to his palace at Split, in modern Croatia.

cards.headline: The Tetrarchy: formed
learned: Diocletian ruled from 284 CE
The Tetrarchy meant four emperors
He split the provinces
He retired in 305 CE

questions.prompt: What was the Tetrarchy?

options.label: A tax paid in four parts

questions.explanation: The Tetrarchy was rule by two senior Augusti and two junior Caesars.

questions.prompt: Why did Diocletian want more than one emperor?

options.label: To have an emperor near every frontier
To let the Senate choose between them
To divide the tax money evenly
options.rationale: The aim was defense and succession.

options.label: To avoid ever living in Rome
options.rationale: The aim was defense and succession.

questions.explanation: Threats came on several frontiers at once, so several emperors could respond.

questions.prompt: From Level 51: which old problem did the Tetrarchy also try to fix?

options.label: The shortage of grain in Rome
The lack of a law of succession

questions.explanation: Rome had never had a fixed law of succession; the Tetrarchy planned who would rise next.

levels.title: The First Christians
levels.objective: After this level you can describe how Christianity began and spread through the Roman world.
levels.summary: Jesus was crucified in Judaea under Pilate. Paul and others carried the faith to the cities of the empire along Roman roads.

cards.headline: A faith from a small province spread along roads that Rome had built.
From Judaea
cards.body: Jesus of Nazareth was a Jewish teacher executed by crucifixion in Judaea under the Roman governor Pontius Pilate, who governed Judaea from 26 to 36 CE. Paul of Tarsus spread Christianity to non-Jews in cities around the eastern Mediterranean.

cards.headline: How it spread
cards.body: Christianity spread mainly in cities, helped by Roman roads, peace and the common Greek language of the East. Christians worshiped one God and refused to sacrifice to the Roman gods or to the emperor.

cards.fact: Early churches looked after their own.
cards.context: Christian communities were led by bishops and cared for their poor, widows and sick, even when the faith itself was under attack.

cards.headline: The faith: spreading
learned: Jesus was crucified under Pilate
Paul spread the faith to non-Jews
It grew in cities along Roman roads
Christians refused to sacrifice

questions.prompt: In which province was Jesus crucified?

options.label: Gaul
options.rationale: He was executed in the East.

options.label: Dacia
options.rationale: He was executed in the East.

questions.explanation: Jesus was crucified in Judaea under the governor Pontius Pilate.

questions.prompt: What helped Christianity spread through the empire?

options.label: It was carried only by the legions
Roman roads, peace and a shared language

questions.explanation: Roads, the Pax Romana and common Greek let the new faith travel between cities.

questions.prompt: From Level 75: which Roman official governed Judaea when Jesus was executed?
questions.explanation: Pontius Pilate was the Roman prefect of Judaea from 26 to 36 CE.

levels.title: Persecution
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why and when Christians were persecuted by the Roman state.
levels.summary: Persecution was local and sporadic until Decius in 250 CE. Diocletian’s Great Persecution from 303 CE was the harshest.

cards.headline: Why would a tolerant empire of many gods persecute one group?
Why Christians were targeted
cards.body: Refusing to sacrifice to the gods and the emperor looked like disloyalty, and Romans feared it would break the peace with the gods. For most of the first two centuries, though, persecution was local and sporadic, not constant.

cards.headline: Empire-wide
cards.body: In 250 CE the emperor Decius ordered everyone in the empire to sacrifice to the gods, the first empire-wide persecution. The Great Persecution under Diocletian, from 303 CE, was the harshest the Christians faced.

cards.fact: Trajan told a governor not to hunt Christians.
cards.context: When Pliny the Younger asked for advice, Trajan replied that they should not be sought out, but punished if accused and they refused to recant. Those who died were honored as martyrs, from a Greek word meaning “witness.”

cards.headline: Persecution: understood
learned: Refusing sacrifice looked disloyal
Persecution was local at first
Decius made it empire-wide in 250 CE
Diocletian’s was the harshest

questions.prompt: Which emperor ordered the first empire-wide persecution, in 250 CE?

options.label: Nero
options.rationale: His persecution was in Rome only.

options.label: Trajan
options.rationale: He said not to hunt Christians.

questions.explanation: Decius ordered everyone in the empire to sacrifice to the gods in 250 CE.

questions.prompt: Why did refusing to sacrifice seem dangerous to Romans?

options.label: Sacrifices paid for the army
options.rationale: The fear was religious and political.

options.label: It risked the peace with the gods
It broke the Twelve Tables
options.rationale: The fear was religious and political.

options.label: Temples would lose their land
options.rationale: The fear was religious and political.

questions.explanation: Romans believed correct rituals kept the pax deorum, so refusing looked disloyal and dangerous.

questions.prompt: From Level 54: which emperor blamed Rome’s Christians for the Great Fire?
questions.explanation: Nero blamed the Christians in Rome for the fire of 64 CE and had many executed.

levels.title: Constantine
levels.objective: After this level you can explain Constantine's rise and his support for Christianity.
levels.summary: Constantine won at the Milvian Bridge in 312 CE, gave Christians tolerance in 313, ruled alone from 324 and called the Council of Nicaea.

cards.headline: Ten years after the Great Persecution began, Christians were free to worship.
The Milvian Bridge
cards.body: In 312 CE Constantine defeated his rival Maxentius at the Milvian Bridge outside Rome. Christian writers said he saw a sign before the battle and had his soldiers fight under a Christian symbol. By 324 CE he had defeated his last rival and ruled the whole empire alone.

cards.headline: A Christian-friendly emperor
cards.body: In 313 CE the Edict of Milan granted religious tolerance to Christians throughout the empire. In 325 CE Constantine called the Council of Nicaea, a meeting of bishops that agreed a common statement of Christian belief.

cards.fact: Constantine was baptized only on his deathbed.
cards.context: He supported the church for most of his reign, but was baptized in 337 CE, as he was dying.

cards.headline: Constantine: crowned
learned: Constantine won at the Milvian Bridge in 312 CE
The Edict of Milan came in 313 CE
He ruled alone from 324 CE
He called the Council of Nicaea

questions.prompt: What did the Edict of Milan grant in 313 CE?

options.label: A new capital in the East

questions.explanation: The Edict of Milan granted religious tolerance to Christians throughout the empire.

questions.prompt: Why was the Council of Nicaea important?

options.label: It ended the Tetrarchy by imperial law
Bishops agreed a shared statement of belief
It moved the Senate to the eastern capital

questions.explanation: In 325 CE the bishops at Nicaea agreed a common statement of Christian belief.

questions.prompt: From Level 84: the Great Persecution began in 303 CE under which emperor?
questions.explanation: Diocletian’s Great Persecution began in 303 CE; the Edict of Milan came just ten years later.

levels.title: Constantinople
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why Constantine founded a new capital on the Bosporus.
levels.summary: In 330 CE Constantine dedicated a new Rome on the Bosporus, closer to the frontiers and between two continents. Today it is Istanbul.

cards.headline: Constantine built a second Rome where Europe meets Asia.
A new capital
cards.body: Constantine dedicated his new capital, Constantinople, on the site of the Greek city of Byzantium in 330 CE. It stood on the Bosporus, the strait between Europe and Asia, controlling the route between the Black Sea and the Mediterranean.
cards.callout: Bosporus: the strait between Europe and Asia

cards.headline: Why move?
cards.body: The new capital was closer than Rome to the threatened Danube and eastern frontiers. It was built as a new Rome, with its own senate, forums and a great hippodrome for chariot racing.

cards.fact: Constantinople is today Istanbul.
cards.context: The city Constantine founded still spans the Bosporus, with districts in both Europe and Asia.

cards.headline: The new Rome: founded
learned: Constantinople was dedicated in 330 CE
It stood on the Bosporus
It was nearer the frontiers
It is Istanbul today

questions.explanation: Constantinople was built on the site of Byzantium.

options.label: It was nearer the threatened frontiers
The Senate refused to meet in Rome
options.rationale: He built a new senate too.

questions.explanation: Constantinople was closer to the Danube and eastern frontiers, where the threats were.

questions.prompt: From Level 65: which riot of racing fans later broke out in Constantinople?
questions.explanation: In 532 CE Blues and Greens rioted in Constantinople in the Nika revolt.

levels.title: Julian the Apostate
levels.objective: After this level you can describe Julian's attempt to restore the old religion.
levels.summary: Constantine’s nephew Julian tried to bring back the old gods in 361 CE. He died in Persia in 363, and his program died with him.

cards.headline: One emperor tried to turn the clock back to the old gods.
The last pagan emperor
cards.body: Julian, Constantine’s nephew, became sole emperor in 361 CE. He rejected Christianity and tried to restore worship of the traditional gods. He was the last Roman emperor to follow the old gods.

cards.headline: A short reign
cards.body: Christians called him Julian the Apostate: an apostate is someone who abandons their faith. He was killed on campaign against Persia in 363 CE, and his religious program died with him.
cards.callout: Apostate: someone who abandons their faith

cards.fact: Julian banned Christians from teaching classical literature.
cards.context: He wanted the old poets and philosophers taught only by people who still honored the old gods themselves.

cards.headline: Julian: remembered
learned: Julian became sole emperor in 361 CE
He tried to restore the old gods
Christians called him the Apostate
He died in Persia in 363 CE

questions.prompt: What did Julian try to restore?
questions.explanation: Julian rejected Christianity and tried to restore the traditional gods.

options.label: He died after a very short reign

questions.explanation: Julian was killed in Persia in 363 CE, and his successors did not continue his program.

questions.prompt: From Level 85: what had Constantine granted Christians in 313 CE?
questions.explanation: The Edict of Milan granted Christians religious tolerance.

levels.title: A Christian Empire
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Christianity became the empire's official religion under Theodosius.
levels.summary: In 380 CE Theodosius made Nicene Christianity the official religion; in the 390s temples closed. After his death in 395 the empire split.

cards.headline: Within a lifetime of the Great Persecution, Christianity became the law.
The official religion
cards.body: In 380 CE, under Theodosius I, Nicene Christianity became the official religion of the empire. In the 390s he banned sacrifices and closed temples. The sacred fire of Vesta was put out and the Vestal Virgins disbanded.

cards.headline: Church and emperor
cards.body: Bishop Ambrose of Milan made Theodosius do public penance for a massacre at Thessalonica, showing the church’s new power. Theodosius was the last emperor to rule both halves of the empire; after his death in 395 CE it was divided between his two sons.

cards.fact: The ancient Olympics ended in a Christian empire.
cards.context: They are traditionally said to have ended in 393 CE under Theodosius.

cards.headline: A Christian empire: established
learned: Christianity became official in 380 CE
Temples closed in the 390s
Ambrose humbled Theodosius
The empire split in 395 CE

options.label: Julian
options.rationale: He tried to restore the old gods.

questions.explanation: In 380 CE, under Theodosius I, Nicene Christianity became the official religion.

options.label: The emperor could appoint any bishop
The church could now challenge an emperor
The old gods still ruled Rome

questions.prompt: From Level 7: what did the Vestal Virgins tend until the 390s?
questions.explanation: The Vestals tended Vesta’s sacred fire, which was put out in the 390s.

levels.title: Disaster at Adrianople
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the Gothic victory at Adrianople and why it mattered.
levels.summary: Goths fleeing the Huns crossed the Danube in 376 CE, rebelled against mistreatment and destroyed a Roman army at Adrianople in 378.

cards.headline: In 378 CE a Roman emperor died on the battlefield against the Goths.
Refugees become rebels
cards.body: The Huns, nomadic horsemen from the Eurasian steppes, were pushing west and driving other peoples before them. In 376 CE Goths fleeing the Huns were allowed to cross the Danube into the empire. Mistreated and exploited by Roman officials, they rebelled.

cards.headline: The battle
cards.body: At Adrianople in 378 CE the Goths destroyed a Roman army, and the emperor Valens was killed. Gothic cavalry arriving during the battle played a decisive part in the Roman defeat.

cards.fact: Afterwards, the Goths stayed.
cards.context: Gothic groups settled inside the empire as allies under their own leaders, a new and risky arrangement for Rome.

questions.explanation: Refugees exploited by Roman officials turned into rebels.

questions.explanation: Varus lost three legions in the Teutoburg Forest; Adrianople was an even worse disaster.

levels.title: Checkpoint: A Changed Empire
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how the empire of 395 differed from the empire of Augustus.
levels.summary: By 395 CE the empire was Christian, ruled by distant monarchs, split in two and defended partly by Goths under their own leaders.

cards.headline: Chapter 9 finale. Would Augustus have recognized the empire of 395?
cards.body: Four changes that made the late empire a different world.

cards.headline: A different empire
cards.body: By 395 CE the empire was Christian, divided into East and West, and defended partly by Germanic allies under their own leaders. It had two capitals, Rome and Constantinople. After Theodosius died in 395 CE, his two sons divided it between them.

cards.headline: Lord, not first citizen
cards.body: Augustus had called himself princeps, “first citizen.” Later emperors ruled more openly as absolute monarchs, surrounded by elaborate court ceremony. Historians sometimes call this the Dominate, from dominus, “lord.”
cards.callout: Dominate: rule by a lord, not a first citizen

It returned to the old gods

From monarch to first citizen

The Senate refused to leave Rome

levels.title: Your Cosmic Address
levels.objective: After this level you can state Earth's address: third planet from the Sun, a star in the Milky Way.
levels.summary: The Sun is a star, Earth is planet three, and our whole solar system lives in the Milky Way.

cards.headline: Every star you see at night is a sun. Ours is just the closest one.
cards.body: The Sun isn't a special kind of object. It's a star, and the nearest one to Earth. The others only look like dots because they're unimaginably farther away.

cards.headline: Your address, zoomed out
cards.body: Start with Earth. It's the third of eight planets orbiting the Sun. The Sun and everything orbiting it make up our solar system.
cards.callout: Earth → planet 3 → the Sun's solar system

cards.fact: Sunlight takes about 8 minutes to reach Earth.
cards.context: So when you look at the Sun (please don't, directly), you're seeing it as it was roughly eight minutes ago.

cards.headline: Now zoom out much, much further
cards.body: The Sun is one of at least 100 billion stars in the Milky Way, a barred spiral galaxy. That faint band across a dark sky? That's our own galaxy, seen from the inside.

cards.headline: Cosmic address: unlocked
learned: The Sun is a star, the closest one
Earth is the third of eight planets
Sunlight is about 8 minutes old when it arrives
Our solar system lives in the Milky Way

questions.prompt: Counting outward from the Sun, which planet is Earth?
questions.explanation: Mercury, Venus, then Earth: third of the eight planets.

options.label: One star among many in the Milky Way
The center of the Milky Way
options.rationale: The Sun orbits within the Milky Way; it isn't its center.

options.rationale: Planets reflect light; the Sun is a star that makes its own.

options.label: The only star in our galaxy
options.rationale: The Milky Way has at least 100 billion stars.

questions.explanation: The Sun is an ordinary star, one of at least 100 billion in the Milky Way.

levels.title: The Sun, Up Close
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what powers the Sun and how dominant it is in the solar system.
levels.summary: The Sun fuses hydrogen into helium, holds 99.8% of the solar system's mass, and is about 4.6 billion years old.

cards.headline: The Sun isn't on fire. It's doing something far stranger.
cards.body: There's no burning in the everyday sense. Deep in its core, the Sun squeezes atoms together.

cards.headline: Nuclear fusion
cards.body: At about 15 million °C, the Sun's core squeezes hydrogen atoms so hard that they fuse into helium. Each fusion releases a little energy, and trillions of them every second add up to the sunlight that reaches you.

cards.fact: The Sun holds about 99.8% of the solar system's mass.
cards.context: Every planet, moon, asteroid and comet together makes up the remaining 0.2%. We're the crumbs.

cards.headline: Middle-aged, not old
cards.body: The Sun formed about 4.6 billion years ago. That sounds ancient, but for a star like ours it's roughly the middle of its life. There's plenty of hydrogen left in its core to keep the fusion going for billions of years more.

cards.headline: Sun: understood
learned: Fusion turns hydrogen into helium in the core
The core is about 15 million °C
The Sun is 99.8% of the solar system's mass
It's about 4.6 billion years old

questions.prompt: What powers the Sun?

options.label: Burning gas, like a campfire
options.rationale: There's no combustion; the Sun has no oxygen fire.

options.label: Heat left over from its formation
options.rationale: Leftover heat would have run out long ago.

options.label: Reflected light from other stars
options.rationale: The Sun makes its own light.

questions.explanation: In its core, the Sun fuses hydrogen into helium, releasing enormous energy.

questions.prompt: Why is it misleading to say the Sun is "on fire"?

options.label: Its energy comes from nuclear fusion, not burning
It's actually cold on the inside
It only reflects light from other stars
options.rationale: The Sun makes its own light.

options.label: It has no fuel left
options.rationale: It has billions of years of hydrogen left.

questions.explanation: Fire is a chemical reaction that needs oxygen. The Sun's energy comes from nuclear fusion: hydrogen atoms fusing into helium under enormous heat and pressure.

questions.prompt: From Level 1: what kind of object is the Sun?

options.label: A planet
options.rationale: Planets don't make their own light.

options.label: A galaxy
options.rationale: A galaxy contains billions of stars.

options.label: A nebula
options.rationale: A nebula is a cloud of gas and dust.

questions.explanation: The Sun is a star, and it's the closest one to Earth.

levels.title: The Rocky Four
levels.objective: After this level you can name the rocky planets and explain why Venus, not Mercury, is the hottest.
levels.summary: Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars are rocky. Venus is the hottest planet thanks to its heat-trapping atmosphere, and Mars is red because of rust.

cards.headline: Mercury is closest to the Sun. So why is Venus hotter?
The inner planets are rocky
cards.body: Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars are small worlds of rock and metal. You could, in principle, stand on any of them. You wouldn't enjoy most of them.

cards.headline: Venus: a runaway greenhouse
cards.body: Venus is wrapped in a thick carbon dioxide atmosphere that traps heat. Its surface is over 450 °C, hotter than Mercury, even though Mercury is closer to the Sun.

cards.fact: Mars is red because it's rusty.
cards.context: Iron oxide (the same stuff as rust) coats Martian dust and rocks, and fine red dust in its thin atmosphere tints the whole planet.

cards.headline: Inner solar system: mapped
learned: Four rocky planets: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars
Venus is the hottest planet
Its CO₂ atmosphere traps heat
Mars gets its red color from iron oxide

questions.prompt: Which of these is NOT one of the rocky inner planets?

options.label: Jupiter
options.rationale: Correct: Jupiter is a gas giant.

questions.explanation: The rocky inner planets are Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars. Jupiter is a gas giant.

questions.prompt: Why is Venus hotter than Mercury?

options.label: Venus is closer to the Sun
Venus has active volcanoes on its whole surface
options.rationale: Volcanism isn't what keeps it so hot.

questions.explanation: Venus's thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat, making it the hottest planet despite being second from the Sun.

options.label: Jupiter

levels.title: Giants of the Outer Dark
levels.objective: After this level you can tell gas giants from ice giants and describe Jupiter's and Saturn's standout features.
levels.summary: Jupiter and Saturn are gas giants, Uranus and Neptune are ice giants. Jupiter outweighs every other planet combined, and Saturn's rings are mostly ice.

cards.headline: Past Mars, the planets stop being rocky and start being enormous.

items.label: Gas giants
points: No solid surface to stand on

items.label: Ice giants
points: Rich in water, ammonia and methane 'ices'

cards.fact: Jupiter has more than twice the mass of all the other planets combined.
cards.context: If the planets were a team, Jupiter would be carrying it.

cards.headline: Saturn's rings are ice
cards.body: Those famous rings aren't solid. They're countless chunks of water ice, with some rock, ranging from dust-sized grains to pieces as big as houses. Each chunk orbits Saturn on its own path, like a tiny moon.

cards.headline: Outer solar system: mapped

Their rings form a solid barrier around them

levels.title: Why We Have Seasons
levels.objective: After this level you can explain that seasons come from Earth's tilt, not its distance from the Sun.
levels.summary: Earth's axis is tilted about 23.5°. Each hemisphere takes turns leaning toward the Sun, which is why seasons are opposite north and south.

cards.headline: Most people get this one wrong: summer isn't when Earth is closest to the Sun.

cards.fact: Earth is closest to the Sun in early January.
cards.context: That's the middle of winter in the Northern Hemisphere. So distance can't be what makes summer.

cards.headline: It's the tilt
cards.body: Earth's axis is tilted about 23.5°. When your hemisphere leans toward the Sun, sunlight hits the ground more directly and days last longer, so more energy lands on each patch of ground. That's summer. Lean away, and the same sunlight arrives at a slant and spreads thin.

cards.headline: Opposite seasons
cards.body: Because the hemispheres lean opposite ways, December is winter in New York and summer in Sydney. Same planet, same distance, different lean.

cards.headline: Seasons: solved
learned: Earth's axis is tilted about 23.5°
Tilt, not distance, causes seasons
Earth is closest to the Sun in January
The hemispheres have opposite seasons

questions.prompt: What mainly causes Earth's seasons?

options.label: Earth's changing distance from the Sun
options.rationale: Earth is closest in January, during northern winter.

options.label: Changes in the Sun's brightness
options.rationale: The Sun's output is nearly constant.

options.label: The Moon's position
options.rationale: The Moon affects tides, not seasons.

questions.explanation: Earth's ~23.5° tilt changes how directly sunlight hits each hemisphere through the year.

questions.prompt: It's July. What season is it in Australia?

options.label: Summer
options.rationale: July is summer in the north, so it's winter in the south.

options.label: It depends on the distance to the Sun

questions.explanation: The hemispheres tilt opposite ways, so northern summer is southern winter.

questions.prompt: Venus is hotter than Mercury (Level 3), and northern summer happens when Earth is farther from the Sun. What do both show?

options.label: Planets closer to the Sun are always hotter
Venus causes Earth's seasons
options.rationale: Venus has no effect on our seasons.

options.label: Earth's orbit is a perfect circle
options.rationale: It's slightly oval, but that isn't the point here.

questions.explanation: Venus's atmosphere traps heat, and Earth's tilt sets the angle of sunlight. In both cases something other than distance is in charge.

levels.title: The Moon's Changing Face
levels.objective: After this level you can explain Moon phases and why we only ever see one side of the Moon.
levels.summary: Phases show how much of the Moon's sunlit half faces us, over a ~29.5-day cycle. The Moon is tidally locked, so the same side always faces Earth.

cards.headline: The Moon doesn't change shape. You're just seeing it from a different angle.
Half lit, always
cards.body: The Sun always lights up half of the Moon. As the Moon orbits Earth, we see different amounts of that lit half: a thin crescent, a half, the full face, then back again. Nothing is covering the Moon; only our viewing angle changes.
cards.callout: A full cycle takes about 29.5 days

cards.fact: We always see the same side of the Moon.
cards.context: The Moon, about 384,400 km away, is tidally locked: it turns exactly once per orbit. The far side isn't permanently dark. It gets as much sunlight as the near side; we just never see it from Earth. Its day and its month last the same time.

cards.headline: Moon: decoded
learned: Phases = how much of the lit half we see
A full phase cycle takes about 29.5 days
The Moon is tidally locked
The far side isn't always dark

questions.prompt: What causes the Moon's phases?

options.label: Earth's shadow covering part of the Moon
options.rationale: That's a lunar eclipse, a different thing entirely.

options.label: How much of the Moon's sunlit half we can see
The Moon changing its actual shape

questions.explanation: The Sun always lights half the Moon; as it orbits, we see more or less of that lit half.

questions.prompt: Why do we always see the same side of the Moon?

options.label: It rotates once for every orbit around Earth
It doesn’t rotate at all as it orbits Earth
options.rationale: It does rotate: exactly once per orbit.

options.label: Its far side is always turned toward the Sun
options.rationale: Both sides get sunlight as the Moon orbits.

options.label: Earth’s shadow always hides the far side
options.rationale: Earth’s shadow only reaches the Moon during a lunar eclipse.

questions.explanation: The Moon is tidally locked: one rotation per orbit keeps the same face toward Earth.

questions.prompt: The Moon’s phases repeat about every 29.5 days. From Level 5: what drives Earth’s yearly cycle of seasons?

options.label: Earth’s changing distance from the Sun
options.rationale: Earth is closest to the Sun in January, during northern winter.

options.label: The Moon’s phases pulling on Earth’s weather
options.rationale: The Moon’s phases don’t cause the seasons.

options.label: Earth’s tilted axis as it orbits the Sun
The Sun’s brightness rising and falling each year
options.rationale: The Sun’s output barely changes over a year.

questions.explanation: The Moon’s phases come from its orbit around Earth. The seasons come from Earth’s ~23.5° tilt as it orbits the Sun.

levels.title: Eclipses and a Cosmic Coincidence
levels.objective: After this level you can tell solar from lunar eclipses and explain why the Moon can exactly cover the Sun.
levels.summary: A solar eclipse is the Moon blocking the Sun; a lunar eclipse is Earth's shadow on the Moon. The Sun is ~400× wider and ~400× farther than the Moon.

cards.headline: By pure luck, the Moon is exactly the right size to blot out the Sun.

items.label: Solar eclipse
points: The Moon passes between the Sun and Earth
The Moon's shadow falls on Earth

items.label: Lunar eclipse
points: Earth passes between the Sun and Moon
Earth's shadow falls on the Moon

cards.fact: The Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon, and about 400 times farther away.
cards.context: Those two numbers cancel out, so the Sun and Moon look almost exactly the same size in our sky. That's why, during a total solar eclipse, the Moon can cover the Sun's bright disc and reveal its faint outer glow.

cards.headline: Eclipses: explained
learned: Solar eclipse: the Moon blocks the Sun
Lunar eclipse: Earth's shadow falls on the Moon
The 400× coincidence makes total solar eclipses possible

questions.prompt: During a lunar eclipse, what is happening?

options.label: Earth's shadow falls on the Moon
The Moon enters its new phase

questions.explanation: In a lunar eclipse Earth sits between the Sun and the Moon, and its shadow falls on the Moon.

questions.prompt: Why can the Moon exactly cover the Sun during a total solar eclipse?

options.label: The Moon and Sun are actually the same size
options.rationale: The Sun is about 400 times wider.

options.label: The Moon is closer to the Sun
The Sun is ~400× wider and ~400× farther away

questions.explanation: The Sun's extra size is balanced by its extra distance, so both look about the same size from Earth.

questions.prompt: From Level 6: why can a lunar eclipse only happen at full Moon?

options.rationale: The Moon’s distance doesn’t follow its phases.

options.label: Full Moons are brighter, so eclipses show up
The Moon briefly stops orbiting at full Moon
Only then does Earth sit between the Sun and Moon

questions.explanation: At full Moon, Earth is between the Sun and the Moon. When the three line up exactly, Earth's shadow falls on the Moon.

levels.title: Light-Years: Measuring the Unmeasurable
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what a light-year measures and how far the nearest star is.
levels.summary: A light-year is a distance: about 9.46 trillion km. The nearest star after the Sun, Proxima Centauri, is about 4.2 light-years away.

cards.headline: A light-year sounds like a unit of time. It isn't.
Distance, measured in light
cards.body: A light-year is how far light travels in one year: about 9.46 trillion kilometers. Astronomers use it because kilometers stop being useful very quickly.

cards.headline: Why measure space in light?
cards.body: Light is the fastest thing there is, about 300,000 km every second. It crosses from the Moon to Earth in just over a second. Yet even light needs years to reach the next star, so astronomers describe distance by how long light takes to cover it.

cards.fact: The closest star after the Sun is Proxima Centauri, about 4.2 light-years away.
cards.context: Its light left before you started reading about this app. Probably.

cards.headline: Cosmic yardstick: acquired
learned: A light-year is a distance, not a time
It's about 9.46 trillion km
Proxima Centauri is about 4.2 light-years away

options.label: Time
options.rationale: It's a common mix-up, but it's a distance.

options.label: Speed
options.rationale: Light's speed is fixed; this is how far it goes in a year.

questions.explanation: A light-year is the distance light travels in one year.

questions.prompt: Proxima Centauri is about 4.2 light-years away. What does that mean?

options.rationale: A light-year measures distance, not age.

options.label: A spacecraft could reach it in 4.2 years
options.rationale: Our fastest probes would take thousands of years.

options.label: Its light takes about 4.2 years to reach us
It's 4.2 times farther than the Sun
options.rationale: It's hundreds of thousands of times farther.

questions.explanation: A light-year is how far light goes in a year, so light from Proxima Centauri left it about 4.2 years before you see it.

questions.prompt: From Level 1: about how long does sunlight take to reach Earth?

options.rationale: That's roughly the distance to Proxima Centauri.

questions.explanation: Sunlight takes about 8 minutes to reach Earth, so the Sun is about 8 light-minutes away.

levels.title: The Life of a Star
levels.objective: After this level you can read a star's temperature from its color and outline how the Sun will end.
levels.summary: Stars are born in clouds of gas and dust. Blue stars are hottest, red coolest. The Sun will become a red giant and then a white dwarf; massive stars can go supernova.

cards.headline: Stars have a life story: birth, a long middle age, and a very dramatic ending.
Color is temperature
cards.body: Look closely and stars have colors. Blue-white stars are the hottest; red stars are the coolest. The Sun sits in between, which is why it looks white-yellow.

events.label: Forms from a collapsing cloud of gas and dust
Fusing hydrogen into helium in its core
Swells into a red giant
Sheds its outer layers and ends as a white dwarf

cards.headline: Bigger stars, bigger endings
cards.body: The Sun won't explode. But stars much more massive than the Sun can end their lives in a supernova: an explosion that can briefly outshine a whole galaxy.

cards.headline: Stellar life cycle: unlocked
learned: Blue stars are hotter than red stars
Stars form in clouds of gas and dust
The Sun will become a red giant, then a white dwarf
Massive stars can end as supernovae

questions.prompt: How will the Sun most likely end its life?

options.label: As a red giant, then a white dwarf
Exploding as a supernova, then a black hole
options.rationale: The Sun isn’t massive enough to explode.

options.label: Collapsing straight into a black hole
options.rationale: The Sun isn’t massive enough for that.

options.label: It will keep shining unchanged forever
options.rationale: It will run short of hydrogen in its core.

questions.explanation: In about 5 billion years the Sun will swell into a red giant, then shrink into a white dwarf.

questions.prompt: A star looks blue-white. What does that tell you?
questions.explanation: A star's color reveals its surface temperature: bluer means hotter.

questions.prompt: From Level 2: when the Sun swells into a red giant, what is it running low on?

options.label: Hydrogen to fuse in its core
Oxygen to keep its fires burning
options.rationale: The Sun doesn’t burn; it fuses hydrogen.

options.label: Helium to fuse in its outer layers
options.rationale: Helium builds up as hydrogen fuses; it’s hydrogen that runs short.

options.label: Heat from the surrounding galaxy
options.rationale: A star makes its own energy.

questions.explanation: A star shines by fusing hydrogen in its core. When the Sun's core runs short of hydrogen, it changes, swelling into a red giant.

levels.title: Checkpoint: Your Place in the Universe
levels.objective: After this level you can trace Earth's address from our planet all the way out to the observable universe.
levels.summary: The Milky Way is ~100,000 light-years across, Andromeda is ~2.5 million light-years away, and the observable universe holds billions of galaxies in a ~13.8-billion-year-old cosmos.

cards.headline: Chapter 1 finale. Let's zoom all the way out.
cards.body: Everything from Levels 1–9 was your neighborhood. Now for the city, the country and the planet.

cards.headline: Our galaxy
cards.body: The Milky Way is about 100,000 light-years across. Light from one edge would take 100,000 years to reach the other.

cards.fact: Andromeda, the nearest large spiral galaxy, is about 2.5 million light-years away.
cards.context: On a dark night you can see it with the naked eye as a faint smudge. It's the most distant thing most people will ever see unaided.

cards.headline: And then everything else
cards.body: The observable universe holds billions of galaxies, each with billions of stars. The universe itself is about 13.8 billion years old.

cards.headline: Chapter 1 complete
learned: The Milky Way is about 100,000 light-years across
Andromeda is about 2.5 million light-years away
The observable universe holds billions of galaxies
The universe is about 13.8 billion years old

options.label: 100,000 years
options.rationale: Far too young: the Sun alone is billions of years old.

options.label: 4.6 billion years
options.rationale: That's the age of the Sun.

questions.explanation: The universe is about 13.8 billion years old, about three times older than the Sun.

questions.prompt: From Level 8: Andromeda is 2.5 million light-years away. What does that mean?

options.label: It takes 2.5 million years to fly there
options.rationale: No spacecraft goes anywhere near light speed.

options.label: It’s 2.5 million kilometers from Earth
options.rationale: A light-year is vastly longer than a kilometer.

options.label: The galaxy itself is 2.5 million years old
Its light took 2.5 million years to reach us

questions.explanation: A light-year is a distance; Andromeda's light has been traveling for about 2.5 million years.

questions.prompt: The Milky Way is about 100,000 light-years across. Roughly how long would light take to cross it?

options.label: About 100,000 seconds
options.rationale: A light-year is a year of light travel, not a second.

options.label: About 13.8 billion years
options.rationale: That's the age of the universe.

questions.explanation: A distance of 100,000 light-years takes light 100,000 years to cross. That's our own galaxy.

questions.prompt: From Level 1: which galaxy is the Sun part of?

options.label: Andromeda
options.rationale: Andromeda is our neighbor, not our home.

options.label: The Large Magellanic Cloud
options.rationale: That's a small satellite galaxy of the Milky Way.

options.label: The solar system
options.rationale: The solar system is inside a galaxy, not a galaxy itself.

questions.explanation: The Sun is one of at least 100 billion stars in the Milky Way.

questions.prompt: Chapter 1 recap: which of these is farthest from Earth?

options.label: Proxima Centauri
options.rationale: About 4.2 light-years: the nearest star after the Sun.

options.label: Neptune
options.rationale: The farthest planet, but still inside our solar system.

questions.explanation: Andromeda is about 2.5 million light-years away, far beyond every star in our own galaxy.

levels.title: Why the Sky Turns
levels.objective: After this level you can explain that day and night, and the stars rising and setting, come from Earth spinning.
levels.summary: Earth spins once a day from west to east, so the Sun and stars appear to rise in the east and set in the west.

cards.headline: The sky isn’t turning. You are.
cards.body: Every sunrise is really your patch of Earth rolling toward the Sun. Stay up all night and you’ll see the stars do exactly the same thing.

cards.headline: One spin, one day
cards.body: Earth spins around its axis, an imaginary line through the North and South Poles, about once every 24 hours. The half facing the Sun has day; the half facing away has night. As Earth turns, you’re carried from one half into the other.

cards.headline: Why everything rises in the east
cards.body: Earth spins from west to east. That turns your eastern horizon toward the Sun first, so the Sun seems to climb up in the east and sink in the west. The Moon, the planets and the stars cross the sky the same way, for the same reason.

cards.fact: At the equator, Earth’s surface moves at about 1,670 km/h.
cards.context: You don’t feel it because you, the ground and the air all move together at a steady speed.

cards.headline: Daily spin: understood
learned: Earth spins once about every 24 hours
Day is the half of Earth facing the Sun
Earth spins from west to east
So the Sun, Moon and stars rise in the east

questions.prompt: What causes day and night?

options.label: The Sun circling Earth
options.rationale: It looks that way, but it’s Earth that turns.

options.label: Earth orbiting the Sun
options.rationale: That takes a whole year, not a day.

options.label: The Moon blocking the Sun
options.rationale: That’s an eclipse, and it’s rare.

questions.explanation: Earth spins about once every 24 hours; the half facing the Sun has day and the other half has night.

questions.prompt: Why does the Sun rise in the east?

options.label: The Sun travels around Earth from east to west each day
options.rationale: Earth’s spin creates the Sun’s daily path, not an orbit of the Sun.

options.label: The eastern sky is closer to the Sun in the morning
options.rationale: Every horizon is the same distance from the Sun.

options.label: Earth spins eastward, turning the east toward the Sun first
Earth’s tilted axis points the east toward the Sun

questions.explanation: Earth rotates from west to east, so your eastern horizon swings into sunlight first and the Sun appears to rise there.

questions.prompt: From Level 1, stars are distant suns. Why do they rise in the east and set in the west, just like the Sun?

options.label: The stars all orbit Earth once every day
options.rationale: Stars are far beyond Earth; they don’t orbit us.

options.label: They are dragged along behind the Sun across the sky
options.rationale: Stars and the Sun each appear to move because of Earth’s spin.

options.label: The Moon’s gravity pulls the stars westward
options.rationale: The Moon doesn’t move the stars.

options.label: Earth’s spin sweeps them all across the sky the same way

questions.explanation: The stars aren’t moving across the sky. Earth’s west-to-east spin makes the Sun and every distant sun appear to rise in the east and set in the west.

levels.title: A Year Around the Sun
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what a year is, why leap years exist, and why the night sky changes with the seasons.
