levels.summary: A year is one orbit of about 365.25 days. The quarter-days add up to leap days, and the night sky shifts as we orbit.

cards.headline: A year is just one lap.
cards.body: Every birthday, Earth has made one full trip around the Sun since the last one.

cards.headline: One lap, 940 million kilometers
cards.body: Earth takes about 365.25 days to orbit the Sun once. In that time it travels roughly 940 million km, which works out to about 30 km every second. Right now you’re moving faster than any rocket has ever launched.

cards.headline: Where the quarter-days go
cards.body: Calendars count 365 days, but each orbit takes about a quarter of a day longer. Those quarters add up to roughly one full day every four years, so we add February 29 in leap years to keep the calendar in step with the seasons.

cards.headline: A different night sky each season
cards.body: At night you face away from the Sun. As Earth moves around its orbit, that view swings toward different parts of space, so each season has its own constellations. Orion, for example, is a winter evening sight in the Northern Hemisphere.

cards.headline: Orbit: understood
learned: A year is one orbit: about 365.25 days
Earth travels about 30 km every second
Leap days catch up the extra quarter-days
The night sky changes as we orbit

questions.prompt: About how long does Earth take to orbit the Sun once?

options.label: 24 hours
options.rationale: That’s one spin on its axis: a day.

options.label: 29.5 days
options.rationale: That’s the Moon’s cycle of phases.

options.label: 4 years
options.rationale: Leap years come every four years; the orbit takes one.

questions.explanation: One orbit of the Sun takes about 365.25 days: one year.

questions.prompt: Why do we add a leap day about every four years?

options.label: Each orbit takes about 365.25 days, not 365
Earth’s orbit slows down every four years
options.rationale: Earth’s orbit doesn’t change like that.

options.label: To keep the calendar in step with the Moon
options.rationale: Leap days track Earth’s orbit around the Sun, not the Moon.

options.label: Because February is too short
options.rationale: February is just where the extra day goes.

questions.explanation: A year is about 365.25 days. The extra quarter-days add up to about one day every four years, so leap years add February 29.

questions.prompt: From Level 5: seasons repeat every year. What happens during one orbit to cause them?

options.label: Earth moves much closer to the Sun, then farther away
options.rationale: Distance isn’t the cause; Earth is closest in January.

options.label: The Sun gets hotter, then cooler
options.rationale: The Sun’s output barely changes over a year.

options.label: Each hemisphere tilts toward, then away from, the Sun
Earth spins faster in summer
options.rationale: Earth’s spin rate stays essentially the same.

questions.explanation: Earth’s axis stays tilted the same way as it orbits, so over one year each hemisphere leans toward the Sun (summer) and then away from it (winter).

levels.title: Connect the Dots: Constellations
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what a constellation is and why its stars usually aren’t near each other.
levels.summary: There are 88 official constellations covering the sky. Their stars only line up from our viewpoint.

cards.headline: Orion isn’t really a hunter, and his stars aren’t even neighbors.
cards.body: Constellations are patterns we see from one spot in space: Earth.

cards.headline: Patterns and regions
cards.body: People have long named star patterns after figures, animals and objects. Today astronomers use 88 official constellations. Each one is a region of sky with set boundaries, like countries on a map, and together they cover the whole sky.

cards.headline: A trick of perspective
cards.body: Stars that look side by side can be wildly different distances away. One might be a few dozen light-years from us, its neighbor in the pattern hundreds. From anywhere else in the galaxy, the same stars would make completely different shapes.

cards.fact: The Big Dipper is not a constellation.
cards.context: It’s an asterism: a familiar pattern inside the constellation Ursa Major, the Great Bear.

cards.headline: Constellations: decoded
learned: Constellations began as named star patterns
There are 88 official constellations
Their stars are usually far apart in space
The Big Dipper is an asterism in Ursa Major

questions.prompt: How many official constellations are there?

options.rationale: That’s the number of zodiac signs; the constellations cover the whole sky.

questions.explanation: Astronomers officially recognize 88 constellations, which together cover the entire sky.

questions.prompt: Two stars sit side by side in the same constellation. What’s most likely true?

options.label: They may be very different distances from Earth
They orbit each other
options.rationale: Some stars do, but most constellation stars are unrelated.

options.label: They are the same distance from Earth
options.rationale: Only their direction matches, not their distance.

options.label: They are the same age
options.rationale: Nothing about a constellation implies that.

questions.explanation: A constellation is a pattern seen from Earth. Stars in it can be at very different distances and just happen to line up from our viewpoint.

questions.prompt: From Level 8: two stars in Orion are 50 and 500 light-years away. What does that mean for their light?

options.label: Their light reaches us at the same moment it leaves
options.rationale: Light takes time to travel: one year per light-year.

options.label: The farther star’s light is 10 times brighter
options.rationale: Distance says nothing about how bright a star is.

options.label: Both lights left them 500 years ago
options.rationale: Each star’s light left it a different time ago.

options.label: The farther star’s light left it about 450 years earlier

questions.explanation: A light-year is how far light travels in a year. Light from a star 500 light-years away left it about 500 years ago; from 50 light-years, about 50 years ago.

levels.title: The North Star
levels.objective: After this level you can find north with Polaris and explain why some stars never set.
levels.summary: Polaris sits above the North Pole, so it stays put while the sky wheels around it. Its height gives your latitude.

cards.headline: One star barely moves all night. It has guided travelers for centuries.
The star above the pole
cards.body: Polaris, the North Star, lies almost directly above Earth’s North Pole. As Earth spins, every other star circles around it while Polaris stays nearly fixed, marking north. It isn’t the brightest star, either: that’s Sirius.

cards.headline: Stars that never set
cards.body: From mid-northern latitudes, stars close to Polaris trace small circles around it and never dip below the horizon. They’re called circumpolar stars. Bonus: Polaris’s height above your horizon, in degrees, roughly equals your latitude.

cards.fact: Polaris won’t be the North Star forever.
cards.context: Earth’s axis slowly wobbles, tracing a circle about every 26,000 years, so the pole points at different stars over the ages. The Southern Hemisphere has no bright pole star at all; navigators there use the Southern Cross to find south.

cards.headline: North: found
learned: Polaris sits almost directly above the North Pole
It marks north; its height gives your latitude
Circumpolar stars never set
Earth’s 26,000-year wobble changes the pole star

questions.prompt: Why does Polaris barely move across the night sky?

options.label: It is the closest star to Earth
options.rationale: The closest star is Proxima Centauri (after the Sun).

options.label: It lies almost directly above Earth’s North Pole
It is the brightest star
options.rationale: The brightest night-time star is Sirius.

options.label: It orbits Earth at the same speed Earth spins

questions.explanation: Polaris sits nearly on the line of Earth’s axis, so as Earth spins, it stays almost fixed while other stars circle it.

questions.prompt: You see Polaris about 40° above the horizon. What does that tell you?

options.label: You are in the Southern Hemisphere
options.rationale: Polaris can’t be seen from the Southern Hemisphere; the Earth itself blocks it.

options.label: It is about 40 light-years away
options.rationale: Its height in the sky shows your latitude, not its distance.

options.label: It is 4 o’clock
options.rationale: Polaris stays put all night, so it can’t tell the time.

options.label: You are at roughly 40° north latitude

questions.explanation: In the Northern Hemisphere, Polaris’s height above the horizon in degrees roughly equals your latitude.

questions.prompt: From Level 11: most stars rise in the east and set in the west. Why don’t the circumpolar stars set?

options.label: Their circles around the pole stay above the horizon
They are too bright to disappear below the horizon
options.rationale: Brightness has nothing to do with setting.

options.label: They orbit Polaris instead of moving with the sky
options.rationale: They only appear to circle it because Earth spins.

options.label: They only rise during the long winter nights
options.rationale: Circumpolar stars are visible all year from mid-northern latitudes.

questions.explanation: Earth’s spin makes every star appear to circle the pole. Stars close to Polaris trace circles small enough to stay above the horizon all night.

levels.title: The Ecliptic: The Planets’ Highway
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why the Sun, Moon and planets all travel along the same narrow band of sky.
levels.summary: The ecliptic is the Sun’s yearly path. The Moon and planets stay near it because the solar system is flat.

cards.headline: The planets don’t roam the whole sky. They stick to one narrow road.
The Sun’s yearly path
cards.body: As Earth orbits, the Sun seems to drift slowly against the background stars, returning to the same spot after a year. The line it traces is called the ecliptic. The constellations it passes through are the zodiac constellations.
cards.callout: Ecliptic = the Sun’s path over a year

cards.headline: A flat solar system
cards.body: The planets all orbit the Sun in nearly the same flat plane, and the Moon orbits Earth close to it too. Seen from inside that plane, we see everything strung along one line: the ecliptic. Spot a bright “star” near where the Sun set? Check if it’s a planet.

cards.fact: Eclipses can only happen when the Moon is on the ecliptic.
cards.context: The Moon’s orbit is tilted slightly, so most months it passes just above or below the Sun’s path. Only when it crosses the ecliptic at the right moment do we get an eclipse.

cards.headline: Planetary highway: mapped
learned: The ecliptic is the Sun’s path over a year
Zodiac constellations lie along it
The planets stay near it because the solar system is flat
Eclipses need the Moon on the ecliptic

questions.prompt: What is the ecliptic?

options.label: The line of Earth’s equator projected onto the sky
options.rationale: That’s the celestial equator, a different line.

options.label: The path the Moon’s shadow takes across Earth
options.rationale: Shadows cause eclipses; the ecliptic is the Sun’s path.

options.label: The Sun’s apparent path across the sky over a year
The band of the Milky Way across the night sky
options.rationale: The ecliptic is set by Earth’s orbit.

questions.explanation: Over a year, the Sun appears to move against the stars along a line called the ecliptic.

questions.prompt: Why do the planets always appear near the ecliptic?

options.label: They are pulled toward the Sun’s path by the stars
options.rationale: Distant stars have no such effect.

options.label: Their orbits lie in nearly the same flat plane as Earth’s
The ecliptic is where the sky is darkest
options.rationale: Darkness has nothing to do with it.

options.label: They orbit Earth along that line
options.rationale: Planets orbit the Sun, not Earth.

questions.explanation: The solar system is flat: the planets orbit in nearly the same plane as Earth, so from Earth they all appear close to the Sun’s path.

questions.prompt: From Level 7: there’s a new Moon every month. Why isn’t there a solar eclipse every month?

options.label: The Moon is too far away to cover the Sun most months
options.rationale: It’s the tilt of the Moon’s orbit, not its distance, that usually prevents it.

options.label: Solar eclipses can only happen in the summer months
options.rationale: Eclipses can happen in any season.

options.label: Earth’s shadow blocks the Moon’s shadow most months
options.rationale: In a solar eclipse it’s the Moon’s shadow that matters.

options.label: The Moon usually passes just above or below the Sun’s path

questions.explanation: The Moon’s orbit is slightly tilted to the ecliptic. Most new Moons pass above or below the Sun; only a line-up on the ecliptic gives a solar eclipse.

levels.title: Wanderers: How Planets Move Across the Sky
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why planets drift against the stars and sometimes appear to loop backwards.
levels.summary: Planets drift against the stars as they orbit. When Earth overtakes an outer planet, it seems to go backwards: retrograde motion.

cards.headline: Every few years, Mars seems to stop, reverse and loop back across the sky.
cards.body: It never actually turns around. You’re watching from a moving planet.

cards.headline: The wanderers
cards.body: Night after night, the stars keep the same patterns. Planets don’t: they slowly shift position against the background stars as they orbit the Sun. The ancient Greeks noticed, and the word “planet” comes from their word for “wanderer.”

cards.headline: Overtaking on the inside lane
cards.body: Earth orbits closer to the Sun than Mars does, so it moves faster. When Earth catches up with Mars and passes it, Mars appears to slide backwards against the stars for a few weeks, then forward again. It’s like passing a slower car: it seems to drift backwards, though both are going forward.

cards.fact: Retrograde motion is only apparent.
cards.context: No planet ever reverses direction in its orbit. The backwards loop is a change in our viewpoint, not in the planet’s path.

cards.headline: Wanderers: explained
learned: Planets drift against the stars as they orbit
“Planet” means wanderer
Earth overtaking Mars makes it seem to go backwards
Retrograde motion is only apparent

questions.prompt: What does the word “planet” originally mean?

options.label: Round world
options.rationale: The name comes from how planets move, not their shape.

options.label: Bright star
options.rationale: Planets were named for moving against the stars.

questions.explanation: Planets drift against the fixed patterns of stars, so the Greeks called them “wanderers.”

questions.prompt: Why does Mars sometimes appear to move backwards across the sky?

options.label: Mars reverses its orbit for a few weeks
options.rationale: Planets never reverse; this is an illusion.

options.label: The Sun pulls Mars backwards
options.rationale: The Sun’s gravity doesn’t make Mars reverse.

options.label: Mars is hidden behind the Moon
options.rationale: That would hide Mars, not move it.

options.label: Earth, on its faster inner orbit, is overtaking it

questions.explanation: Earth moves faster than Mars. As Earth passes Mars, Mars appears to slip backwards against the stars, just like a slower car you overtake.

questions.prompt: From Level 3: which of these planets can show retrograde motion caused by Earth overtaking it?

options.label: Mercury
options.rationale: Mercury orbits inside Earth’s orbit, so Earth never overtakes it.

options.label: Venus
options.rationale: Venus orbits inside Earth’s orbit and moves faster than Earth.

options.label: Earth
options.rationale: We watch from Earth; it can’t appear to move against the stars.

questions.explanation: Mars is the rocky planet just outside Earth’s orbit. Earth overtakes it every couple of years, causing its retrograde loop.

levels.title: Tides: The Moon’s Pull on the Ocean
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why most coasts get two high tides a day and what spring and neap tides are.
levels.summary: The Moon’s gravity makes two bulges of ocean water. Earth spins through both each day; the Sun makes tides bigger or smaller.

cards.headline: The Moon moves oceans. Twice a day.
Two bulges, not one
cards.body: The Moon’s gravity pulls on Earth’s oceans, stretching them into two bulges: one facing the Moon and one on the opposite side of Earth. As Earth spins, most coastlines pass through both bulges, getting two high tides and two low tides about every 24 hours and 50 minutes.

cards.headline: The Sun joins in
cards.body: The Sun pulls on the oceans too, more weakly. Around new and full Moon, the Sun, Moon and Earth line up and their pulls combine into extra-high and extra-low tides: spring tides. Around the quarter Moons they pull at right angles and tides are gentler: neap tides.

cards.fact: Spring tides have nothing to do with spring.
cards.context: They happen twice a month, all year round. The name comes from water “springing” up higher.

cards.headline: Tides: explained
learned: The Moon’s gravity makes two ocean bulges
Most coasts get two high tides a day
Spring tides: Sun and Moon lined up
Neap tides: Sun and Moon at right angles

questions.prompt: What mainly causes ocean tides?

options.label: The Sun’s heat
options.rationale: Heat drives weather, not the tides.

questions.explanation: Tides come mainly from the Moon’s gravity, with a smaller pull from the Sun.

questions.prompt: Why do most coasts get two high tides a day, not one?

options.label: The Moon orbits Earth twice every single day
options.rationale: The Moon orbits once a month.

options.label: Earth spins through two tidal bulges each day
The Sun makes one high tide and the Moon the other
options.rationale: The two bulges both come from the Moon’s pull.

options.label: The ocean sloshes back after each tide
options.rationale: The pattern comes from two tidal bulges.

questions.explanation: There’s a bulge facing the Moon and another on Earth’s far side. Spinning through both gives two high tides a day.

questions.prompt: From Level 6: spring tides happen at new and full Moon. What do those two phases have in common?

options.label: The Moon is closest to Earth
options.rationale: Phase doesn’t depend on the Moon’s distance.

options.label: The Moon is half lit
options.rationale: That’s the quarter Moons, when neap tides happen.

options.label: The Moon is on the far side of the Sun
options.rationale: At new Moon it’s between Earth and the Sun.

options.label: The Sun, Earth and Moon are in a line

questions.explanation: At new Moon the Moon is between Earth and the Sun; at full Moon, Earth is between them. Either way they line up, and their pulls add up.

levels.title: Where the Moon Came From
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the giant-impact explanation for the Moon’s origin and the evidence for it.
levels.summary: The Moon most likely formed from debris after a Mars-sized body hit the young Earth about 4.5 billion years ago.

cards.headline: The Moon may be made of pieces of Earth.
cards.body: The leading explanation starts with one of the biggest collisions in the solar system’s history.

cards.headline: The giant impact
cards.body: About 4.5 billion years ago, soon after Earth formed, a Mars-sized body (scientists call it Theia) is thought to have slammed into it. The crash threw huge amounts of molten rock into orbit, and that debris gathered to form the Moon.

cards.headline: The clues
cards.body: Rocks brought back by Apollo astronauts are chemically very similar to rocks from Earth’s mantle, the layer below the crust. And the Moon has only a small iron core, which fits a Moon built mostly from rocky outer layers rather than Earth’s iron heart. Computer simulations of such a collision can produce exactly this kind of Moon.

cards.headline: Moon origin: reconstructed
learned: The Moon likely formed from a giant impact
A Mars-sized body (Theia) hit the young Earth
That was about 4.5 billion years ago
Moon rocks closely match Earth’s mantle

questions.prompt: What is the leading explanation for how the Moon formed?

options.label: Earth’s gravity captured a large passing asteroid
options.rationale: Capture doesn’t explain the Moon’s Earth-like rocks.

options.label: Debris from a giant collision with the young Earth
It formed from the Sun’s leftover gas
options.rationale: The Moon is rock, formed from a collision.

options.label: It broke away from Mars and drifted to Earth
options.rationale: The impactor was Mars-sized; the Moon didn’t come from Mars.

questions.explanation: A Mars-sized body likely hit the young Earth, and the Moon formed from the debris.

questions.prompt: Which clue supports the idea that the Moon formed from material blasted off Earth?

options.label: The Moon is covered in thousands of impact craters
The Moon always keeps the same face toward Earth
options.rationale: That’s about its spin, not its origin.

options.label: The Moon’s dark “seas” are made of ancient lava
Moon rocks are chemically very similar to Earth’s mantle

questions.explanation: Apollo samples closely match Earth’s mantle rocks, and the Moon has only a small iron core: what you’d expect from debris of Earth’s outer layers.

questions.prompt: From Level 2: the Sun is about 4.6 billion years old. What does the Moon’s age of about 4.5 billion years suggest?

options.label: It formed early, not long after Earth itself
It formed long before the Sun did
It formed only a few million years ago
options.rationale: Billions of years is anything but recent.

options.label: It drifted in from another star system
options.rationale: Its age fits our own solar system’s early history.

questions.explanation: The Moon is only a little younger than the Sun, so it formed early, not long after Earth itself.

levels.title: Craters and Seas on the Moon
levels.objective: After this level you can explain where lunar craters and the dark “seas” came from and why they last so long.
levels.summary: Craters are impact scars preserved for billions of years; the dark maria are ancient hardened lava.

cards.headline: The “Man in the Moon” is made of ancient lava.
Scars that never heal
cards.body: The Moon’s craters were blasted out by asteroids and comets, and range from tiny pits to basins hundreds of kilometers wide. On Earth, wind, rain and shifting plates wear craters away. The Moon has almost no atmosphere, no liquid water and no plate tectonics, so its craters survive for billions of years.
cards.callout: No air, no water, no erasing

cards.headline: Seas without water
cards.body: The dark patches are called maria, Latin for “seas,” because early astronomers thought they might be water. They’re actually vast plains of ancient lava that flooded low areas and hardened. Most of them are on the near side, the side that faces Earth.

cards.headline: Lunar surface: surveyed
learned: Craters come from asteroid and comet impacts
No air, water or plate tectonics erase them
Maria are plains of ancient hardened lava
Most maria are on the near side

questions.prompt: What are the dark patches on the Moon, called maria?

options.label: Oceans of water
options.rationale: The name means “seas,” but they’re dry.

options.label: Shadows of mountains
options.rationale: The patches are dark rock, not shadows.

options.label: Areas the Sun never lights
options.rationale: Sunlight reaches them like the rest of the surface.

questions.explanation: The maria are enormous plains of lava that erupted and hardened long ago.

questions.prompt: Why do craters last so much longer on the Moon than on Earth?

options.label: The Moon is hit by far fewer asteroids than Earth
options.rationale: It’s more that nothing erases the craters.

options.label: The Moon has no weather, water or plate tectonics to erase them
Moon rock is much harder than rock on Earth
options.rationale: The difference is what wears craters away.

options.label: The Moon’s stronger gravity holds craters in shape
options.rationale: The Moon’s gravity is weaker than Earth’s.

questions.explanation: Wind, water and moving plates wear down Earth’s craters. The Moon has none of these, so its craters survive for billions of years.

questions.prompt: From Level 6: why can we see most of the Moon’s maria from Earth?

options.label: The maria reflect more sunlight than the rest of the Moon
options.rationale: They’re actually darker than the rest of the Moon.

options.label: The Moon rotates, so over a month we see every side
options.rationale: The Moon is tidally locked; we see one side.

options.label: The far side is smooth, with no craters or seas
options.rationale: The far side is heavily cratered.

options.label: Most maria are on the near side, which always faces Earth

questions.explanation: The Moon is tidally locked, always showing us the same face, and most of the maria are on that near side.

levels.title: Checkpoint: Reading the Sky
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the everyday motions of the Sun, Moon, stars and planets and the tides they cause.
levels.summary: Spin makes days, orbits make years and seasons, and the Moon’s orbit and gravity drive phases, eclipses and tides.

cards.headline: Chapter 2 finale. Everything in the sky moves for a reason.
cards.body: You now know the reason for almost all of it. Let’s put it together.

cards.headline: Spin, orbit, pull
cards.body: Earth’s spin gives day and night and sweeps the stars across the sky. Its orbit gives the year, the seasons and a changing night sky. And the Moon, circling us, brings phases, eclipses and tides.
cards.callout: Spin → day · Orbit → year · Moon → tides

cards.fact: Each star rises about 4 minutes earlier every night.
cards.context: Earth moves a little along its orbit each day, so the stars get a head start. Over a year those minutes add up to a whole different night sky.

cards.headline: Chapter 2 complete
learned: Earth’s spin: day, night and a turning sky
Earth’s orbit: the year and a changing night sky
The Moon: phases, eclipses and tides
Planets wander; Mars sometimes loops backwards

questions.prompt: Which motion gives us day and night?

options.label: The Moon orbiting Earth
options.rationale: That gives us the Moon’s phases.

questions.explanation: Earth’s daily spin carries each place into sunlight and then into darkness.

questions.prompt: Which star stays almost fixed above the North Pole?

options.label: Sirius
options.rationale: Sirius is the brightest night-time star, not the pole star.

options.label: Proxima Centauri
options.rationale: That’s the nearest star, far from the pole in our sky.

questions.explanation: Polaris lies almost directly above Earth’s North Pole, so it barely moves.

questions.prompt: Why does the night sky show different constellations in different seasons?

options.label: The stars move to new positions
options.rationale: The stars’ patterns stay the same for centuries.

options.label: Earth’s tilt hides some stars
options.rationale: Tilt causes seasons, not which stars face us at night.

options.label: As Earth orbits, night faces a new part of space
The Moon blocks different stars each season
options.rationale: The Moon covers only a tiny patch of sky.

questions.explanation: At night we face away from the Sun. As Earth moves around its orbit, that direction changes, so different constellations are overhead.

questions.prompt: Mars appears to move backwards for a few weeks. What’s really happening?

options.label: Mars briefly reverses direction in its orbit
options.rationale: Planets never reverse; it’s an illusion.

options.label: The Moon’s gravity drags Mars backwards
options.rationale: The Moon doesn’t affect Mars’s motion.

options.label: Mars is passing behind the Sun
options.rationale: Then we couldn’t see it at all.

options.label: Earth is overtaking Mars on its faster inner orbit

questions.explanation: Earth’s faster orbit catches up with and passes Mars, making Mars appear to slide backwards against the stars.

questions.prompt: Chapter 2 recap: which pairing of cause and effect is correct?

options.label: Earth’s tilt → tides
options.rationale: Tilt causes seasons; the Moon’s gravity causes tides.

options.label: The Moon’s gravity → day and night
options.rationale: Earth’s spin causes day and night.

options.label: Earth’s spin → stars rising in the east

questions.explanation: Earth spins west to east, so every star rises in the east. Tides come from the Moon’s gravity, seasons from tilt, and craters from impacts.

levels.title: The First Sky-Watchers
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how ancient cultures used the sky to keep calendars and navigate.
levels.summary: The sky was humanity’s first calendar and map: monuments, floods, eclipses and ocean voyages were all timed by it.

cards.headline: Long before clocks, the sky was the clock.
cards.body: The same patterns you learned in Chapter 2 ran farming, festivals and voyages for thousands of years.

cards.headline: Calendars in stone and stars
cards.body: Stonehenge in England lines up with the midsummer sunrise and the midwinter sunset. In ancient Egypt, the first dawn appearance of the star Sirius each year was linked with the Nile’s annual flood, which made the farmland fertile.

cards.headline: Records that predicted the sky
cards.body: Babylonian astronomers kept careful records of the Moon and planets on clay tablets. Over generations those records revealed repeating patterns, and they used them to predict eclipses.

cards.fact: Polynesian navigators crossed thousands of kilometers of open ocean without instruments.
cards.context: They memorized where stars rise and set on the horizon, and read ocean swells and birds, to steer between islands.

cards.headline: Ancient astronomy: discovered
learned: The sky was humanity’s first calendar
Stonehenge aligns with the solstice Sun
Babylonian records predicted eclipses
Polynesians navigated oceans by the stars

questions.prompt: What is Stonehenge aligned with?

options.label: The North Star on the longest night
options.rationale: Its alignment is with the Sun.

options.label: The first dawn rising of Sirius each year
The path of a total solar eclipse
options.rationale: Eclipses don’t repeat at the same place like that.

options.label: The midsummer sunrise and midwinter sunset

questions.explanation: Stonehenge lines up with the Sun at the solstices: sunrise at midsummer and sunset at midwinter.

questions.prompt: How could Babylonian astronomers predict eclipses without knowing what caused them?

options.label: They measured the Moon’s shadow
options.rationale: They worked from records of when eclipses happened.

options.label: They used telescopes
options.rationale: Telescopes came thousands of years later.

questions.explanation: By recording the Moon and planets for generations, the Babylonians found cycles that repeat, which let them forecast eclipses.

questions.prompt: From Level 11: why could Polynesian navigators use a star’s rising point on the horizon to steer?

options.label: Each star rises at a different point every night
options.rationale: If they did, they’d be useless for steering.

options.label: Each star rises at the same point on the horizon every night
Stars only rise and set in the northern sky
options.rationale: Stars rise all along the eastern horizon.

options.label: The Moon lines up with a new star each night
options.rationale: The Moon’s position doesn’t set where stars rise.

questions.explanation: Earth’s spin makes each star rise in the east at the same point on the horizon night after night, so a known star’s rising point works like a compass bearing.

levels.title: Eratosthenes Measures the Earth
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how a shadow and a well let someone estimate Earth’s size over 2,000 years ago.
levels.summary: Comparing the noon Sun in two cities, Eratosthenes estimated Earth’s circumference remarkably well around 240 BCE.

cards.headline: Around 240 BCE, someone measured the whole Earth without leaving Egypt.
Two cities, one Sun
cards.body: Eratosthenes heard that at Syene, at noon on the summer solstice, the Sun shone straight down a deep well. At the same moment in Alexandria, farther north, a vertical pole cast a shadow about 7° from vertical, roughly one-fiftieth of a full circle.

cards.headline: From angle to planet
cards.body: If Earth is a sphere, the angle difference means the distance between the cities is one-fiftieth of the way around the globe. Multiply that distance by 50 and you get Earth’s circumference. His answer was remarkably close to the modern value of about 40,000 km.

cards.fact: Greek thinkers already knew Earth was round.
cards.context: During lunar eclipses, Earth’s shadow on the Moon is always curved, the shape only a sphere casts every time.

cards.headline: Earth: measured
learned: Eratosthenes measured Earth around 240 BCE
He compared noon shadows in two cities
Angle × distance gave the circumference
Earth’s curved shadow showed it was round

questions.prompt: What did Eratosthenes compare to estimate Earth’s size?

options.label: The length of a day in two cities
The angle of the noon Sun in two cities
The height of two mountains
options.rationale: He used the Sun’s angle, not mountains.

options.label: The Moon’s shadow during an eclipse
options.rationale: He compared the noon Sun in two cities.

questions.explanation: At noon on the solstice, the Sun was straight overhead at Syene but about 7° off vertical at Alexandria. That difference revealed Earth’s curve.

questions.prompt: The shadow angle was about one-fiftieth of a circle. What did Eratosthenes do next?

options.label: Divided the distance between the cities by 50
options.rationale: That would give a tiny number.

options.label: Measured the well’s depth
options.rationale: The well only showed the Sun was overhead.

options.label: Multiplied the distance between the cities by 50

questions.explanation: If the cities are one-fiftieth of the way around Earth, then 50 times the distance between them gives the full circumference.

questions.prompt: From Level 7: during a lunar eclipse, why does Earth’s curved shadow on the Moon show that Earth is round?

options.label: The Moon is round, so every shadow on it looks curved
options.rationale: A flat disc seen edge-on would cast a straight shadow.

options.label: The Sun is round
options.rationale: The shadow’s shape comes from Earth.

options.label: Only full Moons have curved shadows
options.rationale: The shadow’s curve comes from Earth, not the phase.

options.label: Only a sphere casts a curved shadow every time, from every angle

questions.explanation: In a lunar eclipse, Earth’s shadow falls on the Moon. Its edge is always curved, which only a sphere produces from every direction.

levels.title: An Earth-Centered Universe
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the geocentric model and why it lasted for more than a thousand years.
levels.summary: Ptolemy’s Earth-centered model used epicycles to match the planets and lasted about 1,400 years.

cards.headline: For 1,400 years, scholars agreed: Earth sits still at the center.
cards.body: It wasn’t a foolish idea. It fit what people could actually see.

cards.headline: Ptolemy’s universe
cards.body: Around 150 CE, Ptolemy described a model with Earth motionless at the center and the Sun, Moon, planets and stars circling it. To match the planets’ loops, each planet rode on a small circle, an epicycle, that itself moved around Earth. Complicated, yes, but it matched what people saw.

cards.headline: Why it made sense
cards.body: You can’t feel Earth moving. And if Earth orbited the Sun, nearby stars should shift slightly over a year. Nobody could detect such a shift, called parallax, which seemed to prove Earth stood still. The model also predicted planet positions well enough to be useful.

cards.headline: Geocentric model: understood
learned: Ptolemy put a motionless Earth at the center
Epicycles explained the planets’ loops
No one could feel Earth move or see stellar parallax
The model lasted about 1,400 years

questions.prompt: In Ptolemy’s model, what sat at the center of the universe?

options.label: The Moon
options.rationale: The Moon circled Earth in his model.

options.label: The Milky Way
options.rationale: Ptolemy didn’t know our galaxy’s structure.

questions.explanation: Ptolemy’s geocentric model put a motionless Earth at the center, with everything else circling it.

questions.prompt: Why did the lack of an observed stellar shift (parallax) seem to support an Earth-centered universe?

options.label: Stars were thought to be too dim to measure precisely
options.rationale: Stars were plainly visible; the issue was their positions.

options.label: Parallax was thought to happen only near the equator
options.rationale: Parallax would show from anywhere on a moving Earth.

options.label: A moving Earth should shift nearby stars, and none moved
Epicycles were thought to cancel out any parallax
options.rationale: Epicycles were for planets, not star shifts.

questions.explanation: If Earth orbited the Sun, nearby stars should appear to shift during the year. Nobody could detect that, so a still Earth seemed more reasonable.

questions.prompt: From Level 16: how did Ptolemy’s model explain retrograde motion?

options.label: Earth overtaking the outer planets
options.rationale: That’s the modern explanation; Ptolemy’s Earth didn’t move.

options.label: Planets truly reversing direction for a while
options.rationale: Planets in his model circled continuously.

options.label: The Moon passing in front of the planets
options.rationale: The Moon played no part in it.

options.label: Planets riding epicycles as they circled Earth

questions.explanation: With Earth fixed, Ptolemy had each planet loop on a small epicycle, producing apparent backwards motion. Today we know it’s Earth overtaking them.

levels.title: Copernicus Moves the Sun
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the heliocentric model and why it explained retrograde motion more simply.
levels.summary: In 1543 Copernicus put the Sun at the center, making Earth just another planet and explaining retrograde loops naturally.

cards.headline: In 1543, one book quietly demoted Earth to “just another planet.”
The Sun in the middle
cards.body: Nicolaus Copernicus published a model with the Sun at the center and Earth as one of several planets orbiting it. Earth’s daily spin explained the turning sky; its yearly orbit explained the Sun’s path through the stars.

cards.headline: Loops without epicycles
cards.body: In this model, retrograde motion is simply Earth overtaking the outer planets. No extra circles are needed to cause it. Copernicus still assumed perfectly circular orbits, though, so his model needed some small circles of its own to match observations.

cards.fact: Copernicus wasn’t the first.
cards.context: Aristarchus of Samos proposed a Sun-centered arrangement around 1,800 years earlier, but the idea didn’t catch on.

cards.headline: Heliocentric model: understood
learned: Copernicus published a Sun-centered model in 1543
Earth became one of the planets
Retrograde motion = Earth overtaking
His orbits were still perfect circles

questions.prompt: What did Copernicus put at the center of his model?

options.label: The Moon
options.rationale: The Moon orbits Earth in both models.

options.label: Jupiter
options.rationale: Jupiter is one of the orbiting planets.

questions.explanation: Copernicus’s heliocentric model placed the Sun at the center, with Earth orbiting it like the other planets.

questions.prompt: How did the heliocentric model explain retrograde motion?

options.label: As Earth overtaking the slower outer planets
As the Sun pulling planets backwards
As an error in observations
options.rationale: The loops are real, but only apparent.

questions.explanation: With the Sun at the center, retrograde loops follow naturally from Earth passing the outer planets.

questions.prompt: From Level 23: what was one weakness Copernicus’s model shared with Ptolemy’s?

options.label: It kept Earth at the center
options.rationale: Copernicus moved the Sun to the center.

options.label: It still assumed perfectly circular orbits
It couldn’t explain day and night
options.rationale: Earth’s spin explained day and night.

questions.explanation: Like Ptolemy, Copernicus used perfect circles, so he still needed some small extra circles. Ellipses came later, with Kepler.

levels.title: Galileo’s Telescope
levels.objective: After this level you can describe what Galileo saw that challenged the Earth-centered view.
levels.summary: Galileo’s telescope revealed moons circling Jupiter, a full set of Venus phases, lunar mountains and a starry Milky Way.

cards.headline: In 1610, four tiny moons around Jupiter cracked the Earth-centered universe.
Borrowed idea, better instrument
cards.body: Galileo didn’t invent the telescope; it first appeared in the Netherlands in 1608. But he built better ones and, in 1609, pointed them at the sky. He found mountains and craters on the Moon and saw that the Milky Way is made of countless stars.

cards.headline: Moons that don’t orbit Earth
cards.body: Galileo found four moons circling Jupiter: Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto. Here was proof that not everything circles Earth.

cards.fact: Venus has phases, just like the Moon.
cards.context: Galileo saw Venus go through a full set of phases, from crescent to nearly full. Ptolemy’s model couldn’t produce that; a Venus orbiting the Sun could.

cards.headline: Galileo: observed
learned: Galileo turned improved telescopes on the sky in 1609
He found four moons circling Jupiter
Venus shows a full set of phases
The Milky Way is made of countless stars

questions.prompt: What did Galileo discover orbiting Jupiter in 1610?

options.label: A ring system
options.rationale: Jupiter’s faint rings were found much later.

questions.explanation: Galileo found Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto, now called the Galilean moons.

questions.prompt: Why were Jupiter’s moons a problem for the Earth-centered model?

options.label: They proved Jupiter was a star
They showed the Moon was not round
options.rationale: They were about Jupiter, not our Moon.

questions.explanation: In the geocentric model everything circled Earth. Moons circling Jupiter showed that wasn’t true.

questions.prompt: From Level 6: our Moon shows phases because it orbits Earth and we see varying amounts of its lit half. What did Venus’s full set of phases suggest?

options.label: Venus orbits Earth like the Moon
options.rationale: An Earth-orbiting Venus could not show a full set of phases.

options.label: Venus makes its own light
options.rationale: Phases show Venus is lit by the Sun.

options.label: Venus is tidally locked
options.rationale: Phases say nothing about its rotation.

questions.explanation: We see different amounts of Venus’s sunlit half as it orbits the Sun. A full set of phases fits a Sun-centered orbit, not Ptolemy’s model.

levels.title: Kepler’s Ellipses
levels.objective: After this level you can state Kepler’s laws in plain words and explain why planets speed up near the Sun.
levels.summary: Using Tycho Brahe’s data, Kepler found that orbits are ellipses, planets speed up near the Sun, and outer planets take longer.

cards.headline: Planets don’t move in circles. Proving it took the best data of the age.
Ellipses, not circles
cards.body: Johannes Kepler studied the precise naked-eye observations of Tycho Brahe. Circles never quite fit Mars. Ellipses did. His first law: planets orbit the Sun in ellipses, with the Sun at one focus rather than the center.

cards.headline: Faster when closer
cards.body: His second law says a line from the Sun to a planet sweeps out equal areas in equal times. In practice, a planet moves fastest when it’s closest to the Sun and slowest when farthest. His third law adds that the farther out a planet orbits, the longer its year.
cards.callout: Law 2: faster near the Sun · Law 3: farther = longer year

cards.headline: Kepler’s laws: learned
learned: Kepler used Tycho Brahe’s precise observations
Law 1: orbits are ellipses
Law 2: planets move fastest near the Sun
Law 3: farther planets take longer to orbit

questions.prompt: What shape did Kepler find planetary orbits to be?
questions.explanation: Kepler’s first law: each planet orbits the Sun in an ellipse, with the Sun at one focus.

questions.prompt: According to Kepler’s second law, when does a planet move fastest?

options.label: When it is farthest from the Sun
When it is halfway around
options.rationale: Speed changes with distance, not with position in the year.

options.label: It always moves at the same speed
options.rationale: Its speed changes along an elliptical orbit.

options.label: When it is closest to the Sun

questions.explanation: Sweeping equal areas in equal times means the planet must move faster when it’s near the Sun.

questions.prompt: From Level 5: Earth is closest to the Sun in early January. By Kepler’s second law, what follows?

options.label: Earth moves fastest along its orbit in January
Northern winter becomes the warmest season
options.rationale: Distance isn’t what sets the seasons.

options.label: Earth spins fastest on its axis in January
options.rationale: Kepler’s law is about orbital speed, not spin.

options.label: The Moon moves closest to Earth in January
options.rationale: The law applies to Earth orbiting the Sun.

questions.explanation: A planet moves fastest nearest the Sun. Earth is closest in early January, so that’s when it moves fastest along its orbit.

levels.title: Newton’s Gravity
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how one law of gravity covers falling apples, orbiting moons and planets.
levels.summary: Newton’s universal gravitation (1687) showed one force governs falling objects, the Moon and the planets, explaining Kepler’s laws.

cards.headline: The force that drops an apple also holds the Moon in the sky.
One law for everything
cards.body: In 1687 Isaac Newton published his law of universal gravitation. Every object pulls on every other. The pull grows with their masses and weakens with the square of the distance: twice as far, a quarter of the pull. On the Moon, surface gravity is only about one-sixth of Earth’s, so you would weigh about one-sixth as much there.
cards.callout: Twice as far → ¼ the pull

cards.headline: Heaven and Earth, united
cards.body: Newton showed that the gravity making things fall on Earth also keeps the Moon in orbit and the planets circling the Sun. His law explained why Kepler’s laws work, turning a description into an explanation.

cards.headline: Gravity: understood
learned: Newton published universal gravitation in 1687
Every object pulls on every other
Double the distance → a quarter of the pull
His law explained Kepler’s laws

questions.prompt: What did Newton show about gravity?

options.label: Gravity only works near the surface of Earth
options.rationale: His key insight was that it works everywhere.

options.label: One force makes apples fall and holds the Moon in orbit
It pushes planets away from the Sun
It only pulls on large, heavy objects like planets
options.rationale: Every object pulls on every other.

questions.explanation: Newton’s universal gravitation: one force explains falling objects on Earth and the motions of the Moon and planets.

questions.prompt: If you doubled the distance between two objects, what would happen to their gravitational pull?

options.label: It would drop to a quarter

questions.explanation: Gravity weakens with the square of the distance: twice as far means 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4 of the pull.

questions.prompt: From Level 17: what connects Newton’s law to the ocean tides?

options.label: The Moon’s gravity pulls on Earth’s oceans
Tides come from Earth’s orbit around the Sun
options.rationale: Tides are mainly the Moon’s pull.

options.label: Newton’s law says water isn’t affected by gravity
options.rationale: Gravity pulls on everything, including water.

options.label: Tides happen only at the equator

questions.explanation: Newton’s gravity acts between all masses. The Moon’s pull on the oceans creates the tidal bulges.

levels.title: Measuring the Solar System
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the astronomical unit and how astronomers measured the size of the solar system.
levels.summary: Kepler gave the solar system’s shape; transits of Venus and later radar gave its size: 1 AU ≈ 150 million km.

cards.headline: Knowing the shape of the solar system isn’t the same as knowing its size.
A map without a scale
cards.body: Kepler’s laws told astronomers the relative distances of the planets: Mars is about 1.5 times farther from the Sun than Earth, for example. But without one real distance in kilometers, the map had no scale. Every distance in the solar system depended on that one missing number.

cards.headline: Chasing Venus
cards.body: In 1761 and 1769, astronomers spread around the world to time Venus crossing the face of the Sun. Comparing their views let them work out the Earth–Sun distance. Today radar and spacecraft pin it down very precisely.

cards.fact: 1 astronomical unit (AU) is about 150 million km.
cards.context: It’s the average Earth–Sun distance, and the solar system’s standard yardstick.

cards.headline: Solar system: measured
learned: Kepler gave relative distances, not a scale
Transits of Venus (1761, 1769) set the scale
Radar and spacecraft now measure it precisely
1 AU ≈ 150 million km

questions.prompt: What is an astronomical unit?

options.label: The distance light travels in a year
The width of the solar system
The distance from Earth to the Moon
The average distance between Earth and the Sun

questions.explanation: One astronomical unit is the average Earth–Sun distance, about 150 million km.

questions.prompt: Why did astronomers still need to measure one real distance after Kepler?

options.label: Kepler’s laws gave proportions but no kilometers
Kepler’s laws had turned out to be wrong
options.rationale: His laws were right; they lacked a scale.

options.label: To search for new planets beyond Saturn
options.rationale: The goal was the size of the known system.

options.label: To measure the exact speed of light
options.rationale: The goal was the Earth–Sun distance.

questions.explanation: Kepler’s laws fixed the proportions of the solar system. One measured distance, like the Earth–Sun distance, set the scale for all of it.

questions.prompt: From Level 1: sunlight takes about 8 minutes to reach Earth. What distance does that light cover?

options.label: About 1 light-year
options.rationale: Light takes a full year for that.

questions.explanation: Sunlight crosses the Earth–Sun distance, 1 AU or about 150 million km, in about 8 minutes.

levels.title: New Planets: Uranus and Neptune
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Uranus was found by telescope and Neptune was predicted by mathematics.
levels.summary: Herschel spotted Uranus in 1781. Tugs on Uranus’s orbit let Le Verrier predict Neptune, found in 1846 almost exactly where predicted.

cards.headline: One planet was found with a telescope. The next was found with a pencil.
A planet no one had seen
cards.body: In 1781, William Herschel spotted a slow-moving object that turned out to be a new planet: Uranus. It was the first planet discovered with a telescope. Every planet out to Saturn had been known since ancient times. Uranus is so faint that earlier astronomers had recorded it and mistaken it for a star.

cards.headline: Found by mathematics
cards.body: Uranus didn’t quite follow its predicted path, as if something unseen were tugging it. Using Newton’s gravity, Urbain Le Verrier calculated where that unseen planet should be. In 1846 Johann Galle looked there and found Neptune, within about a degree of the prediction.

cards.headline: New planets: discovered
learned: Herschel discovered Uranus in 1781
It was the first planet found by telescope
Neptune was predicted from Uranus’s wobbles
Galle found it in 1846, right where predicted

questions.prompt: How was Neptune discovered?

options.label: It was spotted by chance during a comet search
A space probe photographed it on a flyby
options.rationale: That was in 1846, long before spacecraft.

options.label: Its position was predicted by math, then observed
Ancient astronomers saw it with the naked eye
options.rationale: Neptune is far too faint for that.

questions.explanation: Le Verrier used gravity to predict Neptune’s position from tugs on Uranus’s orbit; Galle found it there in 1846.

questions.prompt: What was special about Herschel’s discovery of Uranus in 1781?

options.label: It was the first moon ever discovered by telescope
It was the first planet discovered with a telescope
It was the closest planet to Earth at the time
It was predicted by mathematics first

questions.explanation: All planets out to Saturn were known since ancient times. Uranus was the first found with a telescope.

questions.prompt: From Level 27: which law did Le Verrier use to predict Neptune’s position?

options.label: Kepler’s first law of elliptical orbits
options.rationale: Ellipses describe orbits but don’t explain tugs between planets.

options.label: The law of the tides
options.rationale: Tides are one effect of gravity, not a tool for finding planets.

questions.explanation: Newton’s gravity predicts how planets tug on each other. The unexplained tug on Uranus pointed to Neptune.

levels.title: Checkpoint: How We Know
levels.objective: After this level you can trace how observation and reasoning moved humanity from an Earth-centered sky to modern astronomy.
levels.summary: From Eratosthenes to Bessel, better observations kept testing ideas, until stellar parallax proved that Earth moves.

cards.headline: Chapter 3 finale. The last ancient objection falls.
cards.body: For 2,000 years, no one could see the stars shift as Earth moved. Then someone did.

events.label: Eratosthenes measures Earth
Ptolemy’s Earth-centered model
Copernicus puts the Sun at the center
Galileo finds moons around Jupiter
Newton’s law of gravity
Bessel measures stellar parallax

cards.fact: In 1838 Friedrich Bessel finally measured a star shifting as Earth orbits.
cards.context: The star, 61 Cygni, moved by a tiny angle over the year: the first measured distance to a star, and direct proof that Earth goes around the Sun, as Copernicus had argued.

cards.headline: Chapter 3 complete
learned: Eratosthenes measured Earth around 240 BCE
Copernicus and Galileo displaced the Earth-centered view
Kepler described orbits; Newton explained them
Bessel’s 1838 parallax proved Earth moves

questions.prompt: Who first estimated Earth’s circumference from shadows?
questions.explanation: Around 240 BCE, Eratosthenes compared the noon Sun in two cities to estimate Earth’s size.

questions.prompt: What did Kepler discover about the shape of orbits?
questions.explanation: Kepler’s first law: planets move in ellipses with the Sun at one focus.

questions.prompt: Which observation did the Earth-centered model fail to explain?

options.label: The full set of phases of Venus
The Sun rising in the east
The Moon’s phases
options.rationale: Both models explained the Moon’s phases.

questions.explanation: Galileo saw Venus show a full set of phases, which only makes sense if Venus orbits the Sun.

questions.prompt: Why was Bessel’s 1838 measurement of stellar parallax so important?

options.label: It revealed a new planet beyond Neptune
It showed stars move faster than planets
It showed Earth really does move around the Sun
It proved that the Moon orbits Earth

questions.explanation: Parallax is the shift of a nearby star caused by Earth’s orbit. No one had seen it before; Bessel did.

questions.prompt: Chapter 3 recap: what put the final piece in place for why the planets move as they do?

options.label: Adding more epicycles to Ptolemy’s model
options.rationale: Epicycles described motion inside the wrong model.

options.label: Eratosthenes’ shadows in a deep well

questions.explanation: Kepler described how planets move; Newton’s universal gravitation explained why, uniting motion on Earth and in the heavens.

levels.title: More Than Meets the Eye: The Spectrum
levels.objective: After this level you can explain that visible light is one small part of the electromagnetic spectrum.
levels.summary: Radio waves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays are all light, differing only in wavelength.

cards.headline: Your eyes are missing almost everything.
cards.body: Most of the light in the universe is invisible to us. Astronomers have learned to see it anyway.

cards.headline: One spectrum, many names
cards.body: Radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays are all the same thing: light. What makes them different is wavelength. Radio waves are the longest, gamma rays the shortest, and visible light is a thin sliver in between.

cards.headline: Same speed, every kind
cards.body: Every kind of light, from radio to gamma rays, crosses space at the speed of light. Within the visible band, the colors are wavelengths too: red is the longest and violet the shortest.

cards.fact: Human eyes see only wavelengths from about 380 to 700 nanometers.
cards.context: Anything longer, like infrared, or shorter, like ultraviolet, is invisible to us. Some animals, such as bees, can see ultraviolet.

cards.headline: Spectrum: revealed
learned: Visible light is a small part of the spectrum
Radio → gamma rays: long to short wavelengths
All light travels at the same speed
Red is the longest visible wavelength; violet the shortest

questions.prompt: What makes radio waves, visible light and X-rays different?

options.label: How fast each one travels through space
options.rationale: They all travel at the speed of light.

options.label: Which objects are able to give them off
options.rationale: The key difference is a property of the light itself.

options.label: Whether they are made of particles
options.rationale: They are all forms of light.

questions.explanation: They are all light. The difference is wavelength: radio waves are longest, gamma rays shortest.

questions.prompt: Which list goes from longest wavelength to shortest?

options.label: Gamma rays → visible light → radio waves
Visible light → radio waves → X-rays
options.rationale: Radio waves are longer than visible light.

options.label: X-rays → radio waves → gamma rays
options.rationale: Radio waves are the longest of all.

questions.explanation: Radio waves are the longest, visible light sits in the middle, and X-rays (then gamma rays) are the shortest.

questions.prompt: From Level 8: light-years are based on the speed of light. Does a light-year mean the same distance for radio waves?

options.label: Yes: every kind of light travels at the same speed
No: radio waves are much slower than visible light
options.rationale: All light travels at the same speed.

options.label: No: only visible light counts as real light
Only for radio waves from nearby stars
options.rationale: The speed doesn’t depend on the source.

questions.explanation: All electromagnetic radiation travels at the speed of light, so a light-year is the same distance whichever kind of light you measure with.

levels.title: Starlight’s Fingerprints
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how spectra reveal what stars are made of.
levels.summary: Each element leaves its own lines in a spectrum, so starlight reveals what stars are made of: mostly hydrogen and helium.

cards.headline: We know what stars are made of without ever touching one.
Lines like barcodes
cards.body: Spread starlight into a rainbow and you’ll find thin dark lines crossing it. Each chemical element absorbs and emits light only at its own set of wavelengths, so each makes its own pattern of lines, like a barcode.

cards.headline: Reading a star
cards.body: By matching the lines in a star’s spectrum to elements measured in the lab, astronomers can tell what the star contains. The answer, for almost every star: mostly hydrogen and helium.

cards.fact: Helium was discovered in the Sun before it was found on Earth.
cards.context: In 1868 astronomers saw an unknown line in the Sun’s spectrum. The new element was named after Helios, the Greek word for the Sun.

cards.headline: Starlight: decoded
learned: Each element leaves its own spectral lines
Spectra reveal what stars are made of
Stars are mostly hydrogen and helium
Helium was found in the Sun in 1868

questions.prompt: What are stars made of, mostly?

options.label: Iron and nickel, like Earth’s core
options.rationale: Stars are mostly the two lightest elements.

options.label: Oxygen and carbon, like living things
options.rationale: Those are only small traces in stars.

options.label: Rock and ice, like the planets
options.rationale: Stars are hot gas, not rock or ice.

questions.explanation: Their spectra show stars are made mostly of hydrogen and helium.

questions.prompt: How can astronomers tell which elements are in a distant star?

options.label: By collecting samples with space probes
options.rationale: No probe has ever reached another star.

options.label: By measuring how bright the star looks
By matching the lines in its spectrum to known elements
By timing how long its light takes to arrive

questions.explanation: Each element leaves its own pattern of spectral lines. Matching those patterns reveals a star’s ingredients.

questions.prompt: From Level 2: why does it make sense that stars are mostly hydrogen and helium?

options.label: They were formed from melted rock
Helium is heavier than all other elements
options.rationale: Helium is one of the lightest elements.

options.label: Stars fuse hydrogen into helium in their cores

questions.explanation: A star like the Sun shines by fusing hydrogen into helium, so its main fuel and its main product are exactly what spectra show.

levels.title: How Telescopes Work
levels.objective: After this level you can tell refracting from reflecting telescopes and explain why bigger mirrors see more.
levels.summary: Refractors use lenses, reflectors use mirrors. A bigger aperture gathers more light, so the largest telescopes are reflectors.

cards.headline: A telescope is a light bucket. Bigger bucket, more universe.
Lenses or mirrors
cards.body: Refracting telescopes, like Galileo’s, gather light with lenses. Reflecting telescopes gather it with curved mirrors. Isaac Newton built the first practical reflector in 1668.

cards.headline: Why size matters
cards.body: A wider mirror or lens collects more light, so it can see fainter objects and show finer detail. That’s why astronomers keep building bigger telescopes. All the largest are reflectors: a huge lens would sag under its own weight, but a mirror can be supported from behind.

cards.fact: The biggest optical telescopes today have mirrors about 10 meters across.
cards.context: Mirrors that size are built from many smaller segments fitted together. Telescopes with mirrors more than 30 meters wide are already under construction.

cards.headline: Telescopes: understood
learned: Refractors use lenses; reflectors use mirrors
Newton built the first practical reflector in 1668
Bigger apertures see fainter and finer
The largest telescopes are reflectors

questions.prompt: What does a reflecting telescope use to gather light?

options.label: A radio antenna
options.rationale: Radio telescopes are a different kind.

questions.explanation: Reflecting telescopes gather light with curved mirrors; refractors use lenses.

questions.prompt: Why are the world’s largest telescopes all reflectors?

options.label: Mirrors show more colors than lenses
Newton banned large lenses
options.rationale: He built a reflector; he didn’t ban lenses.

options.label: Huge lenses sag, but mirrors can be supported from behind
Mirrors are cheaper to carry into space
options.rationale: Most large telescopes are on the ground.

questions.explanation: A giant lens can only be held at its edge and sags under its own weight. A mirror can be supported across its whole back.

questions.prompt: From Level 25: Galileo’s telescope used lenses. Why could later, bigger telescopes see much fainter objects?

options.label: They used brighter lenses
options.rationale: Lenses don’t add light; they collect it.

options.label: They were built on taller mountains only
options.rationale: Height helps a little; size matters most.

options.label: They magnified the stars more
options.rationale: Stars stay points of light even when magnified.

options.label: Their larger mirrors or lenses collect more light

questions.explanation: A larger aperture gathers more light, so bigger telescopes reveal fainter objects than Galileo’s small lenses could.

levels.title: Why Put Telescopes in Space?
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what Earth’s atmosphere does to starlight and what Hubble gained by leaving it.
levels.summary: Air makes stars twinkle and blocks much of the spectrum. Above it, Hubble (1990) takes sharp images across more wavelengths.

cards.headline: Twinkling is beautiful. For astronomers, it’s a problem.
The trouble with air
cards.body: Stars twinkle because moving pockets of air bend their light back and forth, blurring what telescopes see. The atmosphere also blocks most ultraviolet light and X-rays, and much infrared, from ever reaching the ground.

cards.headline: Hubble, above it all
cards.body: The Hubble Space Telescope launched in 1990 and orbits above the atmosphere, so its images are free of that blurring. It’s also the only space telescope designed to be repaired and upgraded by astronauts in orbit.

cards.fact: Hubble helped measure the age of the universe.
cards.context: Its sharp observations of distant galaxies helped pin the universe’s age at about 13.8 billion years, a number you met back in Level 10.

cards.headline: Space telescopes: explained
learned: Moving air makes stars twinkle
The atmosphere blocks most UV and X-rays
Hubble launched in 1990, above the air
Astronauts can repair and upgrade Hubble

questions.prompt: Why do stars twinkle?

options.label: They flicker as they burn their fuel
options.rationale: The star’s light is steady; the flicker happens here.

options.label: Moving air in Earth’s atmosphere bends their light
The Moon’s light interferes with them
options.rationale: Twinkling happens with or without the Moon.

options.label: They are spinning very fast
options.rationale: Spinning doesn’t make a star twinkle.

questions.explanation: Turbulent air bends starlight back and forth, making stars appear to twinkle.

questions.prompt: Besides sharper images, what else do telescopes gain by going to space?

options.label: A closer view of the stars
options.rationale: A few hundred km closer makes no difference.

options.label: Protection from meteors
options.rationale: Space actually has more debris risk.

options.label: Access to light the atmosphere blocks, like ultraviolet and X-rays
Freedom from the Sun’s gravity
options.rationale: They’re still in orbit around Earth.

questions.explanation: The atmosphere absorbs most ultraviolet and X-ray light and much infrared. From space, telescopes can see those wavelengths.

questions.prompt: From Level 31: which kinds of light are mostly blocked before they reach the ground?

options.label: Visible light and radio waves
options.rationale: Both reach the ground, which is why we see and use radio.

options.label: Only light from distant galaxies
options.rationale: Blocking depends on wavelength, not distance.

questions.explanation: Earth’s atmosphere absorbs most ultraviolet and X-ray light, which is why those telescopes must go to space.

levels.title: Listening to the Sky: Radio Astronomy
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what radio telescopes detect and why they are so large.
levels.summary: Radio telescopes catch long radio waves that pierce dust and work day or night. Linked dishes act like one giant telescope.

cards.headline: Some telescopes don’t need darkness. They work at noon, through clouds.
A new window
cards.body: In the early 1930s, Karl Jansky picked up radio waves coming from the Milky Way. Radio astronomy was born. Radio waves pass through cosmic dust and Earth’s clouds, and radio telescopes can observe in daylight.

cards.headline: Why the dishes are huge
cards.body: Radio waves are very long, so seeing fine detail takes an enormous dish. Astronomers go further by linking many dishes into arrays that work together like one much larger telescope.

cards.fact: The Very Large Array in New Mexico links 27 radio dishes.
cards.context: Spread out over up to 36 km, they work together like a single dish of that size, sharp enough to map the radio sky in fine detail.

cards.headline: Radio sky: tuned in
learned: Radio waves pass through dust and clouds
Radio telescopes work day and night
Jansky founded radio astronomy in the 1930s
Arrays link dishes into one giant telescope

questions.prompt: What did Karl Jansky detect in the early 1930s?

options.label: The first planet beyond Neptune
options.rationale: He detected radio waves, not a planet.

options.label: Radio waves coming from the Milky Way

questions.explanation: Jansky’s detection of radio waves from the Milky Way launched radio astronomy.

questions.prompt: Why are radio telescopes usually so much bigger than optical ones?

options.label: Radio sources are much closer than stars
Radio waves are very long, so fine detail needs a huge dish
Radio waves travel more slowly than light
options.rationale: They travel at the speed of light.

options.label: Radio telescopes must block the daylight

questions.explanation: The longer the wavelength, the bigger the dish must be to see fine detail. Radio waves are the longest of all.

questions.prompt: From Level 33: a bigger aperture shows finer detail. How do radio astronomers get an aperture bigger than any single dish?

options.label: By cooling the dishes to very low temperatures
options.rationale: Cooling reduces noise; it doesn’t enlarge the aperture.

options.label: By pointing the dishes at brighter sources
By using lenses instead of dishes
By linking many dishes into one array

questions.explanation: Linked dishes work together like one telescope as large as the spread of the array.

levels.title: Seeing Heat: Infrared and Webb
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why infrared light reveals hidden and very distant objects.
levels.summary: Infrared passes through dust and catches the stretched light of the first galaxies. Webb, launched in 2021, is built for it.

cards.headline: The newest great telescope sees in heat.
Seeing through dust
cards.body: Infrared is the light we feel as heat. It passes through clouds of dust that block visible light, revealing stars forming inside them. And light from the most distant galaxies has been stretched by the expanding universe into infrared.

cards.headline: The James Webb Space Telescope
cards.body: Webb launched on December 25, 2021. Its main mirror is 6.5 meters across, made of 18 gold-coated segments. It orbits the Sun about 1.5 million km from Earth, behind a sunshield that keeps it extremely cold, as an infrared telescope must be. That five-layer sunshield is about the size of a tennis court.

cards.headline: Infrared: unveiled
learned: Infrared is light we feel as heat
It reveals stars forming inside dust
Distant galaxies’ light is stretched into infrared
Webb (2021): 6.5 m mirror, very cold

questions.prompt: What kind of light is the James Webb Space Telescope built to see?

options.label: Radio waves
options.rationale: That’s the job of radio dishes.

options.label: X-rays
options.rationale: X-ray telescopes like Chandra do that.

questions.explanation: Webb is an infrared telescope, built to see through dust and to catch the stretched light of distant galaxies.

questions.prompt: Why is infrared ideal for watching stars being born?

options.label: Infrared passes through the dust clouds where stars form
Newborn stars give off only infrared light
options.rationale: They give off many kinds of light.

options.label: Infrared travels faster than visible light
options.rationale: All light travels at the same speed.

options.label: Dust clouds are brighter in ultraviolet
options.rationale: The point is to see through the dust.

questions.explanation: Stars form inside dusty clouds that block visible light. Infrared passes through that dust.

questions.prompt: From Level 34: why does it help that Webb works in space?

options.label: It can repair itself more easily there
Much infrared light never reaches the ground
Infrared light only exists in space
options.rationale: Infrared exists everywhere, even as heat on Earth.

options.label: It is closer to the distant galaxies
options.rationale: A million km is nothing on galactic scales.

questions.explanation: Earth’s atmosphere blocks much infrared light, so an infrared telescope does its best work in space.

levels.title: Getting to Orbit
levels.objective: After this level you can explain that an orbit is falling around a planet, and what escape velocity means.
levels.summary: Orbiting means falling while moving sideways so fast you keep missing. The ISS does it at 28,000 km/h; escaping takes 11.2 km/s.

cards.headline: Astronauts aren’t floating. They’re falling, and missing.
Falling around Earth
cards.body: Throw a ball and it curves down to the ground. Throw it fast enough and the ground curves away beneath it as quickly as it falls. That’s an orbit. The International Space Station does this at about 28,000 km/h, circling Earth about every 90 minutes.

cards.headline: Why astronauts float
cards.body: Gravity in orbit is still strong. Astronauts float because they and their spacecraft are falling together, so nothing presses them against the floor.

cards.fact: To leave Earth for good, you need about 11.2 km per second.
cards.context: That’s escape velocity: about 40,000 km/h. Slower, and Earth’s gravity eventually pulls you back or holds you in orbit.

cards.headline: Orbits: understood
learned: An orbit is falling while moving sideways
The ISS circles Earth about every 90 minutes
Astronauts float because they fall together
Escape velocity is about 11.2 km/s

questions.prompt: Why do astronauts float inside the space station?

options.label: There is no gravity at that height
options.rationale: Gravity in orbit is still strong.

options.label: The station spins to cancel gravity
options.rationale: The station doesn’t spin for gravity.

options.label: They and the station are falling around Earth together
Space is a vacuum, so nothing weighs anything

questions.explanation: Astronauts and their spacecraft fall together around Earth, so nothing pushes them against the floor.

questions.prompt: A probe launches at more than 11.2 km per second. What can it do that the space station can’t?

options.label: Stay in the same spot above Earth
options.rationale: Escaping carries it away, not in place.

options.label: Orbit much closer to the ground
options.rationale: Escape speed takes it away from Earth.

options.label: Float without any gravity acting on it
options.rationale: Gravity still acts on it as it leaves.

options.label: Leave Earth for good instead of orbiting

questions.explanation: At about 11.2 km/s, escape velocity, a spacecraft can break free of Earth’s gravity instead of falling around it.

questions.prompt: From Level 27: which force makes a spacecraft fall around Earth in orbit?

options.label: The Sun’s light pressure
options.rationale: That’s a tiny push, not what shapes an orbit.

options.label: The Moon’s tidal pull
options.rationale: The Moon’s pull is small near Earth.

questions.explanation: Newton’s gravity is what makes an orbiting spacecraft keep falling toward Earth, just like the Moon.

levels.title: Robot Explorers
levels.objective: After this level you can describe how robotic probes like Voyager explored the outer planets.
levels.summary: The twin Voyagers (1977) toured the giant planets; Voyager 2 alone visited Uranus and Neptune; Voyager 1 is now interstellar.

cards.headline: The farthest thing humans ever built is still sending messages home.
The grand tour
cards.body: Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 launched in 1977. Between them they flew past Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. Voyager 2 is still the only spacecraft to have visited Uranus, in 1986, and Neptune, in 1989.

cards.headline: Into interstellar space
cards.body: In 2012 Voyager 1 crossed into interstellar space, the most distant human-made object. Each Voyager carries a Golden Record of sounds and images from Earth, a message for anyone who might one day find it.

cards.fact: Voyager 1’s radio signals take more than 20 hours to reach Earth.
cards.context: Traveling at the speed of light, each message from the edge of the solar system is almost a day old when it arrives, and the gap grows every year.

cards.headline: Robot explorers: logged
learned: The Voyagers launched in 1977
They flew past all four giant planets
Voyager 2 alone visited Uranus and Neptune
Voyager 1 reached interstellar space in 2012

questions.prompt: Which spacecraft is the only one to have visited Uranus and Neptune?

options.label: Voyager 1
options.rationale: Voyager 1 left the planets after Saturn.

options.label: The James Webb telescope
options.rationale: Webb orbits far from the giant planets.

questions.explanation: Voyager 2 flew past Uranus in 1986 and Neptune in 1989, the only spacecraft ever to visit them.

questions.prompt: What is special about Voyager 1’s location today?

options.label: It has reached interstellar space, farther than any human-made object
It is orbiting Neptune’s largest moon
It has landed on the surface of Pluto
options.rationale: No spacecraft has landed on Pluto.

options.label: It has returned to orbit around the Earth

questions.explanation: Voyager 1 entered interstellar space in 2012 and is the most distant object humans have made.

questions.prompt: From Level 29: Herschel found Uranus with a telescope in 1781. How did Voyager 2 add to that?

options.label: It discovered Uranus a second time
It gave humanity its only close-up visit to Uranus
It brought rock samples back from Uranus
options.rationale: No mission has returned samples from Uranus.

options.label: It landed on the surface of Uranus
options.rationale: Uranus has no solid surface to land on.

questions.explanation: Herschel spotted Uranus from Earth; Voyager 2’s 1986 flyby remains the only close-up visit.

levels.title: Humans on the Moon
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the Apollo Moon landings and what they brought back.
levels.summary: Apollo 11 landed on July 20, 1969. Twelve astronauts walked on the Moon by 1972 and brought back 382 kg of samples.

cards.headline: Only twelve people have ever walked on another world.
One small step
cards.body: On July 20, 1969, Apollo 11 astronauts Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin became the first people to walk on the Moon. Between 1969 and 1972, six Apollo landings put twelve astronauts on its surface.

cards.headline: Bringing the Moon home
cards.body: The Apollo astronauts brought back 382 kg of Moon rocks and soil. Scientists are still studying them, and they’re among the best evidence for how the Moon formed.
