cards.fact: The last Moonwalkers left in December 1972.
cards.context: Their footprints are still up there. With no wind or rain on the Moon, nothing wears them away.

cards.headline: Moonwalk: recorded
learned: Apollo 11 landed on July 20, 1969
Armstrong and Aldrin walked first
Twelve astronauts walked on the Moon by 1972
They brought back 382 kg of samples

questions.prompt: Who were the first two people to walk on the Moon?

options.label: Yuri Gagarin and Valentina Tereshkova
options.rationale: They were early spaceflight pioneers but never went to the Moon.

options.label: John Glenn and Alan Shepard
options.rationale: They flew early US missions, not Moon landings.

options.label: Galileo and Kepler
options.rationale: They studied the sky centuries earlier.

questions.explanation: Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin walked on the Moon during Apollo 11 on July 20, 1969.

questions.prompt: Why are the Apollo samples still valuable today?

options.label: They are the only rocks from space on Earth
options.rationale: Meteorites from space fall to Earth too.

options.label: They prove the Moon is made of cheese
They were used to fuel later rockets
Scientists keep studying them to learn how the Moon formed

questions.explanation: The 382 kg of Apollo samples keep yielding new evidence, including about how the Moon formed.

questions.prompt: From Level 18: what did Apollo samples reveal about where the Moon came from?

options.label: The Moon is made of the same rock as Mars
options.rationale: The match is with Earth, not Mars.

options.label: The Moon is older than the solar system
options.rationale: It formed about 4.5 billion years ago.

options.label: Moon rocks are chemically very similar to Earth’s mantle
The Moon was captured from the asteroid belt

questions.explanation: Apollo rocks closely match Earth’s mantle, supporting the idea that the Moon formed from debris of a giant impact.

levels.title: Checkpoint: The Tools of Astronomy
levels.objective: After this level you can match each kind of light and instrument to what it lets astronomers study.
levels.summary: Each wavelength needs its own tools: radio dishes, infrared and X-ray telescopes in space, and spacecraft that go and look.

cards.headline: Chapter 4 finale. One sky, many kinds of light.
cards.body: Every kind of light shows something the others miss. Here’s the full toolkit.

cards.headline: X-rays: the hottest things
cards.body: X-ray telescopes reveal extremely hot gas, like the gas swirling around black holes. Because Earth’s atmosphere absorbs X-rays, they must work in space. NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory launched in 1999.

cards.headline: Match the light to the job
Or just go there
cards.body: Some questions can’t be answered from a distance. Robotic probes like Voyager 2 flew past Uranus and Neptune, and Apollo astronauts brought 382 kg of the Moon home to study.

cards.headline: Chapter 4 complete
learned: X-ray telescopes see extremely hot gas, only from space
Radio passes through dust; infrared sees star birth
Spectra reveal what stars are made of
Each wavelength needs its own tools

questions.prompt: What do spectral lines tell astronomers about a star?

options.label: How far away the star is
options.rationale: Distance comes from other methods, like parallax.

questions.explanation: Each element leaves its own lines, so a spectrum reveals a star’s composition.

questions.prompt: Which kind of telescope can observe through clouds and in daylight?

options.label: An X-ray telescope on the ground
An optical reflector on a mountain
options.rationale: Clouds and daylight stop optical telescopes.

options.label: An ultraviolet telescope at sea level

questions.explanation: Radio waves pass through clouds and dust, and radio telescopes can observe during the day.

questions.prompt: An astronomer wants to study the extremely hot gas around a black hole. Which tool fits best?

options.label: A radio telescope in a desert
options.rationale: Radio is better for cooler gas and dust.

options.label: A small refracting telescope
options.rationale: Visible light won’t show that hot gas well.

options.label: An infrared telescope inside a dust cloud
options.rationale: Infrared suits dust and cool objects.

options.label: An X-ray telescope in space, like Chandra

questions.explanation: Extremely hot gas glows in X-rays, and only space telescopes can see X-rays.

questions.prompt: Why was Hubble placed above Earth’s atmosphere?

options.label: To escape blurring and see light the air blocks
To get much closer to the stars
options.rationale: A few hundred km makes no difference to star distances.

options.label: To escape the pull of Earth’s gravity
options.rationale: Hubble orbits Earth; gravity still holds it.

options.label: To travel onward to other planets
options.rationale: It stays in orbit around Earth.

questions.explanation: Above the atmosphere, Hubble avoids blurring and can see ultraviolet light that never reaches the ground.

questions.prompt: Chapter 4 recap: which pairing of tool and discovery is correct?

options.label: Radio telescope → Galileo’s moons of Jupiter
X-ray telescope → Helium in the Sun
options.rationale: Helium was found in the Sun’s visible spectrum.

options.label: Spectroscope → helium found in the Sun
Infrared telescope → the first Moon rocks
options.rationale: Moon rocks came back with Apollo astronauts.

questions.explanation: Helium was discovered in 1868 as a line in the Sun’s spectrum, before it was found on Earth.

levels.title: Mercury: The Scorched Survivor
levels.objective: After this level you can describe Mercury’s extreme temperatures and its lack of atmosphere.
levels.summary: The smallest, innermost planet has almost no air, so it bakes by day and freezes by night, yet keeps ice at its poles.

cards.headline: The planet closest to the Sun has ice on it.
Small, fast and close
cards.body: Mercury is the smallest planet and the closest to the Sun. It races around its orbit in just 88 Earth days, the shortest year in the solar system.

cards.headline: No blanket
cards.body: Mercury has almost no atmosphere to hold heat. Its surface reaches about 430 °C in the day, then plunges to about −180 °C at night, one of the biggest temperature swings of any planet.

cards.fact: Mercury has ice in craters near its poles.
cards.context: The floors of some polar craters are always in shadow. Sunlight never reaches them, so water ice survives on the planet closest to the Sun.

cards.headline: Mercury: surveyed
learned: Mercury is the smallest planet and closest to the Sun
Its year is only 88 Earth days
No atmosphere: ~430 °C days, ~−180 °C nights
Shadowed polar craters hold ice

questions.prompt: Which is the smallest planet in the solar system?

questions.explanation: Mercury is the smallest planet, and the closest to the Sun.

options.label: Its surface is covered in reflective ice

questions.explanation: Venus’s thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat day and night. Mercury has almost no atmosphere, so its heat escapes.

levels.title: Venus: Earth’s Evil Twin
levels.objective: After this level you can compare Venus and Earth and describe Venus’s surface and odd rotation.
levels.summary: Venus matches Earth’s size but has 90 times the air pressure, acid clouds, and spins backwards so slowly its day outlasts its year.

cards.headline: On Venus, a day is longer than a year.
A twin gone wrong
cards.body: Venus is nearly the same size as Earth. There the resemblance ends: the air pressure at its surface is about 90 times Earth’s, and the planet is wrapped in thick clouds of sulfuric acid.

cards.headline: Backwards and slow
cards.body: Venus spins backwards compared with most planets, so the Sun rises in the west. It spins so slowly that one rotation takes 243 Earth days, longer than its 225-day trip around the Sun.

cards.fact: The Soviet Venera landers reached Venus’s surface.
cards.context: In the 1970s and 1980s they sent back the first pictures from the ground, then were destroyed by the heat and pressure within about two hours.

cards.headline: Venus: surveyed

Its surface pressure is ~90× Earth’s
It spins backwards: the Sun rises in the west
Its day (243 days) outlasts its year (225)

options.label: Frozen carbon dioxide crystals
options.rationale: Its atmosphere is carbon dioxide, but the clouds are acid.

questions.explanation: Venus is covered by thick clouds of sulfuric acid.

questions.prompt: Why is a day on Venus longer than its year?

options.label: Venus orbits the Sun unusually fast
options.rationale: Its 225-day year is ordinary; its spin is the odd part.

options.label: Venus has no day and night at all
options.rationale: It does, just very long ones.

options.label: It rotates so slowly that one spin takes longer than one orbit

options.rationale: Clouds don’t change the length of a day.

questions.explanation: Venus takes 243 Earth days to rotate once but only 225 to orbit the Sun, so its rotation outlasts its year.

questions.prompt: From Level 11: on Earth the Sun rises in the east because Earth spins west to east. What does a western sunrise on Venus tell you?

options.label: Venus spins the opposite way to Earth

options.label: Venus has no axis to spin around

levels.title: Earth: The Planet We Know Best
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Earth’s magnetic field and atmosphere protect life.
levels.summary: A magnetic field from the molten core deflects solar particles; the atmosphere and ozone layer shield us; water covers 71%.

cards.headline: A magnetic shield
cards.body: Molten iron moving in Earth’s outer core generates a magnetic field. That field deflects most of the charged particles streaming from the Sun, which would otherwise strip away atmosphere and harm life. Particles that slip through near the poles make the sky glow as auroras.

cards.headline: Air and ozone
cards.body: Earth’s atmosphere is about 78% nitrogen and 21% oxygen. High up, the ozone layer absorbs most of the Sun’s harmful ultraviolet light before it reaches the ground.

cards.fact: About 71% of Earth’s surface is covered by water.
cards.context: So far, Earth is the only planet known to have life, and all of it depends on that water.

cards.headline: Home planet: understood
learned: Molten iron in the core makes a magnetic field
The field deflects charged particles from the Sun
Air: 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen; ozone blocks UV
Water covers about 71% of Earth

questions.prompt: What is Earth’s atmosphere made of, mostly?

options.label: Oxygen, with a little carbon dioxide
Nitrogen, with about a fifth oxygen

questions.explanation: Earth’s air is about 78% nitrogen and 21% oxygen.

questions.prompt: What generates Earth’s magnetic field?

options.label: The Moon’s pull on Earth’s oceans
Molten iron moving in Earth’s outer core
Sunlight striking the ozone layer
options.rationale: The ozone layer absorbs ultraviolet light.

options.label: Magnetic rocks in Earth’s crust
options.rationale: The field comes from deep inside the planet.

questions.explanation: Moving molten iron in the outer core generates Earth’s magnetic field.

questions.prompt: From Level 1: Earth is the third planet from the Sun. What else about Earth is, so far, unique?

options.label: It is the only planet with an atmosphere
options.rationale: Venus, Mars and the giants all have atmospheres.

options.label: It has the fastest orbit of any planet

questions.explanation: Earth is the only planet known to host life, protected by its magnetic field, atmosphere and ozone layer.

levels.title: Mars: A Planet That Lost Its Water
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the evidence that Mars once had liquid water.
levels.summary: Dry riverbeds and ancient lakes show Mars was once wetter. Rovers like Curiosity and Perseverance are reading that history.

cards.headline: Mars has riverbeds. It just doesn’t have rivers anymore.
A thin, dry world
cards.body: Mars’s atmosphere is thin and mostly carbon dioxide, with less than 1% of Earth’s surface air pressure. Liquid water can’t last on its surface today, so most of its water is frozen in polar ice caps and underground.

cards.headline: Clues of a wetter past
cards.body: Dry river valleys and ancient lake beds show liquid water once flowed on Mars. NASA’s Curiosity rover, which landed in 2012, found that Gale Crater once held a lake. Perseverance landed in 2021 in Jezero Crater, an old lake and river delta, and is collecting rock samples.

cards.fact: Mars has the tallest volcano in the solar system.
cards.context: Olympus Mons towers over the Martian plains. Mars’s red color, meanwhile, comes from iron oxide, the same compound as rust, in its dust and rocks.

cards.headline: Mars: investigated
learned: Mars’s air is thin: under 1% of Earth’s pressure
Riverbeds and lake beds show a wetter past
Curiosity (2012) found an ancient lake in Gale Crater
Perseverance (2021) explores Jezero’s old delta

questions.prompt: Where is most of Mars’s water today?

options.label: In deep oceans beneath the red dust
options.rationale: Its water is frozen, not in oceans.

options.label: In rivers that flow during the summer
options.rationale: Liquid water can’t last on the surface.

options.label: Frozen in polar ice caps and underground

options.rationale: Mars’s thin air holds little water.

questions.explanation: Mars’s thin atmosphere can’t keep water liquid, so most of it is frozen in polar caps and underground.

questions.prompt: From Level 3: Mars is the outermost rocky planet. Why can’t liquid water last on its surface today?

options.label: Mars is closer to the Sun than Earth
options.rationale: Mars is farther from the Sun.

options.label: Mars has no gravity to hold water
options.rationale: Mars has gravity, weaker than Earth’s.

options.label: Mars’s iron oxide dust soaks it up
options.rationale: The dust colors Mars but isn’t the cause.

options.label: Its atmosphere is too thin, under 1% of Earth’s pressure

questions.explanation: Mars’s thin air, less than 1% of Earth’s surface pressure, means liquid water quickly freezes or evaporates.

levels.title: The Asteroid Belt
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the asteroid belt and why it never formed a planet.
levels.summary: Between Mars and Jupiter lies a sparse belt of rocky and metallic leftovers that Jupiter’s gravity kept from forming a planet.

cards.headline: The asteroid belt isn’t like the movies. It’s mostly empty.
Leftovers between the worlds
cards.body: The main asteroid belt lies between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter. Jupiter’s strong gravity stirred up the material there, keeping it from ever gathering into a planet. Most asteroids are rock; some are largely metal.

cards.headline: Less than a Moon
cards.body: All the asteroids in the main belt together have less mass than Earth’s Moon. They’re spread across such a vast space that spacecraft have crossed the belt without hitting anything.

cards.fact: The biggest object in the asteroid belt is a dwarf planet.
cards.context: Ceres is large enough to be rounded by its own gravity and is classified as a dwarf planet, like Pluto.

cards.headline: Asteroid belt: crossed
learned: The main belt lies between Mars and Jupiter
Jupiter’s gravity kept it from forming a planet
All of it together weighs less than our Moon
Ceres, its largest object, is a dwarf planet

questions.prompt: Where is the main asteroid belt?
questions.explanation: The main asteroid belt lies between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter.

questions.prompt: Why didn’t the asteroid belt form a planet?

options.label: It never had enough material to start
options.rationale: Gravity stirring is the main reason.

options.label: Jupiter’s gravity kept stirring it up
The Sun’s heat melted it apart
A planet formed and later exploded
options.rationale: There’s no evidence of an exploded planet.

questions.explanation: Jupiter’s powerful gravity stirred the material in the belt, keeping it from gathering into a single planet.

questions.prompt: From Level 4: Jupiter outweighs all the other planets combined. How does that connect to the asteroid belt?

options.label: Its huge gravity kept the belt’s material from forming a planet
Its mass pulled all the asteroids into its rings
options.rationale: Jupiter’s faint rings are dust, not asteroids.

options.label: It captured the belt’s missing planet as a moon
Its mass makes the belt spin faster than Mars
options.rationale: Its gravity’s effect was to stop a planet forming.

questions.explanation: Jupiter’s enormous mass means strong gravity, which stirred the belt and prevented a planet from forming there.

levels.title: Jupiter’s Storms and Moons
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the Great Red Spot and Jupiter’s four large moons.
levels.summary: The Great Red Spot is a storm wider than Earth. Jupiter’s four big moons range from volcanic Io to giant Ganymede.

cards.headline: Jupiter has a storm bigger than Earth that has lasted for centuries.
The Great Red Spot
cards.body: Jupiter’s Great Red Spot is a giant storm wider than Earth. Astronomers have watched it for more than 150 years, and it’s still spinning, though it has been shrinking over the past century.

cards.headline: Four worlds of their own
cards.body: Jupiter has dozens of moons, but Galileo’s four are by far the largest, and wildly different. Io is the most volcanically active world in the solar system. Ganymede is the largest moon of all, bigger than the planet Mercury. Callisto is one of the most heavily cratered worlds known. And Europa? That’s the next level.

cards.headline: Jupiter system: explored
learned: The Great Red Spot is a storm wider than Earth
It has been observed for over 150 years
Io is the most volcanic world in the solar system
Ganymede is the largest moon, bigger than Mercury

options.label: A giant volcano on its surface
A shadow cast by one of its moons

options.label: An impact crater from an asteroid
options.rationale: Jupiter has no surface for craters.

options.label: Callisto, the cratered one
options.rationale: Callisto is large, but Ganymede is bigger.

questions.explanation: Ganymede is the largest moon in the solar system and is bigger than Mercury.

levels.title: Ocean Worlds: Europa and Enceladus
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why icy moons may hide liquid-water oceans.
levels.summary: Europa and Enceladus hide oceans under ice, kept liquid by tidal flexing from their planets: prime places to look for life.

cards.headline: Some of the solar system’s biggest oceans are on moons, under ice.
Hidden seas
cards.body: Jupiter’s moon Europa has a salty ocean of liquid water beneath its icy shell, possibly holding about twice as much water as all of Earth’s oceans. At Saturn’s moon Enceladus, the Cassini spacecraft saw plumes of water ice spraying from cracks near its south pole.

cards.headline: Kept warm by squeezing
cards.body: These moons are far from the Sun, so what keeps their water liquid? Their giant planets’ gravity squeezes and flexes them as they orbit, heating their interiors. Liquid water, energy and the right chemistry are key ingredients for life, which is why NASA launched Europa Clipper in 2024 to study Europa.

cards.headline: Ocean worlds: discovered
learned: Europa has an ocean beneath its ice
It may hold twice the water of Earth’s oceans
Enceladus sprays plumes of water ice

options.label: Jupiter’s gravity flexing it, heating its interior

questions.explanation: Tidal flexing by Jupiter’s gravity heats Europa’s interior, keeping its ocean liquid.

options.label: Both need an ocean on the surface

levels.title: Titan: A World of Methane Lakes
levels.objective: After this level you can describe Titan’s thick atmosphere and liquid methane lakes.
levels.summary: Saturn’s largest moon has a thick nitrogen atmosphere and lakes of liquid methane; the Huygens probe landed there in 2005.

cards.headline: It rains on Titan. Just not water.
A moon with weather
cards.body: Titan is Saturn’s largest moon and is bigger than the planet Mercury. It’s the only moon with a thick atmosphere, made mostly of nitrogen. Methane rains from its clouds and gathers in lakes and seas of liquid methane and ethane. At about −179 °C, it’s far too cold for liquid water.

cards.headline: Earth’s strange cousin
cards.body: Apart from Earth, Titan is the only world known to have stable liquid on its surface. In 2005 the Huygens probe parachuted through its haze and landed, the first landing ever on a world in the outer solar system.

cards.headline: Titan: landed
learned: Titan is Saturn’s largest moon
It’s the only moon with a thick atmosphere
It has lakes of liquid methane and ethane
Huygens landed there in 2005

options.label: Liquid water, like Earth’s oceans
options.rationale: Titan is far too cold for liquid water on its surface.

questions.explanation: Titan’s lakes and seas are liquid methane and ethane, fed by methane rain.

levels.title: The Tilted and the Windy: Uranus and Neptune
levels.objective: After this level you can describe Uranus’s sideways tilt and Neptune’s supersonic winds.
levels.summary: Uranus rolls on its side with 42-year polar days; Neptune has the fastest winds known. Methane makes both of them blue.

cards.headline: On Uranus, a single day at the pole can last 42 years.
A planet on its side
cards.body: Uranus is tilted about 98°, so it essentially rolls around the Sun on its side. Each pole gets about 42 years of continuous sunlight, followed by 42 years of darkness.

cards.headline: The windiest planet
cards.body: Neptune has the fastest winds in the solar system, over 2,000 km/h. It’s so far out that it takes about 165 years to orbit the Sun: it completed its first orbit since its discovery only in 2011. Voyager 2 remains the only spacecraft to have visited it.

cards.fact: Methane makes Uranus and Neptune blue.
cards.context: Methane in their atmospheres absorbs red light, so the sunlight they reflect back looks blue.

cards.headline: Ice giants: visited
learned: Uranus is tilted about 98°, on its side
Its poles get 42-year days and nights
Neptune has the fastest winds: over 2,000 km/h
Methane makes both planets blue

options.label: Venus, with its thick air

levels.title: Milestone: The Solar System
levels.objective: After this level you can connect the planets, moons and small bodies into one picture of our solar system.
levels.summary: From the Sun’s 99.8% of the mass to Neptune 30 AU out, the solar system is one family shaped by gravity.

cards.headline: Milestone: halfway to Mastery. Let’s put the whole solar system in one picture.
cards.body: Everything you’ve met so far, from the Sun to Neptune, is one family shaped by gravity.

cards.headline: How big is our neighborhood?
cards.body: Neptune, the outermost planet, orbits about 30 astronomical units from the Sun: about 4.5 billion km. Sunlight, which reaches Earth in about 8 minutes, takes about 4 hours to get out there.

levels.title: Pluto and the Dwarf Planets
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what a dwarf planet is and why Pluto was reclassified.
levels.summary: The IAU’s 2006 definition requires a planet to clear its orbit. Pluto doesn’t, so it’s one of five dwarf planets.

cards.headline: Pluto didn’t change in 2006. The definition of a planet did.
Three tests for a planet
cards.body: In 2006 the International Astronomical Union defined a planet: it orbits the Sun, it’s massive enough to be round, and it has cleared the neighborhood around its orbit. Pluto passes the first two tests but shares its region with many other icy bodies, so it’s a dwarf planet.
cards.callout: Orbit the Sun · Round · Clear its orbit

cards.headline: Five dwarf planets
cards.body: The IAU recognizes five dwarf planets: Ceres, Pluto, Eris, Haumea and Makemake. Pluto itself was discovered in 1930 by Clyde Tombaugh.

cards.fact: Pluto has a heart.
cards.context: When NASA’s New Horizons flew past in 2015, it revealed a huge heart-shaped region covered in nitrogen ice.

questions.explanation: Pluto orbits the Sun and is round, but it shares its region with many icy bodies, so it hasn’t cleared its orbit.

levels.title: The Kuiper Belt
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the icy region beyond Neptune and what New Horizons found there.
levels.summary: Beyond Neptune lies the Kuiper Belt, a ring of icy bodies including Pluto. New Horizons explored Arrokoth there in 2019.

cards.headline: Past Neptune, the solar system keeps going, into the deep freeze.
A second belt
cards.body: The Kuiper Belt is a doughnut-shaped region of icy bodies beyond the orbit of Neptune. Unlike the rocky asteroid belt, it’s mostly ice, and far bigger: about 20 times as wide. Pluto is one of its largest known members, and many comets that return every few decades or centuries come from here.

cards.headline: The farthest flyby
cards.body: After passing Pluto, New Horizons kept going. In 2019 it flew past Arrokoth, a small Kuiper Belt object. It’s the most distant object ever explored up close, a frozen leftover from when the planets formed, barely changed in billions of years.

cards.headline: Kuiper Belt: explored

levels.title: Comets: Dirty Snowballs
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what comets are made of and why their tails point away from the Sun.
levels.summary: Comets are icy “dirty snowballs.” Near the Sun they grow a coma and tails that always point away from it.

cards.headline: A comet’s tail can point ahead of it.
Dirty snowballs
cards.body: Comets are chunks of ice, dust and rock, often described as dirty snowballs. Far from the Sun they’re dark and frozen. As one nears the Sun, its ice turns to gas, forming a glowing cloud called a coma and long tails.

cards.headline: Tails that point away
cards.body: Sunlight and the solar wind push a comet’s tails away from the Sun, so they always point outward, even ahead of the comet as it leaves. Many comets have two: a curved dust tail and a straighter tail of charged gas.
cards.callout: Tails point away from the Sun

cards.fact: Halley’s Comet returns about every 76 years.
cards.context: It last swung past Earth in 1986 and will be back in 2061.

cards.headline: Comets: caught
learned: Comets are ice, dust and rock
Near the Sun they form a coma and tails
Tails always point away from the Sun
Halley’s Comet returns about every 76 years

questions.prompt: What are comets made of?
questions.explanation: Comets are dirty snowballs of ice, dust and rock.

questions.prompt: Which way does a comet’s tail point?

options.label: Always behind the comet
options.rationale: As a comet leaves the Sun, its tail can lead.

questions.explanation: Sunlight and the solar wind push the tails away from the Sun, whatever direction the comet is moving.

questions.prompt: From Level 52: where do many comets that return every few decades or centuries come from?

options.label: The surface of the Sun
options.rationale: Comets come from the cold outer solar system.

questions.explanation: Many shorter-period comets come from the icy Kuiper Belt beyond Neptune.

levels.title: Shooting Stars and Meteorites
levels.objective: After this level you can tell meteoroids, meteors and meteorites apart and explain meteor showers.
levels.summary: A shooting star is a sand-grain meteoroid burning up. Meteor showers come from comet debris, like the August Perseids.

cards.headline: Most shooting stars are no bigger than a grain of sand.
Three names, one journey
cards.body: A meteoroid is a small piece of rock or debris in space. When it plunges into Earth’s atmosphere and burns up, the streak of light is a meteor, or shooting star. Any piece that survives to reach the ground is a meteorite.

cards.headline: Showers from comets
cards.body: Meteor showers happen when Earth passes through the trail of dust a comet left behind. Most of those meteors come from particles about the size of a grain of sand, burning up as streaks of light.

cards.fact: The Perseids peak every August.
cards.context: That’s when Earth crosses the debris of Comet Swift–Tuttle, one of the most reliable meteor showers of the year.

cards.headline: Shooting stars: explained
learned: Meteoroid: debris in space
Meteor: the streak of light in our sky
Meteorite: a piece that reaches the ground
Showers come from comet debris trails

options.label: A meteor that is still in space

options.label: The streak of light in the sky

questions.explanation: A meteoroid in space becomes a meteor in the sky; any piece that reaches the ground is a meteorite.

options.label: Earth passing near the asteroid belt

levels.title: The Oort Cloud
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the distant shell of icy bodies thought to surround the solar system.
levels.summary: Far beyond the Kuiper Belt, a vast shell of icy bodies is thought to surround the solar system: the source of long-period comets.

cards.headline: The solar system’s true edge may be a shell of ice no one has ever seen.
A giant shell
cards.body: The Oort Cloud is thought to be a giant spherical shell of icy bodies surrounding the whole solar system, perhaps reaching 100,000 astronomical units from the Sun. That’s about 100,000 times the Earth–Sun distance.

cards.headline: Known only from comets
cards.body: No object has ever been seen in the Oort Cloud itself. Astronomers infer it from comets that take thousands of years or more to orbit the Sun: their paths trace back to a distant shell all around us.

cards.fact: Voyager 1 will take about 300 years to reach its inner edge.
cards.context: And that’s the fastest-moving, most distant spacecraft we have.

cards.headline: Oort Cloud: imagined
learned: The Oort Cloud is thought to surround the solar system

options.label: Comets that orbit in under 10 years
Comets with no tails at all

options.label: Comets that take thousands of years to orbit

questions.explanation: Very long-period comets, taking thousands of years or more per orbit, are thought to come from the distant Oort Cloud.

levels.title: Inside the Sun
levels.objective: After this level you can name the Sun’s layers and describe how energy travels from its core to its surface.
levels.summary: Energy from the core crosses the radiative and convective zones to the ~5,500 °C photosphere. The corona is over a million °C.

cards.headline: The Sun’s outer atmosphere is hundreds of times hotter than its surface.
Layer by layer
cards.body: From the inside out: the core, where fusion happens; the radiative zone; the convective zone, where hot gas rises and sinks like boiling water; the photosphere, the visible surface; the chromosphere; and the corona.
cards.callout: Core → radiative → convective → photosphere → chromosphere → corona

cards.headline: A slow journey out
cards.body: Energy made in the core can take many thousands of years to work its way out through the Sun’s layers. Once it reaches the surface, light crosses to Earth in about 8 minutes.

cards.fact: The Sun’s surface is about 5,500 °C. Its corona tops 1 million °C.
cards.context: Why the outer atmosphere is so much hotter than the surface below is still one of solar physics’ big puzzles.

cards.headline: Solar interior: mapped
learned: Core → radiative → convective → photosphere → chromosphere → corona
The photosphere is ~5,500 °C
The corona tops 1 million °C
Energy takes thousands of years to escape the core

questions.prompt: Which layer of the Sun is its visible surface?

options.label: The core
options.rationale: The core is deep inside, where fusion happens.

questions.explanation: The photosphere is the Sun’s visible surface, at about 5,500 °C.

questions.prompt: What is surprising about the Sun’s corona?

options.label: It is the coldest part of the Sun
It can only be seen from Mars
options.rationale: It’s visible from Earth during total eclipses.

options.label: It is far hotter than the surface beneath it

questions.explanation: The corona is over 1 million °C, far hotter than the ~5,500 °C surface, a puzzle scientists still study.

questions.prompt: From Level 7: when can we most easily see the Sun’s corona from Earth?

options.label: During a lunar eclipse
options.rationale: Then Earth’s shadow falls on the Moon.

options.label: At sunrise on the summer solstice
options.rationale: The bright surface still hides it.

options.label: At full Moon
options.rationale: The Moon isn’t near the Sun at full Moon.

questions.explanation: In a total solar eclipse the Moon covers the Sun’s bright disc, revealing the faint corona around it.

levels.title: Sunspots and the Solar Cycle
levels.objective: After this level you can explain sunspots and the Sun’s roughly 11-year activity cycle.
levels.summary: Sunspots are cooler, magnetically tangled patches whose numbers rise and fall over an ~11-year solar cycle.

cards.headline: The Sun has spots, and they come and go on a schedule.
Dark, but not cold
cards.body: Sunspots are patches of the Sun’s surface where intense magnetic fields hold back the flow of heat. They’re cooler than the gas around them, so they look dark. They’re still thousands of degrees, just less bright than their surroundings.

cards.headline: An 11-year rhythm
cards.body: The number of sunspots rises and falls over a solar cycle that lasts about 11 years. At solar maximum the Sun is spotty and active; at solar minimum it can go days with no spots at all.

cards.fact: Galileo watched sunspots too.
cards.context: In the early 1600s he was among the first to observe them through a telescope, and used their motion to show that the Sun rotates.

cards.headline: Sunspots: tracked
learned: Sunspots are cooler, magnetically active patches
They look dark next to hotter gas
Their numbers follow an ~11-year cycle
Galileo used them to show the Sun rotates

options.label: About 1 year
options.rationale: The cycle is much longer than a year.

options.label: About 29.5 days
options.rationale: That’s the Moon’s cycle of phases.

questions.explanation: Sunspot numbers rise and fall over a solar cycle of about 11 years.

questions.prompt: Why do sunspots look dark?

options.label: They are cooler than the surrounding surface
They are holes that show empty space
options.rationale: They’re part of the Sun’s surface.

options.label: They are shadows cast by planets
options.rationale: Planet shadows are tiny and don’t look like spots.

options.label: They are clouds of cold dust above the Sun
options.rationale: They’re regions of the surface itself.

questions.explanation: Strong magnetic fields hold back heat, so sunspots are cooler, and therefore dimmer, than the gas around them.

questions.prompt: From Level 25: besides Jupiter’s moons and Venus’s phases, what else did Galileo observe with his telescope?
questions.explanation: Galileo observed sunspots in the early 1600s and used their motion to show that the Sun rotates.

levels.title: Solar Storms and Auroras
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how solar wind and eruptions cause auroras and space weather.
levels.summary: The solar wind and eruptions like flares and CMEs drive auroras and space weather that can disrupt satellites and power grids.

cards.headline: The Sun has weather, and it reaches all the way to us.
Wind and storms
cards.body: The Sun constantly blows a stream of charged particles into space: the solar wind. Sometimes it erupts. Solar flares are sudden bursts of radiation, and coronal mass ejections hurl huge clouds of charged particles into space.

cards.headline: When storms arrive
cards.body: When those particles reach Earth, our magnetic field steers many of them toward the poles, where they make the sky glow as auroras. Strong storms can also disrupt satellites, radio communications and power grids.

cards.fact: The Carrington Event of 1859 is the strongest solar storm on record.
cards.context: It produced auroras seen far from the poles. A storm like it today could seriously disrupt technology.

cards.headline: Space weather: forecast
learned: The Sun blows a solar wind of charged particles
Flares and CMEs are solar eruptions
Auroras glow where particles hit near the poles
Solar storms can disrupt technology

questions.prompt: What is the solar wind?

options.label: Wind blowing across the Sun’s surface
A stream of charged particles from the Sun
Gas blown off comets
options.rationale: Comet tails are pushed by it, but it comes from the Sun.

questions.explanation: The solar wind is a constant stream of charged particles flowing out from the Sun.

options.label: The poles are closest to the Sun
options.rationale: The poles aren’t closer to the Sun.

options.label: Ice at the poles reflects sunlight upward
options.rationale: Auroras are glowing air, not reflections.

options.label: Earth’s magnetic field steers solar particles toward the poles
The polar air is thinner, so light escapes

questions.explanation: Earth’s magnetic field channels charged particles toward the poles, where they make the upper air glow.

options.label: They would reach Earth’s atmosphere directly
They would be absorbed by the ozone layer

options.label: They would bounce back to the Sun
options.rationale: Without a field, nothing would deflect them.

questions.explanation: Earth’s magnetic field deflects most solar particles. Without it, far more would strike the atmosphere directly.

levels.title: How the Solar System Formed
levels.objective: After this level you can outline how the Sun and planets formed from a collapsing cloud of gas and dust.
levels.summary: A collapsing, spinning cloud flattened into a disk: the Sun at its center, rocky planets inside the frost line, giants outside.

cards.headline: Every planet, moon and comet began as part of one cloud.
A spinning cloud collapses
cards.body: About 4.6 billion years ago, a cloud of gas and dust began collapsing under its own gravity. As it shrank it spun faster and flattened into a disk, with the young Sun forming at the center. That’s why the planets still orbit in nearly the same plane.

cards.headline: The frost line
cards.body: Close to the young Sun it was too hot for ices to form, so only rock and metal could clump into planets: small, rocky worlds. Farther out, beyond the frost line, ices could condense too. With far more material to build from, the giant planets grew huge.

cards.headline: Origins: reconstructed
learned: The solar system formed ~4.6 billion years ago
A spinning cloud collapsed into a flat disk
Inside the frost line, rocky planets formed
Outside it, ices helped the giants grow

questions.explanation: Near the Sun only rock and metal could condense. Farther out, ices could too, so the outer planets had much more material and grew into giants.

levels.title: Checkpoint: The Sun’s Domain
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the Sun and everything it influences, from its core to the Oort Cloud.
levels.summary: The solar wind blows a bubble, the heliosphere, around the planets. Voyager 1 crossed its edge in 2012.

cards.headline: Chapter 6 finale. Where does the solar system actually end?
cards.body: It depends on what you measure: the planets, the solar wind, or the Sun’s gravity.

cards.headline: The Sun’s bubble
cards.body: The solar wind blows a vast bubble around the Sun and planets called the heliosphere. Its outer edge, the heliopause, is where the solar wind gives way to interstellar space. Voyager 1 crossed it in 2012.

cards.headline: But gravity reaches farther
cards.body: The Sun’s gravity still holds on far beyond the heliosphere. The Oort Cloud, thought to reach as far as 100,000 AU, is the outermost part of the solar system, which Voyager 1 won’t reach for about 300 years.

levels.title: Parallax: Measuring the Stars
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how parallax measures the distance to nearby stars.
levels.summary: Nearby stars shift slightly as Earth orbits; the smaller the shift, the farther the star. Gaia has measured over a billion.

cards.headline: Blink one eye, then the other. That jump is how we measure the stars.
cards.body: Hold a finger in front of your face and it seems to hop against the background. Stars do the same as Earth moves.

cards.headline: A six-month baseline
cards.body: As Earth orbits the Sun, a nearby star appears to shift slightly against more distant stars. Measure the star in January and again in July, from opposite sides of Earth’s orbit, and that tiny shift reveals its distance.

cards.headline: Closer shifts more
cards.body: The closer a star is, the bigger its parallax shift. Astronomers even named a unit after it: a parsec, the distance at which the shift would be one arcsecond, is about 3.26 light-years.

cards.fact: The Gaia spacecraft has measured more than a billion stars.
cards.context: This European Space Agency mission has mapped the positions and distances of stars across our galaxy using parallax.

cards.headline: Star distances: measured
learned: Parallax: nearby stars shift as Earth orbits
Bigger shift = closer star
1 parsec ≈ 3.26 light-years
Gaia has measured over a billion stars

options.label: The star moving through space

options.label: Earth’s daily spin on its axis

questions.explanation: As Earth moves around its orbit, our viewpoint changes, so nearby stars seem to shift against distant ones.

questions.explanation: Closer stars show larger parallax shifts, so Star A is nearer.

levels.title: Bright or Close? Luminosity
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the difference between how bright a star looks and how bright it really is.
levels.summary: A star’s apparent brightness depends on its luminosity and its distance, fading with the square of distance.

cards.headline: The brightest star in the sky isn’t the most powerful. It’s just close.
Two kinds of bright
cards.body: How bright a star looks from Earth depends on two things: how much light it really gives off, its luminosity, and how far away it is. A modest star nearby can outshine a powerhouse far away.

cards.headline: Fading with distance
cards.body: A star’s brightness falls with the square of its distance. Move a star twice as far away and it looks only a quarter as bright; ten times as far, a hundredth.
cards.callout: Twice as far → ¼ as bright

cards.fact: Sirius, the brightest night-time star, is about 8.6 light-years away.
cards.context: It’s more luminous than the Sun, and relatively close. Many far more powerful stars look fainter because they are much farther away.

cards.headline: Starlight: weighed
learned: Apparent brightness depends on luminosity and distance
Brightness falls with the square of distance
Sirius looks brightest partly because it’s close
Luminosity is a star’s true output

questions.prompt: What is a star’s luminosity?

options.label: How bright it looks from Earth

How far away it is in light-years
How hot its surface is in degrees
options.rationale: Temperature is related, but luminosity is total output.

questions.explanation: Luminosity is a star’s true light output, regardless of distance.

questions.prompt: A star is moved to twice its distance. How bright does it look?
questions.explanation: Brightness falls with the square of distance: twice as far means 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4 as bright.

questions.prompt: From Level 27: which other effect weakens with the square of distance, just like starlight?

options.label: How fast a planet spins on its axis
options.rationale: Spin rate doesn’t depend on distance from anything.

questions.explanation: Newton’s gravity and starlight both spread out and weaken with the square of the distance.

levels.title: The H–R Diagram
levels.objective: After this level you can read the basic pattern of the Hertzsprung–Russell diagram.
levels.summary: Plot stars by luminosity and temperature and a pattern appears: the main sequence, with giants above and white dwarfs below.

cards.headline: Put every star on one chart and a hidden pattern jumps out.
Luminosity versus temperature
cards.body: The Hertzsprung–Russell diagram plots stars by how luminous they are and how hot their surfaces are. It’s named after Ejnar Hertzsprung and Henry Norris Russell, who developed it independently in the early 1900s.

cards.headline: Where the stars fall
cards.body: Most stars fall along a diagonal band called the main sequence, and the Sun sits near its middle: a thoroughly average star. Red giants sit in the upper right: cool but very luminous. White dwarfs sit in the lower left: hot but dim. A star’s place on the chart tells you what stage of life it’s in.

cards.headline: H–R diagram: read
learned: The H–R diagram plots luminosity against temperature

A star’s position shows its life stage

questions.explanation: The H–R diagram plots each star’s luminosity against its surface temperature.

questions.explanation: Temperature runs left to right on the H–R diagram, hottest on the left, so a blue-white star sits to the left of a red one.

levels.title: The Main Sequence
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why a star’s mass decides its temperature and lifetime.
levels.summary: Main-sequence stars fuse hydrogen. The most massive burn out in millions of years; red dwarfs can last trillions.

cards.headline: Life on the main sequence
cards.body: A main-sequence star is fusing hydrogen into helium in its core. Stars spend most of their lives this way, which is why most stars on the H–R diagram fall on the main sequence. The Sun will spend about 10 billion years there in total.

cards.headline: Mass sets the pace
cards.body: A more massive star has a hotter, denser core, so it fuses its fuel much faster. It shines hotter and brighter, but the most massive stars last only a few million years. The smallest, red dwarfs, use fuel so slowly they can shine for trillions of years.
cards.callout: More mass → hotter, brighter, shorter life

cards.fact: Our nearest stellar neighbor is a red dwarf.
cards.context: Proxima Centauri is small, cool and dim, far too faint to see without a telescope, but it will outlive the Sun by an enormous margin.

levels.title: Star Partners: Binary Stars
levels.objective: After this level you can explain binary stars and how they let astronomers weigh stars.
levels.summary: Many stars orbit partners. Watching two stars orbit lets astronomers weigh them with the laws of gravity.

cards.headline: Our Sun is a bit of a loner.
Stars in pairs
cards.body: Many stars orbit a companion. Our nearest neighbor, Alpha Centauri, is a system of three stars, including Proxima Centauri. Even Sirius has a small, faint partner, Sirius B, which is a white dwarf.

cards.headline: Weighing stars
cards.body: You can’t put a star on a scale, but two stars orbiting each other obey the laws of gravity. Measure the size and timing of their orbit, and you can calculate their masses. Binary stars are how astronomers first weighed stars. Some pairs even pass in front of each other, dimming like clockwork: eclipsing binaries.

cards.headline: Binary stars: weighed
learned: Many stars orbit companions
Alpha Centauri has three stars
Sirius has a white dwarf partner
Binary orbits reveal stars’ masses

questions.prompt: How many stars are in the Alpha Centauri system?
questions.explanation: Alpha Centauri has three stars, including Proxima Centauri.

questions.prompt: Why are binary stars so useful to astronomers?

options.label: They are always brighter than single stars
Their orbits reveal the stars’ masses
They show where black holes are

questions.explanation: Using the laws of gravity, the size and period of a binary’s orbit give the stars’ masses.

questions.prompt: From Level 27: which law lets astronomers turn a binary star’s orbit into a mass?

options.label: The law of the tides
options.rationale: Tides are an effect of gravity, not the tool.

options.label: The inverse square law of light

questions.explanation: Newton’s gravity links orbit size and period to mass, whether for planets or pairs of stars.

levels.title: Stellar Nurseries
levels.objective: After this level you can describe how stars form inside nebulae.
levels.summary: Stars form in cold, dense clouds of gas and dust. The Orion Nebula, 1,300 light-years away, is the nearest big nursery.

cards.headline: Stars are being born right now, and you can see one nursery yourself.
From cloud to star
cards.body: Stars form inside cold, dense clouds of gas and dust. Gravity pulls clumps of the cloud together. As a clump shrinks, its center gets hotter and denser, until it’s hot enough for fusion to begin. A star is born.

cards.headline: The nearest nursery
cards.body: The Orion Nebula, about 1,300 light-years away, is the nearest large region of star formation. Look at the sword hanging from Orion’s belt on a dark night and you’ll see it as a fuzzy patch.

cards.fact: Hubble photographed the “Pillars of Creation” in 1995.
cards.context: These towering columns of gas and dust in the Eagle Nebula are full of forming stars, one of the most famous images in astronomy.

cards.headline: Star birth: witnessed
learned: Stars form in cold, dense clouds
Gravity pulls clumps together until fusion ignites
The Orion Nebula is the nearest big nursery
Hubble imaged the Pillars of Creation in 1995

options.label: On the surfaces of old stars

questions.explanation: Stars form in cold, dense clouds of gas and dust, where gravity pulls clumps together.

options.label: Its core becomes hot enough for fusion to begin

options.rationale: Comets have no effect on this.

options.label: It cools until it freezes solid

questions.explanation: As the clump shrinks, its core heats up until hydrogen fusion ignites. Then it’s a star.

levels.title: Red Giants and Planetary Nebulae
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Sun-like stars swell and shed their outer layers.
levels.summary: When the core runs low on hydrogen, a Sun-like star swells into a red giant, then puffs off its outer layers as a planetary nebula.

cards.headline: Someday the Sun will swallow Mercury and Venus.
Swelling up
cards.body: When a Sun-like star’s core runs low on hydrogen, the core contracts and heats up while the star’s outer layers swell enormously. It becomes a red giant. The Sun is expected to grow large enough to engulf Mercury and Venus, and possibly Earth.

cards.headline: A glowing farewell
cards.body: Late in life, a Sun-like star sheds its outer layers into space as a glowing shell of gas called a planetary nebula. Despite the name, it has nothing to do with planets: early astronomers thought these round glows looked like planets’ disks through small telescopes. Each one glows for only tens of thousands of years.

cards.headline: Red giants: understood
learned: Low core hydrogen → the star swells into a red giant
The Sun may engulf Mercury, Venus and possibly Earth
It then sheds a planetary nebula
Planetary nebulae have nothing to do with planets

options.label: A cloud where planets are forming
options.rationale: Despite the name, it has nothing to do with planets.

options.label: A glowing shell of gas shed by a dying Sun-like star

The dusty ring around a gas giant

questions.explanation: A planetary nebula is the glowing shell of gas a Sun-like star sheds late in its life.

questions.prompt: What happens to a Sun-like star when its core runs low on hydrogen?

options.label: It shrinks into a black hole
options.rationale: Sun-like stars don’t become black holes.

options.label: Its core contracts while its outer layers swell into a red giant
It stops shining immediately
options.rationale: It keeps shining as a red giant.

questions.explanation: The core contracts and heats up while the outer layers swell, turning the star into a red giant.

options.label: Up and to the right: cooler but more luminous
Down and to the left: hotter but dimmer
Nowhere: stars never move on the diagram
options.rationale: A star moves as its life stage changes.

questions.explanation: Red giants are cool but very luminous, so the Sun will move up and to the right on the H–R diagram.

levels.title: White Dwarfs
levels.objective: After this level you can describe white dwarfs and why they slowly cool.
levels.summary: A white dwarf is a dead star’s core: Earth-sized, nearly Sun-massive, so dense a teaspoon weighs tons, and slowly cooling.

cards.headline: A teaspoon of this star would weigh several tons.
A star-sized core in an Earth-sized ball
cards.body: After shedding its outer layers, a Sun-like star leaves behind its exposed core: a white dwarf. It’s about the size of Earth, but with a mass comparable to the Sun’s. That makes it incredibly dense: a teaspoonful would weigh several tons on Earth.

cards.headline: Slowly fading
cards.body: A white dwarf no longer fuses anything. It shines only with its leftover heat and slowly cools over billions of years. The nearest example is Sirius B, the faint partner of the brightest star in the sky. Most stars in our galaxy, the Sun included, will end this way.

cards.headline: White dwarfs: understood
learned: A white dwarf is a dead Sun-like star’s core
It’s about Earth-sized with much of the Sun’s mass
A teaspoon would weigh several tons

options.label: About the size of the Sun

options.label: It no longer fuses, so it just cools off

options.rationale: It no longer fuses at all.

questions.explanation: With no fusion left, a white dwarf only radiates stored heat, slowly cooling over billions of years.

levels.title: Supernovae and Star Stuff
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how massive stars explode and scatter the elements we are made of.
levels.summary: Stars over ~8 Suns’ mass end in core-collapse supernovae, spreading the elements forged in stars, including those in us.

cards.headline: The iron in your blood was made inside a star.
Going out with a bang
cards.body: Stars more than about eight times as massive as the Sun end their lives when their cores collapse. The collapse triggers a supernova, an explosion that can briefly outshine an entire galaxy.

cards.headline: Cosmic recycling
cards.body: Nearly all the elements heavier than hydrogen and helium were made by nuclear reactions inside stars and in stellar explosions. Supernovae scatter them into space, where they become part of new stars, planets and people. The calcium in your bones was forged in stars that died before the Sun formed.

cards.fact: In 1987, a supernova was visible to the naked eye.
cards.context: It exploded in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a small galaxy near the Milky Way: the closest supernova seen in centuries.

cards.headline: Star stuff: traced
learned: Stars over ~8 Suns end in core-collapse supernovae
Heavy elements are forged in stars
Supernovae scatter them into new stars and planets
Your bones and blood contain star-made elements

options.label: Stars more than about eight times the Sun’s mass

options.rationale: Planets don’t decide a star’s fate.

questions.explanation: Stars more than about eight times as massive as the Sun end in core-collapse supernovae.

options.label: They were made by the Big Bang alone

options.label: They were forged inside stars and spread by stellar explosions

options.label: They arrived on comets only recently

questions.explanation: Heavier elements, like the calcium in bones and the iron in blood, were made in stars and scattered by supernovae.

options.label: They measure how loud the explosion was

questions.explanation: Each element leaves its own spectral lines, so a supernova’s spectrum reveals what it contains.

levels.title: Checkpoint: The Lives of Stars
levels.objective: After this level you can trace a star’s life from nebula to its final state based on its mass.
levels.summary: Mass decides everything: Sun-like stars end as white dwarfs, while the most massive leave neutron stars or black holes.

cards.headline: Chapter 7 finale. One number decides a star’s whole life story.
cards.body: That number is its mass.

cards.headline: Two paths
cards.body: A star’s final fate depends mainly on its mass. A Sun-like star swells into a red giant, sheds a planetary nebula and ends as a white dwarf. A star far more massive than the Sun explodes as a supernova and leaves behind something much stranger: a neutron star or a black hole.
cards.callout: Sun-like → white dwarf · Massive → neutron star or black hole

events.label: Collapses from a cloud of gas and dust

learned: A star’s mass decides its fate

questions.explanation: Parallax, the shift as Earth orbits, gives a nearby star’s distance directly.

levels.title: Neutron Stars
levels.objective: After this level you can describe neutron stars and how dense they are.
levels.summary: A supernova can leave a neutron star: about 20 km across, heavier than the Sun, so dense a teaspoon weighs billions of tons.

cards.headline: A star heavier than the Sun, squeezed into the size of a city.
What a supernova leaves behind
cards.body: When a massive star explodes as a supernova, its core can collapse into a neutron star. It’s only about 20 km across, about the size of a city, yet it can hold more mass than the Sun.

cards.headline: Crushed to neutrons
cards.body: Gravity squeezes the core so hard that its matter becomes mostly neutrons, packed tightly together. The result is so dense that a teaspoonful would weigh billions of tons on Earth, far more than a white dwarf’s few tons. Many neutron stars also spin many times per second, with magnetic fields far stronger than Earth’s.

cards.headline: Neutron stars: understood
learned: A neutron star is a supernova’s collapsed core
It is about 20 km across
It can hold more mass than the Sun
A teaspoon would weigh billions of tons

questions.prompt: About how wide is a neutron star?

options.label: About the size of the Sun
About 20 km, the size of a city

questions.explanation: A neutron star packs more than the Sun’s mass into a ball only about 20 km across.

questions.prompt: What makes a neutron star so incredibly dense?

options.label: Gravity crushes its matter into tightly packed neutrons
It is made of solid iron
It absorbs nearby planets
options.rationale: Density comes from collapse, not eating planets.

questions.explanation: The collapsing core is crushed until its matter is mostly neutrons packed tightly together.

options.label: It is lighter than a white dwarf
It is about the same weight

options.label: It weighs nothing, being a star
A teaspoon weighs billions of tons

questions.explanation: A white dwarf teaspoon weighs a few tons; a neutron star teaspoon weighs billions of tons.

levels.title: Pulsars: Cosmic Lighthouses
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what pulsars are and how they were discovered.
levels.summary: Pulsars are spinning neutron stars whose beams sweep past Earth. Jocelyn Bell Burnell discovered the first in 1967.

cards.headline: A signal so regular it was nicknamed “LGM”: little green men.
cards.body: In 1967 a radio telescope picked up a pulse that ticked like a clock. It wasn’t aliens.

cards.headline: Lighthouses in space
cards.body: A pulsar is a spinning neutron star that sends out beams of radio waves. Each time a beam sweeps past Earth, we see a pulse, just like a lighthouse. Some pulsars spin hundreds of times every second.

cards.headline: The discovery
cards.body: The first pulsar was discovered in 1967 by Jocelyn Bell Burnell, then a graduate student, while studying radio signals. The pulses were so regular that her team briefly considered, half-jokingly, that they might be artificial.

cards.fact: The Crab Nebula has a pulsar at its heart.
cards.context: The nebula is the remains of a supernova that Chinese astronomers recorded in 1054.

cards.headline: Pulsars: detected
learned: A pulsar is a spinning neutron star
Its beams sweep past Earth like a lighthouse
Jocelyn Bell Burnell found the first in 1967
The Crab Nebula has a pulsar at its center

options.label: A star that grows and shrinks each day
options.rationale: Pulses come from a spinning beam.

options.label: A spinning neutron star whose beam sweeps past Earth
A planet that reflects starlight in flashes

questions.explanation: A pulsar is a spinning neutron star whose beams sweep past Earth like a lighthouse.

levels.title: Black Holes
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what a black hole is and how one forms.
levels.summary: A black hole is where gravity is so strong nothing escapes. Stellar ones form when very massive stars collapse.

cards.headline: A place where escape velocity is faster than light.
Gravity wins
cards.body: A black hole is a region of space where gravity is so strong that nothing, not even light, can escape. Stellar black holes form when the core of a very massive star collapses at the end of its life, with nothing strong enough to stop the collapse.

cards.headline: Not a cosmic vacuum cleaner
cards.body: Black holes don’t suck everything in. From a safe distance, a black hole’s gravity is the same as that of any object with the same mass. If the Sun were swapped for a black hole of equal mass, the planets would keep orbiting just as they do now.
cards.callout: Same mass → same pull at a distance

cards.headline: Black holes: understood
learned: Nothing, not even light, escapes a black hole
Stellar black holes form from collapsing massive stars
At a distance, their gravity is like any equal mass

options.rationale: Distance isn’t what makes it black.

options.label: It is surrounded by dust clouds

questions.explanation: A black hole’s gravity is so strong that no light escapes, so it appears black.

options.label: Earth would be pulled in immediately
options.rationale: Its gravity at our distance would be unchanged.

options.label: Earth would fly off into space

options.label: Earth would stop orbiting and freeze in place

questions.explanation: At a distance, a black hole’s gravity equals that of any object with the same mass, so Earth’s orbit wouldn’t change, though it would get very cold.

questions.explanation: Near a black hole, escaping would require going faster than light, which nothing can do.

levels.title: The Event Horizon
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the event horizon and what the first black hole image showed.
levels.summary: The event horizon is the point of no return. In 2019 an Earth-sized network of radio dishes imaged M87’s black hole.

cards.headline: In 2019, humanity saw a black hole for the first time. Sort of.
The point of no return
cards.body: Every black hole is surrounded by an event horizon: the boundary beyond which nothing, not even light, can escape. Outside it, light and matter can still get away. Inside it, there is no way back.

cards.headline: An Earth-sized telescope
cards.body: To see something that small and far away, astronomers linked radio telescopes around the world into the Event Horizon Telescope, which works like one Earth-sized dish. In 2019 it released the first image of a black hole: a dark shadow ringed by glowing gas, at the center of the galaxy M87.

cards.fact: M87’s black hole is about 6.5 billion times the mass of the Sun.
cards.context: It isn’t a stellar black hole but a supermassive one, sitting at the heart of a giant galaxy.

cards.headline: Event horizon: seen
learned: The event horizon is the point of no return
The EHT links dishes into an Earth-sized telescope
It imaged M87’s black hole in 2019
That black hole is ~6.5 billion Suns

options.rationale: The horizon is a boundary, not the center.

options.label: The jet of particles it shoots out
options.rationale: Jets come from outside the horizon.

questions.explanation: The event horizon is the point of no return: beyond it, nothing can escape, not even light.

levels.title: The Black Hole at Our Center
levels.objective: After this level you can describe Sagittarius A* and how astronomers found it.
levels.summary: At the Milky Way’s heart lies Sagittarius A*, about 4 million Suns. Stars orbiting it revealed it; the EHT imaged it in 2022.

cards.headline: Our galaxy has a monster at its center, and we watched stars orbit it.
Following the stars
cards.body: About 27,000 light-years away, at the center of the Milky Way, stars race around an invisible object. By tracking their orbits for decades, astronomers worked out its mass: about 4 million times the Sun’s, packed into a region far too small to be anything but a black hole. One star, S2, circles it about every 16 years.

cards.headline: A prize and a picture
cards.body: Reinhard Genzel and Andrea Ghez shared the 2020 Nobel Prize in Physics for this discovery. In 2022 the Event Horizon Telescope released an image of Sagittarius A* itself.

levels.title: Gravitational Waves
levels.objective: After this level you can explain gravitational waves and how LIGO first detected them.
levels.summary: Einstein predicted ripples in spacetime in 1916. LIGO caught them in 2015 from merging black holes 1.3 billion light-years away.

cards.headline: In 2015, humans felt two black holes collide.
Ripples in spacetime
cards.body: Albert Einstein’s general theory of relativity predicted in 1916 that massive objects accelerating violently would send ripples through spacetime itself: gravitational waves. For almost a century, they were too faint to detect.

cards.headline: The first detection
cards.body: On September 14, 2015, LIGO detected gravitational waves from two black holes merging about 1.3 billion light-years away. The discovery earned the 2017 Nobel Prize in Physics. To catch it, LIGO measured a change in length far smaller than the width of a proton.

cards.fact: In 2017, astronomers saw two neutron stars collide, and caught its ripples.
cards.context: The merger sent out gravitational waves and light, and it forged heavy elements like gold.

cards.headline: Gravitational waves: detected
learned: Einstein predicted gravitational waves in 1916
LIGO detected them in 2015 from merging black holes
The discovery won the 2017 Nobel Prize
Merging neutron stars forge gold

options.label: Sound waves traveling through space

options.label: Waves in the ocean caused by gravity
Bursts of radio waves from pulsars

questions.explanation: Gravitational waves are ripples in spacetime, predicted by Einstein and caused by massive objects accelerating violently.

options.label: A supernova in our galaxy

options.label: The Big Bang

levels.title: Finding Exoplanets
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the transit and wobble methods for finding planets around other stars.
levels.summary: Since 1995, astronomers have found more than 5,000 exoplanets, mostly from the dips and wobbles they cause in their stars.

cards.headline: Thousands of planets found, and almost none of them actually seen.
Worlds beyond the Sun
cards.body: An exoplanet is a planet orbiting a star other than the Sun. In 1995 Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz found the first around a Sun-like star, 51 Pegasi b, work that earned the 2019 Nobel Prize in Physics. Today more than 5,000 are confirmed.
cards.callout: 1995: the first around a Sun-like star

cards.headline: Dips and wobbles
cards.body: Most exoplanets are found indirectly. The transit method watches for the small, regular dip in a star’s light when a planet passes in front of it. The wobble method detects the slight back-and-forth motion a planet’s gravity gives its star, measured through shifts in the star’s spectrum.

cards.fact: NASA’s Kepler telescope found thousands of exoplanets.
cards.context: It stared at the same patch of sky for years, watching for tiny dips in starlight as planets crossed their stars.

cards.headline: Exoplanets: detected
learned: An exoplanet orbits a star other than the Sun
The first around a Sun-like star was found in 1995

Wobbles: the star’s spectrum shifts

questions.explanation: As the planet tugs its star back and forth, the star’s spectral lines shift slightly, revealing the unseen planet.

levels.title: The Habitable Zone
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the habitable zone and why liquid water matters.
levels.summary: The habitable zone is where a planet could hold liquid water. It sits closer to dim stars; TRAPPIST-1 has planets in its zone.

cards.headline: Not too hot, not too cold. Planets have a Goldilocks zone.
Just right for water
cards.body: The habitable zone is the range of distances from a star where a planet’s surface could be the right temperature for liquid water. Around dim, cool stars it lies much closer in; around bright stars, farther out.
cards.callout: Dim star → close zone · Bright star → far zone

cards.headline: Not a guarantee
cards.body: Being in the habitable zone doesn’t guarantee water, let alone life. A planet’s atmosphere matters too: too thick and it overheats, too thin and water escapes or freezes.

cards.fact: TRAPPIST-1 has seven Earth-sized planets.
cards.context: This red dwarf about 40 light-years away has several planets in its habitable zone, all orbiting much closer than Mercury does to the Sun.

cards.headline: Habitable zone: mapped
learned: The habitable zone allows liquid surface water
Dim stars have close-in zones
Location isn’t a guarantee: atmospheres matter
TRAPPIST-1 has planets in its zone

questions.prompt: What is a star’s habitable zone?

options.label: The region where a star is born
Where a planet could be the right temperature for liquid water
The part of a star that can be seen
The area where comets form
options.rationale: Comets come from the Kuiper Belt and Oort Cloud.

questions.explanation: The habitable zone is the range of distances where a planet’s surface could hold liquid water.

questions.prompt: Why is the habitable zone around a red dwarf so close to the star?

options.label: Red dwarfs are dim and cool, so planets must be close to stay warm
Red dwarfs have stronger gravity
options.rationale: Gravity isn’t what sets the zone.

options.label: Red dwarfs are bigger than the Sun
Red dwarfs have no planets far away
options.rationale: The zone is set by warmth.

questions.explanation: A dim star gives off little heat, so the zone where water could stay liquid lies close to it.

options.label: It is too far from the Sun

options.label: Its thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps too much heat

questions.explanation: Venus’s thick atmosphere traps heat, pushing its surface over 450 °C. Location alone doesn’t make a planet habitable.

levels.title: The Search for Life
levels.objective: After this level you can describe how scientists look for signs of life beyond Earth.
levels.summary: Scientists hunt for biosignatures on Mars, in ocean moons and in exoplanet air, and SETI listens for signals. None confirmed yet.

cards.headline: Are we alone? We finally have tools that could answer.
Close to home
cards.body: In our own solar system, scientists search places where water exists or once existed: ancient Martian lake beds, where Perseverance is collecting rock samples, and ocean moons like Europa and Enceladus. Liquid water, energy and the right chemistry are the clues to follow.

cards.headline: Reading alien air
cards.body: Around other stars, scientists look for biosignatures: gases, such as oxygen and methane together, that living things could produce. The James Webb Space Telescope can analyze starlight filtering through some exoplanets’ atmospheres to see what gases they hold.

cards.fact: No life has yet been confirmed beyond Earth.
cards.context: Meanwhile, SETI projects listen for radio and other signals that a technological civilization might send.

cards.headline: Search for life: underway
learned: Scientists search Mars and ocean moons for signs of life
Biosignatures are gases life could produce
Webb reads exoplanet atmospheres
No life beyond Earth is confirmed yet

questions.prompt: What is a biosignature?

options.label: A radio signal from aliens
options.rationale: That would be a technosignature, SETI’s target.

options.label: A fossil found on Earth
options.rationale: Biosignatures are signs of life elsewhere.

options.label: The signature on a space mission
A sign, like certain gases, that life might be present

questions.explanation: A biosignature is evidence, such as oxygen and methane together, that life could be producing.

questions.prompt: How can Webb study an exoplanet’s atmosphere without visiting it?

options.label: By analyzing starlight that passes through the atmosphere
By listening to its radio signals

questions.explanation: Gases in the atmosphere absorb specific wavelengths of the starlight passing through, leaving fingerprints Webb can read.

questions.prompt: From Level 47: why are Europa and Enceladus high on the list of places to look for life?

options.label: They are the warmest worlds in the solar system
They have liquid water, energy and the right chemistry
They are the closest moons to Earth

questions.explanation: These moons hide liquid water oceans heated by tidal flexing: key ingredients for life as we know it.

levels.title: Checkpoint: Extreme Objects and Other Worlds
levels.objective: After this level you can compare the remnants stars leave behind and explain how we find other worlds.
levels.summary: White dwarfs are Earth-sized, neutron stars city-sized, black holes have no surface. And thousands of other worlds await.

cards.headline: Chapter 8 finale. From dead stars to living worlds.
cards.body: Here’s what stars leave behind, and where life might be waiting.

cards.headline: What’s left when a star dies

items.label: Neutron star
points: About the size of a city

cards.headline: Listening and looking
cards.body: Pulsars announce neutron stars with radio pulses. Gravitational waves reveal black holes and neutron stars colliding. And transits and wobbles have uncovered thousands of worlds around other stars, some in their habitable zones. Each discovery came from reading a different kind of signal.

cards.headline: Chapter 8 complete
learned: White dwarf: Earth-sized
Neutron star: city-sized, far denser
Black hole: no surface, only an event horizon
Transits and wobbles reveal other worlds

levels.title: Kinds of Galaxies
levels.objective: After this level you can tell spiral, elliptical and irregular galaxies apart.
levels.summary: Galaxies come in three main shapes: spirals with arms and new stars, smooth ellipticals of old stars, and shapeless irregulars.

cards.headline: Galaxies come in shapes, and each shape tells a story.
Three main types
cards.body: In the 1920s Edwin Hubble sorted galaxies by shape. Spiral galaxies have a flat, rotating disk with spiral arms, where young stars are still forming. Elliptical galaxies are smooth, rounded collections of mostly older stars, with little new star formation.

cards.headline: And the rest
cards.body: Irregular galaxies have no clear shape at all. Two of the best known, the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds, are close neighbors of the Milky Way.

cards.fact: Our galaxy is a barred spiral.
cards.context: The Milky Way is a spiral with a bar of stars across its center, as you first learned back in Level 1.

cards.headline: Galaxy types: sorted
learned: Galaxies are spiral, elliptical or irregular
Spirals have arms full of young stars
Ellipticals are smooth and mostly old
The Magellanic Clouds are irregulars

questions.prompt: Which kind of galaxy has a flat, rotating disk with arms winding out from its center?

options.label: Globular
options.rationale: Globular clusters are star clusters, not galaxy types.

questions.explanation: Spiral galaxies have flat, rotating disks with spiral arms.

questions.prompt: An astronomer finds a galaxy of mostly old stars with little new star formation. What type is it most likely?

options.label: Spiral
options.rationale: Spirals are still forming young stars in their arms.

options.label: Barred spiral
options.rationale: Barred spirals also form stars in their arms.

questions.explanation: Elliptical galaxies are smooth collections of mostly older stars with little ongoing star formation.

questions.prompt: From Level 66: where in a spiral galaxy would you expect to find the most stellar nurseries?

options.label: In the halo around the galaxy

options.label: Nowhere: spirals no longer form stars

levels.title: Inside the Milky Way
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the Milky Way’s disk, spiral arms, central bulge and halo.
levels.summary: The Milky Way has a bulge, a disk with arms and a halo. The Sun sits 26,000 light-years out and circles every 230 million years.

cards.headline: The Sun has circled the Milky Way only about 20 times since it formed.
The anatomy of a galaxy
cards.body: The Milky Way has a central bulge of stars, a flat disk about 100,000 light-years across with spiral arms, and a surrounding halo of old stars and globular star clusters. At the very center sits Sagittarius A*.

cards.headline: Our place in it
cards.body: The Sun lies about 26,000 light-years from the center, in a minor spiral arm. It orbits the galactic center too, taking about 230 million years for one lap, a “galactic year.” Since the Sun formed about 4.6 billion years ago, it has made only about 20 laps.

cards.headline: Our galaxy: mapped
learned: The Milky Way has a bulge, a disk with arms, and a halo
The Sun is ~26,000 light-years from the center
One galactic orbit takes ~230 million years
Sagittarius A* sits at the center

options.label: About 13.8 billion years
options.rationale: That’s the age of the universe.

questions.explanation: The Sun takes about 230 million years to circle the Milky Way’s center once.

questions.prompt: Where is the Sun located in the Milky Way?

options.label: At the exact center, near Sagittarius A*
options.rationale: The center is about 26,000 light-years away.

options.label: In the disk, about 26,000 light-years from the center

options.rationale: The Sun is in the disk.

levels.title: When Galaxies Collide
levels.objective: After this level you can explain galaxy collisions and the future merger of the Milky Way and Andromeda.
levels.summary: Galaxies merge over hundreds of millions of years. Andromeda is heading our way, but stars almost never hit each other.

cards.headline: Andromeda is on a collision course with the Milky Way.
Cosmic collisions
cards.body: Galaxies can collide and merge, pulling each other into new shapes over hundreds of millions of years. Andromeda, about 2.5 million light-years away, is moving toward the Milky Way, and the two are expected to merge in about 4.5 billion years.

cards.headline: Crash without a crash
cards.body: When galaxies collide, individual stars almost never hit each other. The spaces between stars are so vast that the galaxies pass through each other, their gravity reshaping both. Mergers like this are one way galaxies grow.

cards.fact: You can see the other half of this collision.
cards.context: From a dark site, Andromeda is visible to the naked eye as a faint smudge, about 2.5 million light-years away and slowly getting closer.

cards.headline: Galaxy collisions: forecast
learned: Galaxies can collide and merge
Andromeda is heading toward the Milky Way
A merger is expected in ~4.5 billion years
Stars almost never hit each other

options.label: The Large Magellanic Cloud only
options.rationale: The big merger is with Andromeda.

options.label: M87
options.rationale: M87 is far away in another cluster.

questions.explanation: Andromeda is approaching the Milky Way, and the two galaxies are expected to merge.

questions.prompt: When two galaxies collide, what happens to most of their stars?

options.label: They are swallowed by black holes
They pass each other without hitting

questions.explanation: The spaces between stars are so vast that stars almost never collide, even when whole galaxies merge.

questions.prompt: From Level 10: Andromeda is about 2.5 million light-years away. Roughly how long until the merger?

options.label: About 2.5 million years
