options.rationale: That’s the age of the universe.

questions.explanation: Andromeda is 2.5 million light-years away but moving slowly by cosmic standards: the merger is expected in about 4.5 billion years.

levels.title: The Local Group
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the small group of galaxies the Milky Way belongs to.
levels.summary: The Milky Way is one of more than 50 galaxies in the Local Group, dominated by us and Andromeda, about 10 million light-years across.

cards.headline: Our galaxy lives in a neighborhood.
The neighborhood
cards.body: The Milky Way belongs to the Local Group, a gathering of more than 50 galaxies about 10 million light-years across. Two big spirals dominate it: the Milky Way and Andromeda. Most of the rest are small dwarf galaxies.

cards.headline: Our satellites
cards.body: The Large and Small Magellanic Clouds are small galaxies orbiting the Milky Way. From the Southern Hemisphere they’re visible to the naked eye as two faint, cloudy patches of light.

cards.fact: Andromeda is the Local Group’s other giant.
cards.context: From a dark site you can spot it with the naked eye as a faint smudge, even though it lies about 2.5 million light-years away.

cards.headline: Local Group: mapped
learned: The Milky Way belongs to the Local Group
It has more than 50 galaxies
The Milky Way and Andromeda dominate it
The Magellanic Clouds orbit our galaxy

questions.prompt: Which two galaxies dominate the Local Group?

options.label: Andromeda and M87
options.rationale: M87 is far outside the Local Group.

questions.explanation: The Milky Way and Andromeda are the two big spirals that dominate the Local Group.

questions.prompt: Where can you see the Magellanic Clouds with the naked eye?

options.label: From anywhere on Earth
options.rationale: They’re in the far southern sky.

questions.explanation: The Magellanic Clouds sit in the southern sky and are visible to the naked eye from the Southern Hemisphere.

questions.explanation: The Large and Small Magellanic Clouds are irregular galaxies, with no clear shape.

levels.title: Dark Matter
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the evidence for dark matter from how galaxies spin.
levels.summary: Galaxies spin too fast for their visible matter. Unseen dark matter, about five times ordinary matter, holds them together.

cards.headline: Most of the matter in the universe is invisible.
Galaxies spin too fast
cards.body: In the 1970s Vera Rubin measured how fast stars orbit in spiral galaxies. Stars far from the center moved as fast as those closer in, far too fast for the visible matter to hold them. Something unseen had to be adding gravity.

cards.headline: An older clue
cards.body: Back in 1933, Fritz Zwicky had noticed that galaxies in the Coma Cluster moved too fast to be held together by their visible mass. Today astronomers estimate there’s roughly five times as much dark matter as ordinary matter.

cards.fact: Dark matter doesn’t shine, absorb or reflect light.
cards.context: We detect it only through its gravity. What it actually is remains one of the biggest open questions in physics.

cards.headline: Dark matter: inferred
learned: Galaxies spin too fast for their visible matter
Vera Rubin’s work in the 1970s made the case
Dark matter is detected only by its gravity
There’s ~5× more dark matter than ordinary matter

questions.prompt: How does dark matter reveal itself?

options.label: It glows faintly in infrared light
options.rationale: It gives off no light at all.

options.label: It blocks the light of stars behind it
It appears as dark spots on telescope images

questions.explanation: Dark matter gives off, absorbs and reflects no light; we detect it only through its gravitational pull.

questions.prompt: What did Vera Rubin find about stars far from the centers of spiral galaxies?

options.label: They orbit much faster than visible matter can explain
They orbit much more slowly than expected
They don’t orbit the center at all
They are all younger than central stars

questions.explanation: Outer stars moved so fast that the galaxy’s visible matter couldn’t hold them: evidence of extra, unseen mass.

questions.prompt: From Level 26: planets far from the Sun orbit more slowly. Why was it surprising that outer stars in galaxies don’t slow down?

options.label: Stars never follow the laws of gravity
options.rationale: They do; the missing mass is the surprise.

options.label: Galaxies have no center to orbit
Outer stars are pushed by the solar wind
It means far more mass is present than we can see

questions.explanation: If most mass were in the bright center, outer stars would orbit slowly, like outer planets. Their high speed means much more unseen mass.

levels.title: Galaxy Clusters and Gravitational Lenses
levels.objective: After this level you can describe galaxy clusters and how their gravity bends light.
levels.summary: Galaxies gather in clusters of hundreds or thousands. Their gravity bends light, magnifying galaxies behind them.

cards.headline: Some of the universe’s best telescopes are made of gravity.
Cities of galaxies
cards.body: Galaxies aren’t spread evenly. Many are gathered into clusters of hundreds or thousands of galaxies, bound together by gravity, much of it from dark matter.

cards.headline: Bending light
cards.body: Einstein’s relativity predicts that mass bends light. A massive galaxy cluster bends and magnifies the light of galaxies far behind it, acting as a natural lens. Webb’s first deep-field image, released in 2022, used exactly this trick to reveal much more distant galaxies.

cards.fact: Most of a cluster’s lens is invisible.
cards.context: There’s roughly five times as much dark matter as ordinary matter, so most of the mass bending that light is matter that gives off, absorbs and reflects no light at all.

cards.headline: Clusters: explored
learned: Galaxies gather in clusters of hundreds or thousands
Mass bends light, as Einstein predicted
Clusters act as natural gravitational lenses
Webb’s first deep field used a lens (2022)

questions.prompt: What is a gravitational lens?

options.label: A special telescope mirror
options.rationale: The lens is natural, made of gravity.

options.label: A lens made of dark glass
A cloud of dust around a star
options.rationale: Dust doesn’t lens light this way.

options.label: A massive object whose gravity bends light from behind it

questions.explanation: A massive galaxy cluster bends and magnifies light from more distant galaxies behind it, like a lens.

questions.prompt: How did Webb’s first deep-field image see such distant galaxies?

options.label: A foreground galaxy cluster magnified their light
It used radio waves instead of infrared
It took pictures from two sides of the galaxy

questions.explanation: A galaxy cluster in the foreground acted as a gravitational lens, magnifying far more distant galaxies.

questions.prompt: From Level 85: what supplies much of the gravity holding galaxy clusters together?

options.label: Hot stars in the clusters
options.rationale: Stars are only a small part of the mass.

options.label: Black holes at every galaxy’s center
options.rationale: Their mass is small compared with the cluster.

questions.explanation: Much of a cluster’s mass, and so its gravity, is dark matter, which outweighs ordinary matter about five to one.

levels.title: Quasars and Active Galaxies
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how feeding supermassive black holes can outshine whole galaxies.
levels.summary: Most big galaxies hide a supermassive black hole. When it feeds, its glowing disk can outshine the galaxy: a quasar.

cards.headline: Some of the brightest objects in the universe are powered by black holes.
Monsters at the center
cards.body: Most large galaxies have a supermassive black hole at their center. When one pulls in large amounts of gas, the gas spirals in, heats up in a swirling disk and glows fiercely, before it crosses the event horizon.

cards.headline: Brighter than a galaxy
cards.body: A feeding black hole’s glowing disk can outshine all the stars of its galaxy combined. The brightest of these are called quasars. They’re among the most distant and luminous objects known.

cards.fact: The first quasar was identified in 1963.
cards.context: Maarten Schmidt realized that the object 3C 273, which looked like a faint star, was actually extremely distant and enormously luminous.

cards.headline: Quasars: understood
learned: Most big galaxies have a supermassive black hole
Feeding black holes heat gas to a fierce glow
Quasars can outshine their whole galaxy

questions.prompt: What powers a quasar?

options.label: Gas heating up as it spirals toward a supermassive black hole
Millions of supernovae exploding at once
Two galaxies colliding head-on
options.rationale: Collisions can feed a quasar, but the power comes from the black hole.

options.label: A giant star at the galaxy’s center

questions.explanation: Gas swirling into a supermassive black hole heats up and glows, sometimes outshining the whole galaxy.

questions.prompt: Why can a quasar outshine an entire galaxy?

options.label: It is closer to Earth than the galaxy
options.rationale: It’s part of the same galaxy.

options.label: It reflects light from nearby stars
Gas heated around its black hole glows more brightly than all the stars combined
It is made of many bright stars packed together
options.rationale: Its light comes from gas around a black hole.

questions.explanation: The disk of gas falling into a supermassive black hole gets so hot it can outshine all the galaxy’s stars together.

questions.prompt: From Level 75: our galaxy has Sagittarius A*. Why isn’t the Milky Way a quasar?

options.label: Sagittarius A* is too small to be a black hole
The Milky Way is too young

questions.explanation: A black hole only shines as a quasar while it’s feeding heavily. Sagittarius A* is relatively quiet today.

levels.title: Hubble’s Expanding Universe
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Hubble showed that galaxies are moving apart and the universe is expanding.
levels.summary: Hubble showed Andromeda is another galaxy, then that galaxies recede faster the farther they are: the universe is expanding.

cards.headline: In 1924, the known universe suddenly got much bigger.
One galaxy among many
cards.body: Fuzzy patches like the Andromeda “nebula” were once debated: were they clouds inside the Milky Way, or separate galaxies? In 1924 Edwin Hubble settled it. Andromeda is a separate galaxy about 2.5 million light-years away, far beyond our own.

cards.headline: Everything is moving apart
cards.body: In 1929 Hubble reported that galaxies are moving away from us, and the farther away a galaxy is, the faster it recedes. This is Hubble’s law, and it means the universe is expanding. Georges Lemaître had proposed the same idea a few years earlier.

cards.headline: No center
cards.body: The expansion has no center. Space itself is stretching, so every galaxy sees the others moving away, like raisins in rising dough that all drift apart from one another.

cards.headline: Expansion: discovered
learned: In 1924 Hubble showed Andromeda is another galaxy
Galaxies recede faster the farther they are
The universe is expanding
The expansion has no center

questions.prompt: What did Hubble report in 1929?

options.label: Galaxies are all moving toward the Milky Way
Galaxies recede faster the farther away they are
Galaxies are fixed in place and never move
Only the nearest galaxies are moving away

questions.explanation: Hubble’s law: the farther away a galaxy is, the faster it recedes, evidence that the universe is expanding.

questions.prompt: Observers in every galaxy would see the other galaxies moving away. What does this tell us?

options.label: The Milky Way is the center of the universe
options.rationale: Every galaxy would see the same thing.

options.label: Galaxies are fleeing one point in space
options.rationale: There is no single point they flee from.

options.label: Space itself is expanding, with no center
Telescopes distort the motion of galaxies

questions.explanation: Because space itself stretches, every galaxy sees the others receding. No galaxy sits at the center.

questions.prompt: From Level 10: Andromeda is about 2.5 million light-years away. Why did Hubble’s 1924 finding about it matter?

options.label: It proved galaxies exist beyond the Milky Way

questions.explanation: Showing that Andromeda lies far outside the Milky Way proved that our galaxy is one of many.

levels.title: Redshift
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what redshift is and how it reveals the expanding universe.
levels.summary: Expanding space stretches light to longer, redder wavelengths. The farther the galaxy, the bigger its redshift.

cards.headline: Distant galaxies look a little redder than they should.
Stretched light
cards.body: As light crosses expanding space, its wavelength is stretched. Red is the longest wavelength of visible light, so stretched light shifts toward the red end of the spectrum. Astronomers call this redshift.

cards.headline: Reading the shift
cards.body: Redshift shows up in spectral lines. Each element leaves lines at its own known wavelengths, and in a distant galaxy those familiar lines appear shifted toward the red. The more distant the galaxy, the bigger the shift.

cards.fact: Redshift is a cosmic yardstick.
cards.context: Because redshift grows with distance, measuring a galaxy’s redshift tells astronomers roughly how far away it is.

cards.headline: Redshift: decoded
learned: Redshift is light stretched to redder wavelengths
Expanding space stretches light
Spectral lines reveal the shift
Farther galaxies show bigger redshifts

questions.prompt: What is redshift?

options.label: Light given off by cool red giant stars
options.rationale: Redshift is stretched light, not star color.

options.label: Red dust dimming the light of distant galaxies
Light squeezed to shorter, bluer wavelengths
Light stretched to longer, redder wavelengths

questions.explanation: Redshift is the stretching of light to longer, redder wavelengths.

questions.prompt: Galaxy X’s spectral lines are shifted much farther toward the red than galaxy Y’s. What can you conclude?

options.label: X is probably farther away than Y
X is probably closer than Y
options.rationale: A bigger redshift means more distant.

options.label: X is made of different elements
options.rationale: The same lines appear, just shifted.

options.label: X contains more red stars
options.rationale: The shift isn’t about star color.

questions.explanation: The more distant a galaxy, the greater its redshift, so X is most likely the farther galaxy.

questions.prompt: From Level 32: why are spectral lines so useful for measuring redshift?

options.label: Spectral lines appear only in red light
Each element’s lines have known wavelengths
They make faraway galaxies look brighter
They reveal each galaxy’s exact age

questions.explanation: Because every element’s lines sit at known wavelengths, a shift toward the red is easy to measure.

levels.title: Checkpoint: A Universe of Galaxies
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the universe’s structure from our galaxy up to the cosmic web.
levels.summary: From the Milky Way to the Local Group, clusters and the cosmic web: a universe of galaxies, all moving apart.

cards.headline: Chapter 9 finale. Zoom out as far as galaxies go.
cards.body: From our home galaxy to the largest structures in the universe.

cards.headline: A ladder of scale
cards.body: The Sun circles the Milky Way once every 230 million years or so. The Milky Way is one of more than 50 galaxies in the Local Group. Beyond that, galaxies gather in clusters of hundreds or thousands, held together largely by dark matter.

cards.headline: The cosmic web
cards.body: On the largest scales, galaxies and clusters form a vast web of long filaments and sheets wrapped around huge, nearly empty voids. And the whole web is stretching as the universe expands, which is why distant galaxies look redshifted.

cards.headline: Chapter 9 complete
learned: Galaxies are spiral, elliptical or irregular
Local Group → clusters → the cosmic web
Dark matter holds galaxies and clusters together
Redshift reveals an expanding universe

questions.prompt: On the largest scales, how are galaxies arranged?

options.label: In one giant sphere around the Milky Way

levels.title: The Big Bang
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what the Big Bang theory says and what it doesn’t.
levels.summary: The universe began about 13.8 billion years ago, hot and dense, and has expanded and cooled ever since. It wasn’t an explosion in space.

cards.headline: Everything you’ve learned about began hot, dense and tiny.
Rewind the expansion
cards.body: If galaxies are moving apart today, they were closer together in the past. Run the clock back far enough and everything was packed into an extremely hot, dense state. The Big Bang theory says the universe began that way about 13.8 billion years ago and has been expanding and cooling ever since.
cards.callout: Hot and dense → expanding and cooling

cards.headline: Not an explosion
cards.body: Despite the name, the Big Bang was not an explosion into empty space. It was the expansion of space itself, happening everywhere at once. The name came in 1949 from astronomer Fred Hoyle, who favored a rival theory.

cards.headline: The first ingredients
cards.body: In its first few minutes, the young universe made the lightest elements: hydrogen, helium and a trace of lithium. What came before the Big Bang, if anything, is a question the theory doesn’t answer.

cards.headline: The Big Bang: understood
learned: The universe began ~13.8 billion years ago, hot and dense
It has been expanding and cooling ever since
The Big Bang was space expanding, not an explosion
The first minutes made hydrogen and helium

questions.prompt: According to the Big Bang theory, how did the universe begin?

options.label: As a cold, empty void that slowly heated up
In an extremely hot, dense state, then expanded
As a single giant star that later exploded
options.rationale: There were no stars at the start.

options.label: As a swarm of galaxies moving inward

questions.explanation: The universe began about 13.8 billion years ago, extremely hot and dense, and has been expanding and cooling ever since.

questions.prompt: Why is it misleading to picture the Big Bang as a bomb going off in space?

options.label: Space itself expanded, everywhere at once
There was no matter until much later
options.rationale: Hydrogen and helium formed within minutes.

options.label: It happened at the center of the Milky Way
Bombs are much hotter than the Big Bang was
options.rationale: The early universe was extremely hot.

questions.explanation: A bomb explodes into space that already exists. The Big Bang was the expansion of space itself, with no center.

questions.prompt: From Level 32: stars are made mostly of hydrogen and helium. Where did those elements first come from?

options.label: The first minutes after the Big Bang

questions.explanation: Hydrogen and helium, with a trace of lithium, formed in the first few minutes after the Big Bang.

levels.title: The Afterglow: Cosmic Microwave Background
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the cosmic microwave background and why it supports the Big Bang.
levels.summary: The Big Bang’s leftover light, released 380,000 years in and stretched into microwaves, still fills the sky. Its discovery backed the theory.

cards.headline: The whole sky glows, faintly, with the Big Bang’s leftover light.
When light broke free
cards.body: For its first 380,000 years or so, the universe was too hot and dense for light to travel far. When it cooled enough for atoms to form, light could finally travel freely. That ancient light still fills the sky as the cosmic microwave background, or CMB.
cards.callout: Released ~380,000 years after the Big Bang

cards.headline: Stretched to microwaves
cards.body: The CMB started as the glow of hot gas. As space expanded over billions of years, that light was stretched to much longer wavelengths, all the way to microwaves. Today it’s only about 2.7 degrees above absolute zero.

cards.fact: It was found by accident in 1965.
cards.context: Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson picked up a steady hiss in their radio antenna and first suspected a fault. It was the CMB, which the Big Bang theory had predicted, so the discovery became key evidence for the theory.

cards.headline: The afterglow: detected
learned: The CMB is the Big Bang’s leftover light
It was released ~380,000 years after the Big Bang
Expansion stretched it into microwaves
Its 1965 discovery backed the Big Bang

questions.prompt: What is the cosmic microwave background?

options.label: Microwaves leaking from Earth’s radio towers
options.rationale: It comes from every direction in the sky.

options.label: The light of the most distant quasars
Leftover light from the early universe
Heat radiating from the Milky Way’s center
options.rationale: It fills the whole sky evenly.

questions.explanation: The CMB is leftover light from the early universe, released when atoms first formed.

questions.prompt: Why does the CMB reach us as microwaves rather than visible light?

options.label: It was always a faint microwave signal
options.rationale: It began as the glow of hot gas.

options.label: Earth’s atmosphere converts it to microwaves
Dust in the Milky Way absorbs its visible light

questions.explanation: As space expanded over billions of years, the CMB’s light was stretched to much longer wavelengths.

questions.prompt: From Level 91: why did finding the CMB give such strong support to the Big Bang theory?

options.label: It proved the Milky Way is at the center
The theory had predicted such a glow
It showed radio waves can’t cross space
It revealed what dark matter is made of

questions.explanation: A hot, dense early universe should leave a leftover glow. Finding it was a strong test the theory passed.

levels.title: The First Stars and Galaxies
levels.objective: After this level you can describe how the first stars and galaxies lit up the early universe.
levels.summary: After the dark ages, massive stars of pure hydrogen and helium lit up and seeded space with heavier elements. Webb hunts their galaxies.

cards.headline: After its first light, the universe went dark for a long time.
The cosmic dark ages
cards.body: After the CMB was released there were no stars yet, just cooling gas, mostly hydrogen and helium, in the dark. Within a few hundred million years after the Big Bang, gravity pulled clumps of that gas together and the first stars lit up.

cards.headline: Giants of two elements
cards.body: The first stars formed from only hydrogen and helium. They’re thought to have been very massive and short-lived. When they died, they scattered the first heavier elements into space, seeding the gas that later stars and planets formed from.

cards.headline: Finding the first galaxies
cards.body: Light from these early galaxies has been stretched into infrared by the expanding universe. That’s why Webb, an infrared telescope, is built to find them. It has already seen galaxies as they were only a few hundred million years after the Big Bang.

cards.headline: First light: found
learned: The cosmic dark ages came before the first stars
The first stars were only hydrogen and helium
They were massive and seeded heavier elements
Webb sees galaxies from the early universe

questions.prompt: What were the first stars made of?

options.label: The same mix as the Sun today
options.rationale: The Sun contains elements made by earlier stars.

questions.explanation: The first stars formed from the Big Bang’s gas: only hydrogen and helium.

questions.prompt: Why were the first stars important for later planets like Earth?

options.label: They gave off the cosmic microwave background
options.rationale: The CMB was released long before them.

options.label: They became the planets of our solar system
options.rationale: Planets form from gas and dust around stars.

options.label: They made heavier elements and scattered them
They created all the hydrogen in the universe
options.rationale: Hydrogen formed in the Big Bang.

questions.explanation: Rocky planets need heavier elements. The first stars forged some and scattered them into space when they died.

questions.prompt: From Level 36: why does Webb look for the first galaxies in infrared?

options.label: Early galaxies were made of infrared stars
options.rationale: The stars shone normally; their light was stretched later.

options.label: Infrared light travels faster than visible light
options.rationale: All light travels at the same speed.

options.label: Visible light can’t travel that far
options.rationale: Distance alone doesn’t block visible light.

options.label: Their light has been stretched into infrared

questions.explanation: The expanding universe stretched light from early galaxies into infrared wavelengths, which Webb is built to detect.

levels.title: Dark Energy
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the discovery that the universe’s expansion is speeding up.
levels.summary: In 1998, distant supernovae showed that the expansion is speeding up. Its unknown cause, dark energy, is about 68% of the universe.

cards.headline: The universe’s expansion is speeding up, and no one knows why.
Expecting a slowdown
cards.body: Gravity pulls everything together, so astronomers expected the expansion of the universe to be slowing down. In 1998 two teams measured distant supernovae to check. The supernovae were fainter than a slowing universe allowed. The expansion is speeding up.

cards.headline: Dark energy
cards.body: Whatever is driving the acceleration is called dark energy, and nobody knows what it is. Yet it makes up roughly 68% of the universe’s energy content. Dark matter is about 27%, and everything made of ordinary atoms, every star, planet and person, is only about 5%.

cards.fact: The discovery won the 2011 Nobel Prize in Physics.
cards.context: Saul Perlmutter, Brian Schmidt and Adam Riess shared it for revealing the accelerating universe.

cards.headline: Dark energy: discovered
learned: The expansion of the universe is speeding up
Distant supernovae revealed it in 1998
The unknown cause is called dark energy
Ordinary matter is only ~5% of the universe

questions.prompt: What did astronomers discover in 1998?

options.label: The expansion of the universe is slowing
The Milky Way is slowly shrinking
The expansion of the universe is speeding up

questions.explanation: Distant supernovae were fainter than expected: the expansion is accelerating.

questions.prompt: Roughly how much of the universe is ordinary matter, the stuff of stars, planets and people?
questions.explanation: Ordinary matter is only about 5%. Dark matter is about 27% and dark energy about 68%.

questions.prompt: From Level 85: how are dark matter and dark energy different?

options.label: They are two names for the same thing
Dark matter glows faintly; dark energy doesn’t
Dark matter adds gravity; dark energy speeds up expansion
Dark energy is made of black holes

questions.explanation: Dark matter’s gravity holds galaxies together; dark energy drives the expansion to accelerate.

levels.title: How Big Is the Observable Universe?
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why the observable universe is larger than 13.8 billion light-years across.
levels.summary: Looking far away means looking back in time. Space kept expanding while light traveled, so the observable universe is ~93 billion light-years wide.

cards.headline: How can we see farther than light has had time to travel?
cards.body: The universe is about 13.8 billion years old, yet the observable universe is far wider than 13.8 billion light-years.

cards.headline: Looking back in time
cards.body: Light takes time to travel, so looking far away means looking into the past. We see the Andromeda galaxy as it was about 2.5 million years ago. The most distant light we can see set out about 13.8 billion years ago.

cards.headline: Space kept stretching
cards.body: While that ancient light was traveling toward us, space kept expanding. The regions that sent it are now much farther away than 13.8 billion light-years. That’s why the observable universe is about 93 billion light-years across.

cards.headline: A horizon, not an edge
cards.body: The observable universe is only the part we can see, limited by how far light has traveled since the Big Bang. It isn’t the edge of the universe. How big the whole universe is, and whether it goes on forever, nobody knows.

cards.headline: The observable universe: measured
learned: Looking far away means looking back in time
Space kept expanding while light traveled
The observable universe is ~93 billion light-years across
It’s a horizon, not the edge of everything

questions.prompt: About how wide is the observable universe?

options.label: About 13.8 billion light-years
options.rationale: That’s the light-travel time, not today’s width.

questions.explanation: Because space kept expanding while light traveled, the observable universe is about 93 billion light-years across.

questions.prompt: What is the edge of the observable universe?

options.label: The outer wall of the whole universe
options.rationale: It’s only the limit of what we can see.

options.label: The place where the Big Bang happened
The limit of how far light has reached us
The farthest reach of Webb’s mirror
options.rationale: It isn’t set by any telescope.

questions.explanation: It’s a horizon, set by how far light has traveled since the Big Bang, not an edge of the universe itself.

questions.prompt: From Level 8: a light-year is a distance. So what do you see when you look at a galaxy 2.5 million light-years away?

options.label: The galaxy exactly as it is today
options.rationale: Its light took time to arrive.

options.label: The galaxy as it will look in the future
options.rationale: Light shows the past, not the future.

options.label: Only light reflected by our own galaxy
options.rationale: The light comes from that galaxy.

options.label: The galaxy as it was long ago

questions.explanation: Its light left 2.5 million years ago, so you see the galaxy as it was then.

levels.title: Integration: From Atoms to Galaxies
levels.objective: After this level you can connect nuclear fusion, stellar lives and galaxy formation into one story.
levels.summary: Big Bang gas became stars; stars forged heavier elements and scattered them; that enriched gas became new stars, planets and you.

cards.headline: The atoms in your body have been on a 13.8-billion-year journey.
From the Big Bang to you

events.label: Hydrogen, helium and a trace of lithium form
The first stars light up
Generations of stars forge heavier elements
The Sun and planets form from enriched gas

cards.headline: The great cycle
cards.body: Stars fuse light elements into heavier ones, just as the Sun turns hydrogen into helium. Massive stars end in supernovae that blast those elements into space. New stars and planets form from that enriched gas, and the cycle repeats.

cards.fact: You are made of star stuff.
cards.context: The calcium in your bones and the iron in your blood were made inside stars that lived and died before the Sun formed.

cards.headline: The cosmic cycle: connected
learned: The Big Bang made hydrogen and helium
Stars forge heavier elements
Dying stars scatter them into space
New stars, planets and people form from them

questions.prompt: Which elements did the Big Bang itself produce?

options.label: Hydrogen, helium and a trace of lithium
Carbon, oxygen and iron
options.rationale: Those were forged later, in stars.

options.label: Every element in the periodic table
Only iron and gold
options.rationale: Those need stars and stellar explosions.

questions.explanation: The Big Bang made only the lightest elements; stars made nearly all the rest.

questions.prompt: Which sequence is in the right order?

options.label: First stars → hydrogen forms → the Sun forms
The Sun forms → first stars → hydrogen forms

options.rationale: The Sun formed billions of years after the first stars.

questions.explanation: The Big Bang made hydrogen; the first stars lit up within a few hundred million years; the Sun formed 4.6 billion years ago.

options.label: It formed in the Big Bang

questions.explanation: Massive stars forged heavy elements and scattered them in supernovae; the solar system formed from that enriched gas.

levels.title: Integration: How We Know What We Know
levels.objective: After this level you can connect each major astronomical discovery to the tool or method behind it.
levels.summary: We can’t visit the stars, so astronomers read their light: spectra, parallax, transits, spin and gravitational waves.

cards.headline: We can’t visit the stars. So how do we know so much about them?
New windows
cards.body: Some discoveries needed entirely new signals. Stars at galaxies’ edges orbiting too fast revealed dark matter. Redshift in galaxies’ spectra revealed the expanding universe. And LIGO first detected gravitational waves in 2015, from merging black holes.

cards.headline: Old tricks still work
cards.body: Some methods needed no telescope at all. Around 240 BCE, Eratosthenes estimated Earth’s size from the Sun’s noon angle in two cities. Careful measurement and reasoning, checked by others, is how astronomy has always worked.

cards.headline: Methods: mastered
learned: Spectral lines reveal what stars are made of
Parallax measures distances to nearby stars
Transits and wobbles find planets
Galaxy spin revealed dark matter

questions.prompt: Which pairing of method and discovery is correct?

options.label: Spectral lines → what stars are made of
Parallax → what stars are made of
Redshift → what planets are made of

questions.explanation: Each element leaves its own lines in a spectrum, so spectra reveal what stars are made of.

questions.prompt: An astronomer wants the distance to a nearby star. Which method fits best?

options.label: Listening for gravitational waves
options.rationale: Those come from colliding black holes and neutron stars.

questions.explanation: Parallax, the star’s tiny shift as Earth orbits the Sun, gives the distance to nearby stars.

questions.prompt: From Level 85: no one has ever seen dark matter. What evidence convinced astronomers it exists?

options.label: Photos of dark clouds between galaxies
options.rationale: Dark matter is invisible, not dark-colored.

options.label: Radio signals from dark matter itself
Stars orbiting faster than visible mass allows

questions.explanation: Galaxies spin too fast for their visible matter, so extra unseen mass must be adding gravity.

levels.title: Integration: Futures of the Sun, Earth and Universe
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the long-term futures of the Sun, Earth, Milky Way and universe.
levels.summary: Polaris won’t stay the pole star. The Sun will brighten, then swell. Andromeda will merge with us, and distant galaxies will slip from view.

cards.headline: Astronomy can forecast billions of years ahead.
cards.body: Here’s the long forecast for the sky, the Sun, Earth and our galaxy.

events.label: Earth’s axis wobbles through a full circle; Polaris won’t stay the pole star
A brightening Sun makes Earth too hot for oceans
The Milky Way and Andromeda merge
The Sun swells into a red giant, later becoming a white dwarf

cards.headline: The universe’s fate
cards.body: Dark energy is speeding up the expansion. If it keeps doing so, galaxies beyond our local neighborhood will eventually drift out of view. The Sun’s own story ends quietly, as a white dwarf that no longer fuses anything and slowly cools.

cards.headline: The future: forecast
learned: Polaris won’t always be the pole star
The Sun will brighten, then become a red giant
The Milky Way and Andromeda will merge

levels.title: Integration: The Big Open Questions
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the major unanswered questions in astronomy and why they matter.
levels.summary: About 95% of the universe is dark and unexplained. The Hubble tension, what came before the Big Bang and life elsewhere are all open.

cards.headline: The best part of astronomy: it isn’t finished.
cards.body: Here are some of the biggest questions still waiting for answers.

cards.headline: The dark 95%
cards.body: Dark matter and dark energy together make up about 95% of the universe, and nobody yet knows what either one is. Ordinary matter, everything we can see, is only about 5%.

cards.headline: Unsolved puzzles
cards.body: Different ways of measuring how fast the universe expands today disagree slightly, a puzzle called the Hubble tension. Why the Sun’s corona is so much hotter than its surface isn’t fully understood. And no one knows what, if anything, came before the Big Bang.

cards.fact: Is anyone out there?
cards.context: No life has yet been confirmed anywhere beyond Earth. Webb can now study the atmospheres of some other worlds for the gases life might leave behind.

cards.headline: Open questions: mapped
learned: About 95% of the universe is still unexplained
The Hubble tension is unresolved
What came before the Big Bang is unknown
No life has been confirmed beyond Earth yet

options.label: The pull between the Milky Way and Andromeda

questions.explanation: Different methods give slightly different values for how fast the universe expands today.

questions.explanation: Dark energy and dark matter together make up about 95% of the universe.
